Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from age, light exposure, and fading, often present significant challenges for Optical Character Recognition (OCR) systems. In response, we propose an end-to-end approach utilizing a multi-adversarial network to improve the quality of degraded handwritten documents. The system involves two adversarial networks - one converting colorized images to black-and-white format, and the other assessing the originality of the generated output - along with a segmentation network to isolate the handwritten text from the document's background. Notably, our method bypasses the need for detailed handwritten text images by instead using binary images of the text as a starting point, and achieving remarkable hand-written text enhancement through subsequent iterations. The effectiveness of our method is validated by extensive experiments and a comprehensive comparison with other widely-used image enhancement techniques on publicly available datasets.

The increasing reliance on digital documentation has led to a pressing need for
efficient methods to convert physical documents into digital formats. This research
addresses the issue of extracting personal information from Indonesian ID card
documents by combining optical character recognition with post-processing
using natural language processing. The proposed method successfully extracted
data from 100 Id Cards, with a notable 96.5% accuracy in recognizing Indonesian
characters and 85% accuracy in character-level accuracy. The results indicate
that the approach is effective in handling local language characteristics and
document types.

In vehicular networks channel estimation is a challenging task because of the high mobility of vehicles.  IEEE 802.11p channel estimation channels are severely affected by time-extension and limited pilot data. To alleviate this problem, we developed a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network-based estimator, which was further optimized by incorporating a temporal averaging mechanism. The optimized estimator was able to improve convergence speed, increase accuracy, and reduce power consumption compared to its non-optimized version. The validity of our solution was verified through MATLAB simulations, which showed that it was compatible with IEEE 802.11p standard.

Astronomical images contain valuable data, but are often constrained by small
telescope apertures or low frame rates. This study presents a method leveraging
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to enhance the resolution and color
fidelity of astronomical images by leveraging label-associated data. Under
conditions where high-resolution images are scarce, a least-squares-based
data augmentation technique is employed to prevent overfitting. Numerical results
demonstrate that this method successfully improves the visual quality of images
without compromising their content.

We present a novel neural network framework that surpasses traditional gradient-free optimization methods, such as batch gradient descent, back-propagation, and Adam, which are prone to getting stuck in local minima. By building on the Universal Approximation Theorem, our framework involves two key components: identifying and understanding data patterns and constructing suitable network architectures. The first component employs the concept of data manifolds, which reveal the inherent relationships between features and targets, and provide valuable insights for understanding the nature of the data. The component of architecture design utilizes the theoretical basis provided by the UAT to recommend network structures. The theoretical foundations of our framework are the topological UAT and the Carathéodory Theorem. The framework's efficacy is demonstrated through the FRED dataset, a complex collection of time-series data, where we achieved a 3.5-fold improvement in the autoregressive integrated moving average (ARIMA) forecasting method, and successfully applied the framework to a real-world stock analysis case.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel operated under the ECFA's auspices from 2013 to 2020. Following the conclusion of its term, the panel received an extension of its activities by ECFA management until the end of 2022. Since then, it has been actively contributing through various webinars and reports. This paper outlines how the panel functioned during its period of operation and highlights the panel's recent contributions.

A proposed optical structure called a dual beam splitter is developed to convert line waves into directed beams using a specialized dual metasurface. The antisymmetric component of the line wave is utilized to create beams through a magnetic layer, while the symmetric component interacts with a dielectric layer to maintain directional stability. Our design effectively uses the parts of the line wave that are typically lost as reflected or transmitted energy. By using a straightforward design with minimal complexity, our concept can be implemented in various optical applications, and its performance can be evaluated through available numerical and experimental assessments.

One of the most pressing issues in developing commercially applicable robots for industrial settings is the considerable time and resources required to retrain existing robots for new tasks due to advancements in technology or shifts in regulations. Similar challenges arise when designing autonomous AI systems for semi-autonomous collaborative applications with humans, particularly in scenarios like collaborative learning or skill acquisition. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel multi-agent learning framework that enables agents to create their own internal knowledge structures by observing and interpreting each other's actions. By doing so, this framework allows the AI agents to quickly adapt to various robots and industries by observing a relatively small number of demonstrations. Our approach is tested and validated through a simulated welding scenario, featuring multiple autonomous AI welding robots working with one human welding robot.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  A novel bias-corrected estimate of the adjustment factor has been proposed and, in the context of median regression, a bias-corrected density estimate has been proposed based on this correction.  This correction factor was tested through various Bayesian and non-Bayesian methods of median estimation, including the maximum likelihood estimator and a multi-stage method.  It was discovered that taking this correction into account significantly improves the accuracy and consistency of these estimators.  Similar techniques can be applied to other M-estimators as well.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing them to benefit from a mutual
relationship. This synergy manifests in two key aspects: accurately establishing
a subject-predicate relationship aids in identifying the corresponding object,
and predicting an object given a subject-predicate relationship can in turn help
verify the subject Predicate-Entity triple. Building on this idea, we have designed
a bi-directional model that simultaneously performs both tasks, which has been
found to significantly improve overall relation extraction outcomes when compared
to a baseline model, particularly in scenarios involving sparse data.

The analysis focuses on how finite-strangeness and/or baryon asymmetry impacts the dissociation properties of U-charge neutral U-charge strange hadrons in a N-dimensional plasma under anisotropic momentum conditions. Using the framework where quasi-particle Debye mass represents the interaction between color charges, and applying minimum uncertainty principles for both longitudinal and transverse motions, researchers investigated the ground state energy and dissociation energy of heavy quarkonia systems. The study reveals that anisotropic momentum conditions and finite baryon or strangeness chemical potentials significantly influence the dissociation energy, with its magnitude depending on whether the longitudinal or transverse Debye mass dominates, which in turn determines if the quarkonia system remains intact or dissociates.

Our study focused on the magnetic arrangement of Tb3RuO7, a material exhibiting Ru-based chains with alternating bond lengths, using neutron diffraction, ab initio calculations, and theoretical modeling. We found that Tb ions create an uneven internal magnetic field that disrupts the magnetic patterns of Ru ions. At a temperature of 18 K, Tb3RuO7 enters a partially disordered state due to the effect of this internal field, similar to the behavior observed in the related compound Dy3RuO7. Our analysis revealed that the magnetic patterns of Tb and Ru ions change significantly within a broad temperature range, indicating the presence of magnetic excitations even in the presence of a magnetic field, even after accounting for the effects of the internal field.

Although deep learning models have achieved remarkable success in image-related tasks, their ability to handle non-image data, especially with periodic patterns, is still limited. While some approaches like the Fourier transform and Fourier neural operators can effectively process periodic signals, they fail to capture the unique features of different periods. To overcome this, we developed a novel neural network that periodically activates in a modulated manner, allowing the model to separately represent the unique features of each period while also capturing the overall pattern. Our model outperforms existing models on tasks involving heat transfer and fluid dynamics by combining the local features with a task-dependent operator, and we further demonstrate its generalizability beyond these applications.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data to adjust a classifier trained on a disparate distribution. In this work, a novel semi-generative approach is proposed that incorporates both causal and effect characteristics from unlabelled data. It is demonstrated that this method achieves consistent classification in situations where pure adaptation methods remain inconsistent in both asymptotic and finite sample contexts. Furthermore, an array of heuristic strategies for determining the degree of intervention on unlabelled data has been developed. Experimental evaluations are conducted using both artificial and real-world datasets to validate the effectiveness of this method.

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the inner workings of deep learning systems remain shrouded in theoretical uncertainty. In our study, we establish a geometric framework for understanding deep learning by examining its key components in relation to high-dimensional data representation and manifold learning theory. Through this geometric lens, we elucidate how neural networks can effectively encode complex data structures, providing insights into their learning and generalization capabilities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that neural networks' representational power enables them to surpass traditional kernel-based methods in certain tasks. By putting deep learning within a broader theoretical context, our work contributes to addressing long-standing questions about its fundamental mechanisms.

We consider the field extension $K(\sqrt[3]{d}, \sqrt{\Delta})/K$ where $d$ is a cube-free integer, $1 < \Delta$ is the square-free part of the discriminant of the order $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt[3]{d}]$, and $K$ is an imaginary cubic field with class number $h_K$. It is demonstrated that for a positive constant $C$ dependent only on certain parameters, the maximum value of $|\Delta|$ for which the extension is not a field is bounded above by an exponential function of $h_K$, specifically $exp(C \cdot log^5(21 \cdot h_K + 1))$, based on a recent result by Baker and Polignac for Pell's equation. This finding supports the main conjecture associated with principal type lattices.

A research project investigates how much relevance conventional variables used by less advanced classifiers contribute to high-performance, state-of-the-art deep learning classifiers used in jet tagging. This is done by applying layerwise relevance propagation to the CRNN jet neural classifier, which is a widely-used jet substructure tagger. By using propagation, the relevance of conventional variables at the input layer is identified and compared to the relevance of variables at subsequent layers. Our experiments reveal a strong correlation between the relevance of conventional variables at the input and the relevance of hidden layers in the CRNN neural classifier. This suggests that these variables may be useful not only for less advanced classifiers, but for more advanced classifiers as well.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, reducing to well-known cases when r equals one. This paper seeks to establish formulas linking these variations together.

Eight sets of layer groups were examined to derive the specific representation characteristics. The characteristics of first order irreducible representations were mapped out within each set. Additionally, a systematic approach to determining site symmetry induced representations was established. These findings provide a comprehensive reference table for applied crystallographers.

Momentum operators are used to create Killing vector fields with geodesic paths. The study focuses on identifying all possible cases in spaces with symmetric distributions of curvature. Specific exceptions occur in higher-dimensional spaces without symmetry. These cases correspond to known physical models, such as two-dimensional quantum systems and hypothetical four-dimensional space-time frameworks, also including a three-dimensional real form representation.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian in the problem. Our proposed solution involves utilizing a complex-valued neural network to approximate the log-likelihood plus a term representing the log-Jacobian, thereby enabling applications even in scenarios where the sign problem arises sporadically.

In a composite Higgs model, we propose the flavor symmetry to originate from the fundamental interaction, thus stabilizing the potential problem of flavor changing effects in chiral models.  The chiral symmetry allows us to analyze the mass spectrum within a systematic and organized framework based on the breaking pattern of the symmetry.  Furthermore, we propose a model where the flavor symmetry breaks down into a subgroup, resulting in a light pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson representing a scalar doublet analogous to the observed Higgs boson.  This doublet interacts with both fermions and gauge bosons in patterns consistent with Standard Model couplings, modified by factors of order V/ f.  We explore a concrete example of chiral symmetry where SU(4) represents the strong interaction and breaks down into SP(4).  Here, we identify the Higgs boson as a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson and investigate the characteristics of extra scalar particles.  Ultimately, we match our theoretical predictions with current LHC findings.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond traditional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception, subtly guiding users' movements to enhance interactivity. This research examines the dangers of VPPM exploitation, beginning with a conceptual framework that confirms their existence and then applying speculative design to identify and mitigate threats. Through practical examples, we demonstrate how current security methods are insufficient and propose enhancements to protect users when using VPPM technologies.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 10 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Recent observations by ALMA have revealed numerous binary star systems within their protostellar formation stages, indicating their significant presence at this point in time. Research has shown that these systems have a wide range of final formation masses. To understand the mass distribution of binary systems through fragmentation theory, we conducted numerical simulations of collapsing clouds with a core forming early on and mass added later. These clouds received external mass in two steps, first increasing the mass by 20% of the core's initial mass after the first collapse, and another 20% after further collapse. By comparing the masses of systems created with and without added mass, we found that while early systems have little added mass, later systems have more. Our results show that final system mass is closely related to the ratio of added mass to initial mass in early systems, and this relationship holds true across a wide mass range. However, in later systems, there is little added mass relative to system mass, breaking this correlation. To account for this discrepancy, we suggest considering the mass distribution of systems at the first collapse point in time. Our findings also indicate that angular momentum effects have a minimal impact on final system mass in this scenario.

This research introduces an enhanced algorithm for separating mixed signals based on their non-Gaussian characteristics. Initially, the original data is reorganized into matrices, followed by the application of the Fast Fixed-Point algorithm to obtain an initial linear mixing matrix. Subsequently, the algorithm leverages the row-normalized matrix's approximate independence in its columns to refine the linear mixing matrix and achieve a highly accurate separation. Consequently, the algorithm requires less data compared to traditional methods and boasts faster computational efficiency. Its performance is substantiated through numerous numerical experiments.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It's known that the bounded quantifier prefix calculus can't be more powerful than the extended polynomial calculus (PC) and that CPT is equivalent to P. We show a more direct connection, with the bounded quantifier prefix calculi simulating PC of equivalent size, which allows us to compare proof complexity with circuit complexity. We also establish a detailed connection between L_{\infty,\omega}^{=}(Q_{b}) and the extended Polynomial Calculus by simulating PC with a size-efficient method, enabling the translation of PC proofs with variable length to shorter RQBP-calculuss proofs. We further demonstrate the extended PC's ability to distinguish specific graph properties, which the PC itself can't do, which is equivalent to the P vs NP problem, highlighting the PC's non-invariance under graph isomorphism.

A subring collection in a ring $R$ is $\sigma$-elementary if subring inclusion implies inclusion in $F_R(\cdot)$, a mapping that takes a subring to the set of its elements in $R$. It's known that upper integral closure collections form a comprehensive list $1 \leq \sigma < \infty$ of possible sizes for a ring's collection of chains with the given property. This paper establishes a new ring type with possible sizes for its collection of chains with the given property, ranging from $\sigma = 1$ to $\infty$.

Social media platforms harbor numerous assertions that evade direct disproof, such as "my rival possesses superior skills." Despite being inherently subjective, these statements significantly influence users' online interactions, prompting an investigation into their structural characteristics. In this paper, we define relations among entities based on the disparity in claim frequencies directed at each entity within a given user subset. By analyzing these implicit relations, we identify consistent structural patterns in various types of unfalsifiable claims, using football and women's fashion domains as case studies. Furthermore, we develop an algorithm to generate single-source hierarchical clusters from the defined relations and their associated confidence levels, enabling a comprehensive visualization of underlying structures in these datasets.

Identifying events in real-time by analyzing social media activities across multiple locations, locations over time, and multiple locations over time is known as spatio-temporal event detection. Traditional approaches struggle with real-time applications due to their inability to process large amounts of unstructured social media data. A new framework has been developed to detect spatio-temporal events by predicting activity levels at specific locations and classifying events based on predicted scores, which has been shown to outperform traditional methods. Framework components include a sliding time window, a fixed geographic area, and a predefined threshold. The proposed system has been successfully tested on the Greater New York City area using Twitter data from the San Francisco Seismic Event and the Super Bowl events.

Gravitational lensing of the cosmic microwave background by large-scale structure is utilized to investigate the universe's early development, particularly by analyzing data through Fourier space statistics such as the bispectrum. A new technique has been developed to calculate the bispectrum involving the CMB temperature, lensing convergence, and galaxy distribution, allowing researchers to extract valuable information about the early universe. The method has been implemented using real data from the Planck satellite and a large-scale structure dataset from the Dark Energy Survey. Although initially slow due to the need to analyze data across multiple celestial coordinates, the method has been accelerated by transforming data into a rotated coordinate system that simplifies the calculation. This optimization has resulted in a significant speedup, making the technique feasible for analyzing full-sky data.

By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training of deep neural networks, we developed a rigorous framework for training certifiable Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs). This approach combines constraint relaxation and modified cross-entropy loss to achieve robustness to potential attacks. The method, demonstrated through empirical tests on standard datasets, allows for training BNNs that are both accurate and certifiably secure on challenging datasets such as MNIST and CIFAR-10, further providing benefits in uncertainty calibration. This innovation facilitates the deployment of BNNs in applications requiring utmost reliability.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020, and China was the first country to identify and control its outbreak.  The pandemic had a profound impact on people's lives, and online rumors about it spread rapidly, causing significant harm.  Understanding the mechanisms behind the spread of these rumors and their effect on individuals is crucial.  This paper investigates the characteristics of rumors related to COVID-19 in China by collecting data from Sina Weibo, and then builds a machine learning model to measure the influence of users who post the rumors.  By applying this model, the paper identifies the key factors that contribute to the spread of rumors, and provides policy recommendations to mitigate their negative effects.

This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. It utilizes several techniques such as discrete wavelet transform, complex wavelet transform, and principal component analysis to reduce the dimensions of the datasets. The reduced data is then classified using a diverse range of machine learning algorithms, including support vector machine, random forest, and maximum likelihood. By comparing the results of these methods, the study evaluates the effectiveness and limitations of each dimensionality reduction technique. It reveals that the choice of method significantly influences the classification accuracy and structural preservation of the hyperspectral images. Furthermore, the study reveals that the structure of the data can be both enhanced or obscured depending on the method employed, emphasizing the need for further advanced methods in hyperspectral image analysis.

Neural networks excel at solving complex tasks but struggle with execution due to
their ability to draw inferences from massive amounts of data, which often leads
to oversized models. The problem is particularly acute in natural language
understanding, where a model must grasp the intricacies of language after being
exposed to vast quantities of text. Such a model, though tiny, is impossible to
manually inspect, making it nearly impossible to identify and fix issues
during development. Researchers have made significant strides in reducing the
size of neural networks, but the application of these techniques to language
models remains limited. Researchers have turned to a new class of techniques
known as compression methods, which not only compress a model's parameters but
also provide insight into its internal workings. This report delves into the
advanced techniques of model compression, highlighting their use in natural
language understanding and the potential benefits of these methods
beyond just size reduction.

A novel predictor for protein tertiary structure has been introduced, utilizing high-level quantum mechanics calculations to model protein atoms and simulate the effects of solvation. This calculation yields the chemical shifts of the protein backbone amide protons, which can then be compared to experimental values. The difference between the calculated and measured chemical shifts serves as an indicator of the accuracy of the protein structure. In addition, a novel refinement technique for protein structure is developed by applying a weighted mean-squared difference between the calculated and measured chemical shifts to the protein's energy function during molecular dynamics simulations. This method was tested using simulated data from small proteins, including the protein G B1 bundle, cytochrome c peroxidase, and cytochrome c, as well as the structure determined through NMR for a 20-amino acid peptide. Our results demonstrate that this approach is capable of accurately predicting protein structure and improving the quality of structures obtained through heteronuclear NMR.

The choice of loss function for a neural network's training significantly influences its final performance. Despite being a crucial decision, it is often made through experimentation rather than a deliberate process. In this research, the effect of commonly used loss functions for multiclass classification was investigated, particularly in terms of accuracy and the distribution of its results over time. Our findings for the specific dataset used show that both categorical cross-entropy losses, but in different ways of calculating the error, have a meaningful connection with accuracy, whereas other types of losses do not have a clear correlation. It's also notable that the two methods produce different accuracy patterns over time, which has significant implications for understanding the network's learning process. Our research reveals that despite being commonly used in the field, not all loss functions for multiclass classification are equally effective, and the type of target data can affect their performance in various ways.

We reframe the parquet theory whole-system Hamiltonian perspective to develop a new viewpoint on the theory's physics of parabolic composition. By applying a novel partitioning approach to the four-particle Hamiltonian, we derive a set of coupled equations for the partitioning of the Hamiltonian's fully interacting four-particle cluster operator. These equations also yield a practical iterative solution method. The results also show that our formalism naturally connects to the established diagrammatic mass-action approximation of parquet theory for many-body systems.

The process of exciton condensation in a system with electron-hole symmetry is computed using a thermodynamically accurate method based on first principles. This involves coupling time-dependent Hartree-Fock theory with classical statistical mechanics. An application of the proposed approach to the material TiSe2 reveals the occurrence of a typical exciton insulator state. This is characterized by the resolution of Se atoms into three phases: an intermediate phase and two metallic phases. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the mechanism driving excitonic phase transition in TiSe2 can be attributed to Fermi surface instability, rather than being the primary cause of the transition. This is in contrast to a common belief that such instability is merely a consequence of the transition.

In recent years, numerous online platforms have enabled users to report issues and enhance their community's safety through feature innovations like comment systems, threaded discussions, and even AI-powered content moderation tools. To effectively address user-reported problems, it's crucial for dispatchers to accurately interpret user-submitted text and identify the core safety concerns. This study delves into a lesser-known aspect of safety reporting: the communication dynamics between dispatchers and users. Using a comprehensive text log from the San Francisco Safety Dispatch platform, we uncover essential dispatcher tasks, their corresponding processes, and a novel dataset, USDS20, which we introduce to study this interaction. Our research reveals that dispatchers and users engage in a collaborative process, with users providing additional context to clarify initial reports, such as false alarms or misplaced subjects. Through this partnership, they often achieve more efficient outcomes, such as relocating subjects to the correct areas, with users playing a vital role in refining and directing the reporting process.

To analyze the impact of a magnetic field on doped hexagonal black phosphorus, a theoretical model incorporating a nematic order has been developed and mathematical equations describing the superconducting state's response to the field have been derived within the BCS framework. Research indicates that the superconducting energy gap in this material is composed of two distinct subgaps that behave differently in isotropic conditions but may become unequal and even vanish in specific directional configurations under a magnetic field. Consequently, the magnetic field can induce a transition to a type-II superconducting state, accompanied by quantum oscillations in the material's properties.

Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. However, human annotators face time constraints when labeling a large batch of selected examples. To address this, we investigated the scenario in which a chosen set of highly informative data includes unfamiliar samples, leading to extended labeling times. From a minimax perspective, we established a lower bound on the minimax risk for a minimax active learning setting. Furthermore, we created a new active learning algorithm, known as Active Explore-Exploit (A3E), which achieves this minimax risk. The key innovation of A3E is a novel query criterion that balances between exploring unknown areas and exploiting known ones. Notably, existing methods may fail to handle unknown samples or require labeling all selected examples, leading to increased time costs. Our approach, in contrast, can efficiently identify and adapt to unknown samples, significantly reducing human annotation time.

Using concepts from information theory, the complexity of music can be treated as a property that changes over time. This research focuses on the average complexity of two musical elements - rhythm and pitch contour in the top 1000 popular songs from the last two decades in the US. The results show an overall increase in both aspects of complexity, with no significant differences among various genres. Notably, the top songs in the US display less complexity compared to those in the UK, indicating genre and geographical influences on musical evolution.

A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate reinforcement extends traditional process models by allowing for dynamic changes in process entries based on past observations.  The current research examines countable process entries with multiple additions and derives key statistical outcomes, including the behavior of visit frequencies and the probability of future additions based on past events.  The examination includes specific instances such as the Polya urn model and the canonical reinforcement process, with findings extending existing statistical outcomes to the stochastically dependent settings of our process.

Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader application is hindered by the expense of obtaining human annotations. To overcome this limitation, we propose VISCLR, a time-efficient VISual Cluster Ranking Learning approach. VISCLR leverages human aptitude for classification by presenting pre-grouped similar tasks. Empirical evidence demonstrates that comparing tasks within the same category yields more reliable human annotations, enabling our method to achieve comparable performance at half the cost. Furthermore, VISCLR's flexibility allows it to be used with various image observation techniques, including both raw images and pre-extracted task features, and our experiments confirm that it enhances the quality of the learned reward in all these scenarios.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties.

Euler's equations for 2D ideal fluids with singularities can be reformed as a weakly singular equation involving a vortex core whose circumference is zero. This equation can be solved for solutions that exhibit specific symmetry and pointwise behavior. The key finding is that such equations have both trivial and non-trivial solutions. Trivial solutions correspond to smooth Navier-Stokes solutions, whereas the latter exhibit a specific density behavior at origin, exhibited by a unique family of solutions. These solutions demonstrate stability in certain contexts, and a related vortex core behavior can also be examined, although such behavior exhibits a loss of stability.

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a causal quantity that can be estimated using the Backfitting algorithm or other methods. A key challenge in conditional causal inference is "conditioning away" covariations, which often results in large estimation variances due to ATE being a difference of two close values. To address this issue, variance-reduced estimators combining neural network-based predictions with augmented inverse probability weighting have been developed. However, these estimators are limited to cases where ATE can be precisely identified. In contrast, in situations where ATE is not identifiable, similar estimators can still yield consistent results, but they are computationally inefficient. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a new class of estimators - the Normalized Augmented Inverse Probability Weighting (NAIPW) estimators - that efficiently utilize augmented model predictions even when ATE is not identifiable. We establish the normality and semi-convergence of this new estimators and conduct simulation experiments to evaluate their performance. We further compare our new estimators with existing methods, including random sampling, and double machine learning, in a range of simulated scenarios.

The role of CPT-odd hadronic vacuum polarization in electron-positron annihilation into tau particles has been ruled out experimentally, but other complex, flavor-specific aspects of tau decays remain mysterious.  These enigmatic problems can be resolved by combining theoretical and experimental research in a collaborative way.  However, in other areas, other issues arise.  The recent discovery of off-shell weak bosons decaying into tau pairs, which has been verified experimentally, presents a challenge for theory in an entirely different way.  While some issues, like the suppression of certain tau decays, can be addressed by combining lattice QCD and experimental research in a combined way, others pose additional difficulties on their own.  The lattice QCD and experimental research in tau physics has been in an inextricably linked relationship for a long time.  With new data coming in from the FEEL'it experiment, this connection will become even tighter.

A typical approach to Bayesian inference for extreme value analysis involves modelling threshold exceedances as a homogeneous Poisson process, which can be effectively achieved using standard Bayesian software, provided the threshold exceedance rate is included among the model parameters. However, this strategy is not always in line with the original intent of the analysis, particularly when the underlying parameters of the extreme value distribution, rather than the threshold, are of primary interest. We identify the issues resulting from estimating the threshold alongside the extreme value parameters, which include difficult-to-interpret posterior samples and sensitive inference resulting from the combination of the extreme value and threshold. To address these challenges, we introduce a straightforward Poisson process transformation, which enables the marginalisation of the threshold and provides meaningful results, which can be readily implemented using standard Bayesian software. We illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed technique through two practical case studies, including one Bayesian inference for a weather analysis and the other being an analysis of historical and future insurance claims in the presence of inflation.

In the context of offline reinforcement learning with corrupted data, we explore a setting where some entries in the dataset are randomly altered. Theoretical analysis shows that in this setting, the value function estimation problem is subject to a level set structure, resulting in an estimation error bound that increases proportionally to $n^{-1/4}$ given a sample size of $n$. This rate is known to be the most efficient possible under certain conditions. A novel, distance-based risk measure is developed to evaluate the effectiveness of an action-value function in this corrupted setting, and a novel regularizer based on policy-induced distributional distance is introduced to ensure robustness against future data shifts. The integration of this novel approach with a level set constrained optimization technique gives rise to LROQL, a new offline Q-learning algorithm that is both robust and general, and under specific conditions, the performance of LROQL in the corrupted setting is nearly as good as it would be in an uncorrupted setting. The performance of LROQL in the robust offline reinforcement learning task is then evaluated through a series of numerical experiments.

This study demonstrates a logarithmic convexity linked to observability at a specific point in time for a one-dimensional heat equation under dynamic boundary conditions, leading to impulse approximate controllability in similar scenarios with dynamic boundaries. Additionally, we provide a detailed estimate for the cost of impulse control. Our research includes a step-by-step procedure for finding the impulsive control of minimal L^2-norm and supports these findings with numerical tests to verify the efficiency of the developed algorithm.

A consensus has not been reached on the definition of out-of-distribution (OOD) text for natural language processing. We propose categorizing OOD into distinct classes and suggest a method for their identification. The first class, anomalous samples, can be found using density estimation methods, whereas the second class, domain shift, requires a reference to a normal distribution for a given domain to identify shifts to unusual domains. We define three categories of OOD: local, global, and cross-domain. Local OOD refers to the replacement of a single token in an input sentence, OOD global refers to the alteration of a sentence's meaning without changing its structure, and OOD cross-domain refers to a transition from one domain to another. We present a method for detecting local OOD at the token level, global OOD at the sentence level, and cross-domain OOD by comparing a sentence to a domain-specific normal distribution. The proposed approach is evaluated on the GLUE benchmark and a custom dataset.

In recent years, various artificial molecular motors operating on the principle of inelastic electron tunneling have been developed. These motors, along with other quantum devices, are expected to be incorporated into future quantum computing and quantum information processing applications. A general mathematical model has been developed to simulate the behavior of quantum engines, incorporating insights from quantum mechanics. This model can be applied to capture the dynamics of quantum devices, including Brownian molecular motors driven by inelastic electron tunneling. Using a quantum stochastic method, we have computed the tunneling current and thermodynamic properties of the Brownian molecular motor, providing a comprehensive understanding of its operation.

Building on a 2019 find by Germain and Konietschke about the general unavailability of synchronous transducers for language recognition with alphabet changes, we investigate the closest equivalent. The research focuses on two key concepts: one-way resynchronizability, a weaker form similar to one-way determinism, and one-balancedness, a stronger analogy to finiteness. Although they are not fully equivalent as shown in the original study, it's been shown that for non-erasing transducers, these concepts are indeed equivalent. For a broader understanding, we also examine how these two ideas relate to the recognizability of languages by 1-safe transducers.

In this study, we examine the standard convolution problem under a variety of constraints relating polynomial degrees and variable counts. Finiteness in the support of multivariate polynomials across n variables leads to the concept of restricted convolution as seen in instances like sum-of-squares for SAT. This paper provides a structural decomposition of the convolution operator and introduces an efficient method for its computation, one which is nearly linear in complexity for certain restricted cases. Specifically, for nearly the same set of instances, our algorithm achieves a complexity of $m^{\Omega(n)}$, where $m$ represents the total degree, and it can be computed in $mO(n \log m)$ operations within the field. Furthermore, for sums-of-squares calculations, an even simpler upper bound of $d^n$ is possible, where $d$ represents the pointwise convolution restriction and the exponent can be reduced to $2.376$. Our findings reveal that even with severe constraints, such as all but a minimum number of variables being limited to first-degree, our method remains efficient, outperforming the traditional brute-force approach by a significant margin, where the complexity is reduced from $m^n$ to $m n$.

The discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B in 1995 marked a significant moment in the field as it was the first of its kind with a confirmed mass. Located approximately 20 light-years away, this ultra-cool dwarf has a mass around 85% of Jupiter's and a age estimated at 4-8 billion years. Due to its age, GJ 229A's atmosphere should have cooled down, which would have affected its spectral characteristics. However, certain spectral features in its spectrum, particularly around 2.15 micrometers, are not fully understood. By analyzing multi-epoch observations with the NIRSpec instrument on the JWST, a comprehensive study of its atmospheric composition was conducted. By comparing various models of different cloud depths, a broad range of possibilities for the opacity of its high-altitude clouds were identified as being between 0.005 cm^-1 and 0.02 cm^-1. Additionally, a temperature of 730 K and a surface gravity of 5.20 cm s^-2 were found to be the best fit for the observed spectral data. These results also shed light on the atmospheric composition of late-T dwarfs, which is a significant area of study in the field of exoplanetary science.

To look for a previously unobserved exotic state with the properties 0^{--}, we suggest using a particular arrangement of the particles charmonium and diphoton, denoted as $J/\Psi\gamma$. Our analysis indicates that if the Fierz interaction exists, it can lead to the formation of a nonet of exotic states with zero spin and negative parity, and we calculate the masses of these states to be 3262, 3440, 4150, and 4607 MeV. Our study also shows that the placement of the $Y(4230)$ and $Y(4380)$ resonances can be attributed to the dominant hybrid components of the light scalars, and it is proposed that the $Y(4230)$ and $Y(4380)$ may in fact be the isoscalar members of the hybrid and Fierz states, respectively, and that $Y(4230)$ and $Y(4380)$ can be produced through the $J/\Psi\gamma$ process. Our findings also reveal the potential for the $Y(4230)$ and $Y(4380)$ to be created in $e^+e^-$ collisions, and we have determined their production cross sections, and it is recommended that the $Y(4230)$ and $Y(4380)$

A crucial goal of the LHCb experiment is to establish the $C\!P$ violation measurement in $S$ quark mixing by making a precise prediction for the phase $\phi_s$ and width difference $\Delta\Gamma_s$. In addition to completing this measurement, studies of $C\!P$ violation in $S$ quark mixing could help us understand the size of $\phi_s$ and whether it aligns with the Standard Model. Recent findings from 2015-2018 data reveal a $\phi_s$ measurement of $-0.0074\pm0.0029\mathrm{~rad}$ and a $\Delta\Gamma_s$ upper limit of $0.17\pm0.07\mathrm{~ps}^{-1}$, which suggests the possibility of further improvements based on a combined analysis of $S$ and $C$ body spectra and isolated candidate decays from 2015-2020 data.

The spread of airborne diseases, such as COVID-19, within confined indoor settings is heavily influenced by the turbulent mixing of the environment. Researchers have been using well-mixed models due to the difficulty in obtaining detailed information about the complex flow patterns in these spaces. A study was conducted in an urban bus to assess the effectiveness of the well-mixed assumption for an indoor setting with complex geometry and varying pressure conditions. Wind tunnel experiments were performed with an infected source of SARS-CoV-2, using bacteriophage as a proxy, under different conditions. The experiments involved an infected source of bacteriophage at the front of the bus, near the front window, and near the rear window. The well-mixed model was able to accurately predict the concentration of airborne particles at various points within the bus. The model was also able to quantify the risk of an infected person, seated at various points within the bus, infecting a susceptible person. The results suggest that well-mixed models can be a useful tool for predicting disease transmission in urban buses, and potentially other indoor settings with complex geometries and varying pressure conditions.

To ascertain intrinsic characteristics such as log ft values and single particle matrix elements for E\beta transitions in E2 and E1 channels, a shell-model analysis was conducted on the recently measured forbidden beta decay of $^{135}$Te ($7/2^+$ to $6^+$) and $^{137}$Te ($7/2^+$ to $6^+$) E2 transitions. Furthermore, single particle matrix elements for various Single Particle Shell Model E\beta transitions were also computed for these isotopes. By incorporating a simple mean field with the standard WS06 Woods-Saxon potential, we obtained matrix elements for various Single Particle Shell Model E\beta transitions as well as the log ft values associated with the forbidden beta decay of $^{135,137}$Te. Our calculated log ft values for $^{135,137}$Te were found to be lower than experimental values, which can be attributed to the inclusion of the spin-orbit term in the WS06 potential.

Double-sided auctions are commonly used financial matching systems that facilitate transactions.  A significant issue with these systems is their complexity, which often makes them susceptible to errors.  Our research addresses this problem by developing fully formalized rules for double-sided auctions, which apply to both demand futures and commodity futures markets.  Our approach allows for tracking and managing live orders in markets that have multiple sessions.  Our approach is based on an automated verification method that ensures the soundness of the auction rules through mathematical proof.  Our work builds on existing research, but differs in several aspects such as considering order expiration, session-based trading and different pricing methods for futures.  Our approach is consistent with real-world trading platforms such as those used by the Chicago Mercantile Exchange.

We utilized heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying both theoretical and experimental data to calculate the mass of these mesons. Additionally, by examining the decay widths of bottom mesons, we derived upper limits on their corresponding coupling values. Our research also featured a phase shift analysis using these couplings, which allowed us to present the final mass values and provide estimates with confidence intervals for the $F$-wave bottom mesons.

R. C. Baker initially proposed a theory in 1974 that every nonexpansive mapping from the plane to itself can be broken down into horizontal and vertical slices, where each piece maps to a single point in the plane. This concept has stood the test of time despite the passage of over four decades. In this context, we introduce a more generalized concept: periodic decompositions for mappings defined on the plane, which encompasses the original decomposition as a special case. Furthermore, we identify key characteristics of such decompositions and provide illustrative examples of their applications.

A popular technique in nonlinear systems analysis, Dynamic Mode Decomposition, approximates an underlying linear operator using a particular snapshot, facilitating various properties of its spectrum in describing a system. However, nonlinearity and computational constraints can lead to inaccurate approximations by limiting the operator's Hilbert space. Here, a new kernel-based dynamic mode decomposition is developed, employing a specific kernel to expand the available Hilbert space for more precise operator approximation. By incorporating a specific shift operator, a unique kernel is derived, enabling the application of dynamic mode decomposition in understanding complex, high-dimensional systems. A new optimization method, kernel learning for robust dynamic mode decomposition, uses gradient ascent to learn the desired kernel, eliminating the need for specific kernel selection. This method is demonstrated on various examples, including low-dimensional systems like the Burgers equation and a Lorenz 96 model, as well as removing a spurious mode in a turbulent channel flow simulation.

Online chess communities have grown to massive proportions, with 2.8 million members on r/chess as of 2021. Building on our previous work's analysis of the 2018 world chess championship, we now examine all games from titles that year back to 2009. To achieve this, we establish an original scoring system to quantify opening similarity and coherence, then determine the most prominent sequences. Ultimately, our method enables a numerical assessment of uncertainty for chess experts' predictions regarding the outcomes of the 2021 chess world championship between Carlsen and Nepomniachtchi.

This research derives an original formula in millisecond pulsar theory, describing the white dwarf's core temperature as a function of its age. A crucial variable in this derivation is the pulsar's initial birth mass. To determine these core temperatures and initial masses, we employed the Akaike Information Criterion on a set of numerical pulsar evolution simulations. Our findings indicate that the pulsar's initial mass significantly impacts its subsequent evolutionary path. These results can be applied to analyze millisecond pulsar data from the eFELP project of the eFEL collaboration.

A method to derive constants of motion beyond local bounds for ODE-based Lagrangian systems is outlined, including a practical example that illustrates its utility for dissipative mechanical systems and its implications on solution existence under specific conditions when time dependence is constant.

Recent advancements in computer graphics and vision have made it possible to create more immersive and interactive 3D environments, accessible via head-mounted displays. Currently available datasets, however, are limited in two dimensions, lacking the depth required for realistic 3D human-computer interactions. Our team has developed a novel dataset in response to this limitation, consisting of real-world 3D shapes captured from RGB-D images, and rendered as a human in VR. We invite researchers to participate in a associated challenge with corresponding papers, inviting novel approaches for efficient retrieval of similar 3D shapes within the dataset, given a subset of its rendered contents via a graphical interface.

HD80606b, a planet with a very long and uneven orbit around its host star, undergoes dramatic changes in brightness and temperature that provide unique insights into exoplanet atmospheres. However, its complex orbital path makes predicting its position difficult. By analyzing the time it takes HD80606b to transit HD80606 in various directions from Earth, researchers can create a more accurate schedule for observing the planet with the James Webb Space Telescope. To refine this timeline, a collaborative team used a global network of radio telescopes to precisely time the planet's transit in 2019. By applying a statistical model to this data, combined with existing information about the system's orbital plane, they were able to create a more reliable schedule, including a predicted visit with the space telescope in April 2022.

Investigating isentropic collapse of a spherical, isotropic fluid in General Relativity, we discovered that isentropic surfaces can emerge once departure from isotropy occurs. Similarly, if we restrict ourselves to isentropic surfaces, collapse remains viable but results in an infinite set of singularities. However, if we assume a fluid with a linear equation of state, we found that collapse can be achieved while maintaining entropy levels, yet even in this scenario, some singularities remain unavoidable.

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have confirmed that a specific expression for entropy applies to all black holes when expressed in terms of the null generator of the horizon. This null generator becomes degenerate specifically at the occurrence of an extremal black hole. By analyzing the properties of this degenerate generator, we have confirmed that it satisfies the requirements for a steady state, leading to the conclusion that it remains unchanged along its entire trajectory. This confirms that an extremal black hole's entropy can be expressed as the product of this null generator's complexity and its temperature, which becomes zero in the extremal case. Furthermore, we have verified that an extremal black hole's entropy remains invariant under any smooth transformation of the horizon, supporting the hypothesis that this property is intrinsic to the horizon itself.

A key requirement for effective robotic learning in unstructured settings is capable physical interaction.  Interaction End-Effector Exploration Drive (I-EEED) serves as a control mechanism facilitating exploration by decoupling the robot's interaction end-effector from its supported object.  As a result, I-EEED has found successful applications in a range of tasks including 3D reconstruction, supporting vulnerable loads, and teaching skills to learning agents.  Despite its potential, current I-EEED implementations struggle due to the under-explored interaction between end-effector and supported object.  To overcome this limitation, we introduce an I-EEED system driven by electric muscle actuators and equipped with a haptic feedback interface.  By integrating multiple actuation methods, our system can provide multi-directional interaction forces, while the incorporation of haptic feedback interface enables a more natural I-EED exploration.  The effectiveness of our I-EEED system has been validated through simulated and real-world robotic interaction tasks, demonstrating its potential to outperform existing I-EED systems.

A generalized version of the Poincaré algebra has been developed that introduces colour indices.  Using the Fock-Schwinger parameter and a coloured version of the Poincaré operator, projections have been made onto massless and massive spin-2 fields.  These projections have led to the derivation of the gravitational field's quadratic action in both the massive and massless forms, as well as the field strength action for the massive case.  Similarly, the Schwarzian action for a coloured particle has been obtained through the Poincaré orbit method.  Notably, the obtained actions can serve as the basis for studying  coloured gravity and particles within the framework of an associated coloured spacetime.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices in the graph, running in O(n^(k+1)) time, where 'n' represents the total number of edges and 'k' is the source vertex count. We've also developed a fixed-parameter algorithm伟大的基于源汇顶点数之和, 耗时 $O(n \log n + k^6 \log k)$. Our novel approach combines the use of planar subgraphs and positional layouts. We've further developed a fixed-parameter algorithm基于图块数量, 运行 $O(n^{\omega}(k+1))$ 时间, 其中$\omega<2.373$是矩阵乘法指数.

Image-based goal navigation is a key memory-based task for real-world robotic applications.
To navigate efficiently, robots must choose between multiple remembered memories and discard unnecessary ones.
However, existing methods for distilling memories are either computationally expensive or not well-suited for navigation tasks.
We present a novel approach called MemoNav, which combines a self-supervised method with a reinforcement learning strategy to filter out unhelpful memories.
The first component involves using self-supervised contrastive learning to filter out similar memories and remove unnecessary ones, which are then paired with samples from the main experience.
The derived policy method chooses the most helpful memories to navigate to the goal, avoiding distractions and not included in the main experience.
The two methods work together to create a robust policy that selects the most helpful memories to navigate to the goal.
The experimental results on the TUORB and KITTI datasets show that MemoNav outperforms existing methods by either filtering unnecessary memories or selecting the most helpful memories to navigate to the goal.

To enhance coverage and data rates within indoor spaces, small cells have been successfully integrated into the commercial 4G and 5G networks starting with the first femtocells deployed in 2008 and macro-femto integration in 2013. Although small cells have achieved significant commercial success, they face challenges in meeting the demands of emerging 6G use cases, such as immersive immersive experiences, immersive immersive experiences, immersive immersive experiences, immersive experiences, and immersive experiences, and other similar applications. In response to these challenges, the paper explores the limitations of current small cell technologies and proposes potential advancements needed for 6G applications. It emphasizes the need for improved power efficiency, user authentication, mobility management, and other essential components to support diverse 6G scenarios. The paper then suggests possible future directions for small cell evolution, including RAN sharing, AI-powered optimization, edge computing integration, and other innovative solutions. Lastly, the paper highlights various research topics relevant to the RAN, core network, and emerging 6G use cases, and concludes by providing an overview of the ongoing research efforts in this area.

We've developed a comprehensive framework to model complex interactions between multiple entangled systems using hypergraphs. This approach can be applied to various processes and is particularly useful for capturing system dynamics that traditional methods can't fully capture. By illustrating with examples from neurobiology and chemistry, our framework's general nature is showcased. Nonetheless, a key focus remains on characterizing the general behavior in diffusive systems within this framework.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems through an entropy production method, focusing on out-of-time-ordered correlator behavior and entanglement patterns in eigenstates. Utilization of complete eigenbases from numerical methods or analytical solutions enables a thorough analysis of operator entanglement. We extend our findings to the 1+1 dimensional free scalar field and demonstrate how our entropy approach aligns with results from reduced density matrix calculations for two-point functions.

The equation-of-state (EoS) of nuclear matter is characterized by two key aspects: its saturation density and the saturation binding energy per nucleon. The properties of dense nuclear matter can be investigated by measuring light elements, particularly those involving the nuclear triple-alpha reaction, which involves fusing three alpha particles to form a 12C nucleus at a 31 MeV excitation energy, known as the Hoyle state. The residue of this resonance is believed to facilitate the fusion of alpha particles and ultimately leads to the synthesis of carbon stars. The theoretical component of the Hoyle state's decay has been estimated but the experimental verification is still pending. A new approach to directly measure the decay of the Hoyle state using a Time Projection Chamber (TPC) has been proposed in this study. By detecting the stable decay products of the reaction, the proposed method can determine the theoretical binding energy and excitation energy of the Hoyle state, thereby validating the theoretical predictions. By detecting the decay component of the Hoyle state directly using a TPC, the proposed method can determine the theoretical binding energy and excitation energy of the Hoyle state, thereby validating the theoretical predictions.

Significant breakthroughs in understanding and predicting crack behavior are
needed for several applications. A theoretical model is developed to analyze
the dynamics of a fracture line in a 2D material. We demonstrate how a new
model can produce both oscillating crack patterns and branching cracks at their
tips. Key factors influencing these phenomena are the intrinsic properties of
materials, such as their surface tension and relaxation periods. Oscillatory
instability occurs when a certain type of stress exceeds the materials' intrinsic
properties. Similarly, tip-splitting instability occurs when the rate at which
cracks form exceeds the materials' intrinsic period. These findings are
supported by simulations of fracture patterns, confirming the importance of
materials' intrinsic properties in predicting stable crack patterns.

In a general setting, we examine the properties of finite state channels with feedback and state information, specifically focusing on the scenarios where the channel statistics are either known in advance or unknown to the user. Our research demonstrates that under certain conditions, the achievable capacity region is finite when the system includes a limited number of states and is unknown to the user, leading to the conclusion that the achievable capacity region is also finite when the system contains a limited number of states and the user has access to the mutual information between the channel output and the system's state. This phenomenon is analogous to the self-stabilizing nature of random walks with a limited number of steps. As a result, we develop a general algorithm for estimating a lower bound on the achievable capacity region, which can be implemented in a limited number of steps and relies on a limited amount of channel output data. This finding has significant implications for the design of adaptive communication systems, particularly in scenarios where the system dynamics are complex and changing, leading to a simplified understanding of the achievable capacity region, $C_{\text{CS}}$, which can be estimated within a limited number of steps as $O(|\mathcal{S}|)$, where $|\mathcal{S}|$ represents the system's state space size. This outcome is notable as it suggests that the achievable capacity region can be estimated efficiently within a limited number of steps, even when the system's dynamics are complex and challenging to model accurately.

A theoretical approach based on the Majorana transformation has been developed to identify topological superconductivity in the 2D attractive Rashba Hubbard model for low-lying fillings. Through numerical calculations of the finite system's many-body wave function, the ground state's symmetry and the critical coupling strength for a given spin imbalance have been determined. Employing the tight-binding model, the numerically obtained critical coupling strength agrees well with the theoretical value. A specific expression for the 3rd order Chern number of the Fermi surface has been derived, enabling the prediction of topological superconductivity in the low-lying fillings within this model.

This study focuses on creating and utilizing a labeled dataset for verifying facts within scientific documents presented in tabular format. Conducted as a competition under the SemEval 2021 framework, this task brings together researchers from natural language processing and visual graph metrics to develop effective models for automating fact-checking processes in commercial and educational settings. This paper outlines the details of the dataset created, along with the results of participating teams' submissions to the challenge. The dataset used for this task is based on credible sources such as journals, books, and online databases that provide visual and textual representations of facts. The results indicate that human-level accuracy can be achieved in verifying facts when textual and visual information are combined. The set of participating models submitted to the competition is comprised of twelve models, whose sources and architectures are detailed in this study. The results indicate that models incorporating textual cues outperform those incorporating visual elements when attempting to verify facts within complex scientific and medical datasets. The set of participating models submitted to the competition is comprised of twelve models, whose sources and architectures are detailed in this study. This analysis explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics, delving into common justifications for complex formalism and offering additional perspectives to support its necessity. By examining these factors, we hope to clarify the underlying reasoning for employing complex numbers in Quantum mechanics.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

They're based on assumptions including a confined or unconfined aquifer with a thin bottom, specific and variable but thin top boundaries, and a bottom permeability much lower than the sides. While side and top boundaries may vary greatly in hydraulic conductivity, the bottom is much less conductive. Examples of such situations involve sand or gravel deposits in a glacial environment.

Starting points for these equations are Darcy's Law and the water continuity equation. They don't rely on assumptions regarding the aquifer's shape or the boundary properties of the sides and bottom. However, some simplifications are necessary due to the difficulty in theoretically determining the boundary properties. These assumptions regarding the boundaries are: (a) the sides are impermeable; (b) the bottom is confined by a clay layer; and (c) the top boundary is exposed to the atmosphere.

In power stations with fuel flexibility, there's an increased risk of sulfur dioxide forming in the flue gas outlet due to natural gas being replaced by high-sulfur fuels like coal. This paper presents an anode plasma concept for generating ozone as well as direct UV emission, which can effectively remove sulfur dioxide in post-treatment applications. The proposed solution involves a double-layer anode plasma device with a dielectric barrier, allowing it to be used both for primary treatment of flue gas and for treating gas at the exit. The effectiveness of this device was evaluated through numerical simulations using a comprehensive model that considers the chemical kinetics and transport properties in a plasma zone.

As interest in neuromorphic computing grows, engineers face a key challenge in simulating the technology to evaluate and refine their designs. Testing novel algorithms and architectures on a simulated chip requires accurate models, which are in short supply, particularly for energy-efficient designs. This problem hampers innovation in neuromorphic computing by making it difficult to compare new designs with existing benchmarks. This research addresses the need by creating a set of standardized digital circuits using SystemC, which represents spiking neural activity. By providing these models, we enable engineers to measure performance metrics such as power consumption, energy efficiency, and processing efficiency. Our models have been verified against mathematical calculations and can accurately simulate a memory element with 16-bit resolution. We also demonstrate their effectiveness by comparing their performance on neuromorphic architectures against real hardware benchmarks.

Deploying machine learning in dynamic environments like stock trading, where the presence of competing agents like bots or human traders can outperform individual predictions, presents significant challenges.
Effective performance requires more than just prediction accuracy - a transparent explanation of how that accuracy was achieved is equally important.
We introduce a innovative approach, called Indecision Trees, for predicting the outcome of future competitions between comparable entities, such as horses in races or stocks in the market, over which information may be incomplete.
This method enables us to draw conclusions not only about our own observations but also about opposing parties' hidden information, resulting in an argument-based prediction supported by a level of confidence.
This reasoning process is underpinned by a solid mathematical framework rooted in quantitative update theory, allowing us to learn and make predictions even when information is partially unknown.
We put our approach to the test using three different datasets, and compare its performance with that of a leading alternative method, demonstrating its effectiveness in predicting outcomes under uncertain conditions.

The DTW distance is widely applied in time series analysis across various fields,
despite its high computational cost stemming from its dynamic time alignment
property. To reduce this expense, early abandoning (EA) prunes DTW by halting
calculations when the lower bound exceeds the current maximum. Calculating
the LB often demands LBMA, an operation more costly than comparing values. To
address this, we developed a data structure that efficiently calculates LBMA in
constant time. By doing so, EA can be made as fast or faster than the DBN search,
making EA a viable option for similarity search where speed is crucial. By
skipping LBN calculations, EA prunes DTW at the beginning of its computation,
resulting in an LBN speedup of over 100 times in our tests.

Current educational tools and environments used to teach software testing are primarily designed for instructing instructors, not students. An innovative approach has been implemented in an educational setting, where teaching assistants provide two types of feedback - traditional feedback and inquiry-based feedback - based on data collected from a study focusing on teaching strategies for software testing. The investigation aimed to determine the effectiveness of these feedback mechanisms by analyzing the test cases and directory structures students created, and the results showed that - although students initially struggled more with inquiry-based feedback - both forms of feedback had comparable long-term effects on students' testing skills. In domains such as medicine, generating trustworthy AI decisions requires not just accuracy but also clarity and reliability. Since machine learning techniques lack these qualities when applied to textual data, we propose a framework for generating transparent explanations by integrating rule extraction from multiple sources, including supervised and unsupervised deep learning methods. This framework combines the strengths of data-driven and logic-based approaches by using unsupervised deep learning to identify relevant concepts, associated high-frequency words, and associations, then utilizing induction and stratification logic programming techniques to generate rules that explain the data. The proposed system is demonstrated by its success in trained a DNN classifier on the JAM 2019 dataset for disease sub-type classification in histopathology.

Over-smoothing significantly constrains the complexity of Graph Convolutional Networks, making it crucial to understand the root cause. A thorough examination of the over-smoothing phenomenon and Graph Convolutional Networks is presented in this article, including an estimation of the upper limit for its occurrence. The study sheds light on the pivotal elements contributing to over-smoothing and offers empirical evidence validating various countermeasures to mitigate it.

Dark matter particles interacting with visible matter through a common vector or axial boson mediator are investigated within the standard model extended framework. The analysis involves dark matter production alongside a Z boson in proton-proton proton collisions at a 13 TeV proton center-of-mass energy at the LHC, resulting in a final state comprising a charged lepton-neutrino pair from a Z boson decay and at least one pint of jet activity. The data collected by the CMS experiment in 2016 at a 95% confidence level is analyzed using multiple mediator scenarios, including those decaying into a dark matter particle pair, where the mediators include a Z boson, a scalar, a pseudoscalar, and a vector particle. The analyses focus on the production of a Z boson in association with a scalar or a vector particle decaying into a charged lepton-neutrino pair, where the product decays into a mediator. The analyses found no significant deviation from standard model expectations in excess data collected corresponding to 35.9 fb^-1 of proton-proton collisions at a 13 TeV proton center-of-mass energy. The results show exclusion limits on the production cross-sections of dark matter in the specified mass ranges for different mediator scenarios, including a 750 GeV mass range exclusion for a dark matter particle interacting with a 750 GeV Z boson.
