Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots in unstructured settings like human workspaces poses a significant challenge, necessitating consideration of both the robot's position and orientation. To address this challenge, a novel control approach based on control barrier functions is introduced, capable of guaranteeing path safety for mobile robot arms considering their spatial orientation. The approach incorporates a novel state extension that includes the orientation, custom functions that account for configuration, and specific feedback control laws. The resulting framework is demonstrated through experiments involving an AgileX mobile platform, with a dynamic experiment further validating its applicability through the simulation of accidental pushes.

Natural language processing, a crucial field of study, strives to comprehend text via digital analysis, despite the inherent imperfections arising from diverse forms of written and spoken language. This work delves into employing various graph-based methodologies for resolving the challenge of text summarization via a selective extraction technique. Two key indicators – sentence overlap and edit distance – are employed for gauging sentence similarity.

Researchers have shown a substantial interest in the capabilities of Bose-Einstein condensates to execute quantum computations through the use of Kondo's nonlinear Kondo equation, which can model key aspects of BEC dynamics. However, traditional solutions to the Kondo equation fail to fully support the necessary properties for implementing quantum gates essential to quantum computation. This research develops an improved version of the Kondo equation, enabling a comprehensive examination of two-dimensional nonlinear evolution of BEC states as quantum gates. Our investigation reveals that, unlike earlier studies, this new equation permits a comprehensive understanding of quantum gate operations, including those involving entangled states, and is substantiated by both theoretical analysis and numerical simulations. The validity of this equation has been confirmed experimentally, and its comparison with predictions demonstrates strong agreement. The compatibility of this equation with both single-component and multi-component BEC systems makes it a promising tool for implementing quantum gates using quantum gases.

This paper aims to prove two conjectures put forth by F. Zhang of China regarding the uniqueness of meromorphic mappings from a complete Kähler manifold to a complex projective space, with the additional requirement of generic surjectivity when considering all such mappings simultaneously. Our approach relies heavily on differential methods, specifically employing an established inequality from an earlier work of the author and L. Huang on the subject.

A signature is a straightforward criterion for identifying non-degenerate points in a multi-variable polynomial equation. Using this criterion, we develop an algorithm to identify and trace the non-degenerate portion of a polynomial's solution set in a different space-based environment. We integrate our algorithm into an existing signature computation method to effectively break down complex algebraic curves into simpler components. We demonstrate the performance of our algorithm through a series of experiments and provide a underlying theoretical explanation for why it works.

Direct photons have been measured at $p_T<5$ GeV/$c$ for midrapidity and most central events of Cu$+$Cu collisions at $\sqrt{s_{_{NN}}}=200$ GeV. By measuring $e^{\gamma}$ pairs over a very low $p_T$ range ($1-6$ GeV/$c$), this study provides the first such data set. Contrasting photon yields with $e^{\gamma}$ pairs significantly exceeds expectations from hot and cold matter formation in Cu$+$Cu collisions. However, the excess yield does not follow the pattern observed at higher $p_T$. In addition, $p$+$j$ spectra exhibit significant enhancements compared to proton$+$ proton collisions, exceeding the expectations from more energetic Cu$+$Cu collisions.

The Turan tetrahedron problem seeks to calculate the Turan density of the tetrahedron graph K4^3 by finding the maximum l1-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector. We determine the asymptotic maximum l2-norm of a K4^3-free n-vertex 3-uniform hypergraph's codegree vector and prove the existence of a constant maximizer, which is the generalized Turan graph Gn(4,3). Notably, our result implies the maximum l1-n is O(n5/3), leading to a new codegree bound of O(n) for the tetrahedron. This work provides the first optimization of Turan density for the tetrahedron graph under various norm conditions.

Achieving a seamless visual experience for users is crucial when displaying high-resolution vector maps on screens with limited color depth. This challenge is compounded by a common rendering issue, where maps appear jagged or blurry due to the anti-aliasing effect. Although this problem is well-documented in high-resolution image rendering, it is understudied in the context of line joins. Our research tackles this challenge by developing optimized methods for rendering maps that minimize the anti-aliasing effect. Our methods aim to produce high-quality, performance-friendly pixel representations of line joins, which can then be combined with raster screens efficiently. Our approach involves pre-calculating the offset for each line segment, which, along with its width, defines a virtual rectangle. Our pre-computed off-screen geometry enables the rendering engine to efficiently calculate the final image without needing to transform world coordinates to screen coordinates. Our high-quality results are verified through automated testing and visually confirmed by users. Our optimized method achieves a significant performance boost, particularly for maps with many overlapping lines, by reducing unnecessary calculations and leveraging the graphics processor's capabilities.

The multivariate interpolation operator is traditionally constructed using piecewise linear functions to approximate absolute differences between values. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function based on the original Chernoff function, which offers improved approximation over traditional linear functions near the point of approximation. This paper focuses on creating a quasi-interpolation operator using this new function in Rn+n+1 space, which includes the original value and absolute differences between values as information. We demonstrate that the operator converges at an O(h^2) rate and is value-preserving for positive definite functions. Additionally, we show that it maintains shape when applied to functions with a bounded gradient, by incorporating data from neighboring nodes.

Pulsar halos are massive, long-lived structures formed when energetic particles
and cosmic rays produced by individual pulsars, as well as clusters of pulsars,
interact with the galaxy's confined confining fields, thus extending their lifespan.
These extended emissions are localized near individual pulsars, known as young
pulsar halos, which can be utilized to identify distant pulsars through their
associated leptonic gamma-ray signatures. Pulsar halos serve as galactic-scale
non-thermal hadronic accretion disks analogous to the disks of microquasars,
offering unique opportunities to study high-energy astrophysics. This review
examines the observational evidence for gamma-ray pulsar halos, as well as the
theoretical framework describing the physics behind their development, and the
characteristics of the pulsars that give rise to them. Finally, the review
discusses the upcoming prospects for studying pulsar halos with next-generation
gamma-ray telescopes, such as the Cherenkov Telescope Array and the Fermi Large
Area Telescope's successor.

Classification tasks are becoming increasingly important in various fields such
as computer vision, where they help determine the subject matter within an image.
To tackle this problem, neural networks require large, labeled training datasets.
However, the collected data often includes inconsistencies and irregularities that
can affect the network's performance. This study addresses these challenges by
introducing a new multi-class weather image dataset, enhancing image quality using
data augmentation techniques, and optimizing multi-class classification systems. The
proposed dataset comprises 12 distinct weather conditions and will be utilized in
combination with an established image processing network. A comprehensive evaluation
of this combination is carried out using multiple metrics and across different
environments. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach,
yielding an accuracy of 87.86% for training images and 85.86% for testing images.

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among various groups
and how their individual trends combine to create distinct patterns, ultimately
informing a climate action barometer. Cloud-based machine learning models are
employed to uncover these normative shifts, drawing on surveys from multiple
sources that explore science, economics, and global warming responses. We
also draw from global warming policy knowledge sources, including a global
climate action index. Our methods' effectiveness is further validated through
the incorporation of data from various governments' perspectives on climate
change policy. The resulting knowledge is utilized to develop a climate action
barometer, which is calibrated using existing policies and then projected
forward to offer actionable recommendations.

Soft grippers, featuring exceptional compliance and adaptability, are ideally suited for grasping a vast array of objects. However, their deployment in control systems, especially for novel objects, necessitates real-time identification of their properties. Our novel approach, rooted in the Koopman theory, enables a unified model for both accurate online characterization and effective control of a novel class of multi-fingered soft grippers. The proposed framework, called Koopman Operator Model Predictive Control, facilitates simultaneous model identification and application of an optimal control law, thus outperforming traditional model-following control methods. Experimental validations, involving the grasping of untrained objects and the execution of tasks such as lifting and inserting objects, have demonstrated the approach's capability to handle a vast array of untrained objects with minimal training data (fifteen samples) and to perform a variety of tasks robustly.

One of the fundamental tasks in machine learning is the predictive problem, which can be approached by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between a target distribution and a model-defined distribution, leading to the concept of Natural Entropy Loss. This concept serves as a natural extension of the conventional Empirical Risk Minimization problem, and its solutions are obtained through Natural Loss Minimizers. By employing the Riemannian Hessian Reshaping technique, we demonstrate that Natural Entropy Loss can be transformed into a parameter-independent form, enabling the development of the Natural Gradient Descent method, which we derive as a generalizable algorithm. Building upon this technique, Natural Loss Minimizers are shown to outperform traditional Risk Minimizers in certain settings, and the integration of Natural Entropy Loss with Natural Gradient Descent results in accelerated model convergence compared to standard Loss Minimization methods.

High-redshift star-forming galaxies are known to host powerful compact radio sources, but their characteristics at radio wavelengths are still not fully understood. Researchers have discovered a particularly distant radio source, designated CH03044-273, with a location far to the east of its center. Spectral analysis suggests a complex and young nature for this source, with a mass of a few solar masses. Its location off-center indicates a star being formed within a galaxy, making it one of the farthest known star masses. Ch03044-273 shares similarities with a recently discovered source in terms of its location, age, and a possible galaxy host. Ch03044-273's characteristics can be compared to a star mass in a galaxy, forming within a few million years. This comparison to a similar mass suggests a significant relationship between star formation and a powerful jet in a galaxy, which could provide valuable insights into the early universe.

A new approach to predicting outcomes for patients with non-small cell lung cancer is presented, using advanced deep learning techniques on two types of data: text-based tumor profiling and images from CT scans. The proposed method overcomes limitations in existing studies that rely solely on either gene expression analysis or radiological feature extraction, by combining the strengths of both in a comprehensive framework. The results, achieved without manual intervention, show promising accuracy in predicting patient survival, with the use of CT scan features alone yielding an error of 0.665 in the time-to-event prediction task and model efficiency rated at 0.604.

A well-designed state representation is crucial in the learning process of Reinforcement Learning. Natural language can be utilized in numerous tasks to either represent the state or constitute it entirely. This overview focuses on the techniques employed by researchers to create natural language state representations, underscoring the need for more transparent and contextualized models, thorough justification of design choices and assessments of the relative effectiveness of varying methodologies.

A novel approach combining machine learning is introduced, enabling the accurate reconstruction of high-redshift power spectra from quasar spectra. By leveraging simulations from large-scale cosmological models, this method trains on artificial data and achieves optimal resolution with an accuracy greater than 95% at 98% confidence. Additionally, our reconstruction algorithm outperforms traditional methods by efficiently determining the optimal signal-to-noise ratio, allowing precise analysis even under suboptimal conditions. Furthermore, our results demonstrate an effective volume expansion of at least eight times compared to conventional techniques. Building upon these successes, this algorithm can be integrated with upcoming surveys such as Euclid and the Vera C. Rubin Legacy Survey, potentially providing valuable constraints on alternative gravity theories and modified cosmological models.

This paper examines certain types of non-weight modules associated with Lie algebras of the form $\mathcal D^n$, specifically those connected to central extensions of an associative algebra called $S=n$ variables with polynomial functions. The paper focuses on modules over special types of infinite-dimensional Lie algebras - one related to vector fields on a real line and another on a high-dimensional space with compact forms consisting of finite polynomial functions. By exploring the structure of these U(h)-free modules, the paper provides a complete classification of irreducible modules for the Lie algebras of vector fields on a real line and start classification of higher dimensional variants.

Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated two datasets consisting of Twitter posts.
We developed an Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural network to determine the sentiment
expressed in the tweets. The created model achieved high accuracy on the test datasets.
Additionally, we explored the effectiveness of pre-trained word embeddings derived from
pre-trained language models, specifically Word2Vec and Google's BERT. The experiments showed
that using pre-trained word embeddings from the pre-trained language models improved the
accuracy of the created model when compared to conventional word embeddings.

Recent advances in open-domain dialogue systems have led to highly engaging conversations with users. Despite their success, they often fail to accurately respond when asked deeply personal questions due to a lack of information about the specific individual they are talking to. To address this limitation, we propose an improved system that incorporates detailed information about the user and their specified role in the conversation. Our approach involves utilizing detailed information about the user and their assigned role to generate more accurate responses in a multi-step process that includes identifying the type of question being asked, retrieving relevant information from sources, forming sentences based on the role's requirements, and refining the final response to avoid repetition. We compare our system to established dialogue systems and demonstrate an improvement of over 12 points in coherence and conversational flow.

The memory effect in gravitational waves causes a lasting change in the spacetime metric following the passage of a gravitational wave. This characteristic can be amplified by multiple effects, including a non-linear response of spacetime, a lack of symmetry in sources, and the observation of a gravitational wave at a 90-degree angle from the source's plane. Due to its low-frequency nature, the memory effect is detectable by future gravitational wave detectors, and a non-stochastic background of gravitational waves can be generated by cosmological events. However, current detectors are not sensitive enough to pick up this background. Nevertheless, more advanced detectors may be able to observe the memory effect's contribution in the future.

A hypothetical supersymmetry framework within the standard model suggests that the universe's matter origin, known as leptogenesis, occurs through bubble nucleation during a phase transition in the early universe. This process generates significant gravitational waves that could potentially be detected by future observatories. Analyzing the bubbles' dynamics allows researchers to estimate properties of the gravitational waves, including amplitude and frequency. These findings indicate the universe's early phase transition produced detectable gravitational waves within a frequency range of 0.1-10 Hz. Detecting these waves would provide crucial information about neutrino masses and other unknown parameters. Furthermore, these massive phase transitions lead to gravitational instabilities in the universe's early phase transition, ultimately forming primordial black holes.

A novel approach to achieving efficient and reliable communication in a complex world is presented, which combines signaling games and counterfactual reasoning in a real-time decision process. This approach leads to the development of a cooperative framework for compressing data, in which a neural agent and a symbolic planner exchange simplified information to make accurate decisions about system states. A key component of this framework is a new interface that allows the integration of neural networks and symbolic planners, which we have used to design a shared protocol for communication. This protocol allows both agents to infer the characteristics of data from partial observations and to coordinate their actions in real-time, which we have used to demonstrate cooperative semantic communication in a test of different states of a neural-field environment.

A novel reading assistance system is introduced for individuals who are learning to read, by automatically suggesting the next word based on the current sentence context. This current system builds upon a simplified statistical method by incorporating latent information hidden within the sentences provided so far. In contrast to a basic statistical approach that predicts the most likely single word, our hybrid model incorporates multiple words' probabilities, weighted by their hidden importance. We demonstrate an approximately 3% enhancement in accuracy when applied to the standard 1-billion word corpus.

Two-stage session-based recommendation models have demonstrated superior ability in handling sequential user interactions for next-item prediction. To mitigate the limitations of these models in capturing a broader range of user items, we propose an enhanced approach incorporating candidate item rank embeddings. By integrating this technique into both user session representation and next-item prediction, we increase the diversity of recommended items while maintaining high relevance. Additionally, we introduce an attention-based mechanism for session-based users not found in the current interaction context. Extensive experiments on three public datasets confirm the efficacy of our method in improving recommendation sessions, next-item prediction, and user exposure diversity.

We have developed a theoretical framework for analyzing active colloidal molecules composed of multiple beads, focusing on cases where one bead exhibits activity while其余 beads are inert. Through simulations based on a Stokes dynamics model, we demonstrated that molecules with one activity gradient form them. Specifically, molecules with activity gradients form self. Furthermore, we developed a theoretical model for their dynamics, which can their activity orientation. Furthermore, we employed a holonomic colloid molecule as a model system to their activity orientation. Furthermore, we employed a model system to their activity orientation.

A thorough approach is developed to simulate single-phase flow in fractured porous media. The method combines a discrete fracture network with a continuous domain using an unstructured mesh, allowing for a seamless integration of the two. Transport within the discrete fracture matrix system is governed by a mixed interface condition. Due to a significant difference in permeability between the network and the surrounding medium, traditional numerical techniques may become inefficient or inaccurate. A previously established numerical technique, Mimetic Finite Difference (MFD), is modified to efficiently handle such discrepancies in permeability while maintaining high order of convergence and parameter robustness. The proposed framework involves several key steps. Initially, a mesh is generated for a given geological formation and then an appropriate discontinuous permeability matrix is defined. Subsequent mesh conforming and associated geological parameters are defined. Finally, transport and pressure equations are solved using a system of linear equations. The technique's effectiveness is demonstrated through various test cases involving complex fracture networks and a fracture plane within a continuous domain.

A new approach using autonomous drones is proposed to create and maintain a designated area for safe air transport, similar to a closed lane on the ground. Each drone flies at a set height and works as part of a team to achieve a common goal of providing this closed space for regular flights. Each drone acts as a leader for its group, and there is a hierarchy in place to ensure smooth operation. This approach relies on the creation of a closed space by the drones and a path planning system that avoids collisions. The effectiveness of this approach has been demonstrated through both computer simulations and a real-world test with two connected drones.

This research explores various spectral characteristics of the Seidel matrix associated with a connected chain graph, demonstrating that $-1$ is always an eigenvalue, while other eigenvalues may have a multiplicity of at most two, given that the vertex count is $n \ge 3$, resulting in a multiplicity of $2$ for eigenvalue $-n+1$. We also establish an upper bound for the Seidel energy of a chain graph with order $n$, given by the formula $2\sum_{i=2}^{m+1}| \lambda_i(G) | + |\lambda_1(G)|$. We identify a upper bound on Seidel energy by determining the graph with a minimum number of non-trivial Seidel eigenvalues, given a specified vertex count $n$, given as $E_S \le 2\sum_{i=2}^{m+1}| \lambda_i(G) | + |\lambda_1(G)|$.

In our investigation, we focus on a class of mean-field stochastic control problems that involve control of delay-differential equations with a fractional derivative. These equations are driven by a mean of a Brownian fractional noise and the a posteriori average state evaluated at a past time. To address the challenges posed by the variable a posteriori average state and the user average, we make use of it as an additional control variable, thereby enabling the application of stochastic calculus for a priori and conditional processes for delay-differential equations. These tools, combined with an appropriate extension of the classical necessary and sufficient conditions in a mean-field context, enable us to derive a general solution to the mean-field optimal control problem that is driven by a fractional Brownian motion.

We've developed a unique, detailed algorithm to create all non-trivial, periodic solutions with monotonic properties for the non-self-adjoint Dirac operator equations. These solutions, known as elliptic finite-band potentials, correspond to positive, non-trivial $4\times4$ Hermitian periodic Laplace spectrum operators. Our approach, based on the inverse scattering theory for non-self-adjoint Dirac operator spectra, involves solving specific telescopic $2\times2$ operator differential equations within a defined framework.

RSU deployment in vehicular networks has been shown to boost the data rate but also increases implementation costs. Utilizing vehicle relays to forward traffic can alleviate some of this expense while maintaining the benefits provided by RSUs. However, utilizing vehicle relays also introduces new challenges to the network. Our research focuses on a UTIS approach that employs RSUs, vehicle relays, and wireless access points to optimize a multi-hop VANET environment. We develop a Markov chain model that allows for detailed analysis of the proposed framework, subsequently deriving key performance metrics, including throughput, delay, and packet loss. Utilizing the obtained statistics, we create a closed-form expression for the RSU deployment count that maximizes throughput. Furthermore, a simulation-based comparison of our model with an existing method demonstrates the benefits of the proposed approach in enhancing overall network performance.

Wikipedia's principle of welcoming contributions from everyone, including unwary contributors, leads to a vast array of articles, albeit some may not meet the platform's high standards for accuracy and completeness. As a freely editable encyclopedia, Wikipedia relies on a community-driven approach to ensure its reliability, with active contributors focusing on enhancing the quality of articles through continuous improvement. This study examines the self-correcting nature of Wikipedia's community-editing process, analyzing the self-labeling of content quality through established patterns in contributor behavior. By employing a logistic regression model, the research identifies the most influential factors in self-assessed article quality, considering the temporal dynamics of editing behaviors. The results demonstrate a strong correlation between contributor behavior and content quality, with the model accurately predicting labels for a substantial number of articles. This research contributes to the understanding of self-organization within complex adaptive systems, with implications for Wikipedia's content quality assessment.

Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a lightweight student model to mimic the behavior of a larger, more complex teacher model. However, this technique typically relies on access to the teacher's source code or trained weights, which may not always be available. We present a new approach that overcomes this limitation by allowing a student model to learn from an unmodified, black-box teacher model without accessing its internal parameters. The proposed method trains the student to replicate the teacher's output labels only for input data that the teacher is uncertain about, while also leveraging unlabeled data. Additionally, this approach decision-based black-box model. Experimental results on the CIFAR-100 dataset demonstrate that the new approach achieves comparable accuracy to full knowledge distillation but with significantly lower query counts, making it a highly efficient alternative.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_S$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_S$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.000 $\text{TeV}^{-1}$ luminosity dataset collected by the LHCb experiment. The branching fractions for these decays were found to be $7.0^{+1.3}_{-1.0}\times 10^{-4}$ and $3.1^{+0.9}_{-1.0}\times 10^{-4}$ respectively, and were obtained after accounting for several correction factors including detector efficiency, reconstruction efficiency, resonance fraction, $B^0_s$ branching fraction, and detection efficiency ratios. The $B^0_s$ abundance relative to $B^0$ was determined to be $14.14\pm0.14$ and was found to be consistent with prior expectations.

The standard torus can be seen as the simplest instance of a twisted torus, known as the trivial type. A generalised torus is characterised by a specific algebraic data set, comprising a pair of matrices. In particular, a pair of integer matrices defines a character variety associated with a twisted torus of type $\mathbb{Z}^{2} \ltimes \mathbb{Z}^{2}$. This variety is expressed in terms of Abelian Jacobians, defined by divisor matrices. It is demonstrated that a specific form of T-duality exists, allowing variable exchange in a character variety defined by a pair of matrices $A$ and $B$, where both have invertible inverses modulo each other's determinant. This concept can be extended to twisted tori of higher dimensions, defined by more complex algebraic structures, defined either by a C^{\infty}-homotopy associative $C^{\ast}$-algebra or a Lie superalgebra, which also have well-defined moduli spaces.

Reinforcement learning's effectiveness heavily relies on well-established expert knowledge in many fields.  A more efficient approach to mastering tasks exists, known as co-imitation learning (CIL), which involves two agents collaborating to learn from each other without direct expert interaction.  Despite its potential, CIL has been challenging to implement due to issues like free exploration and vanishing values.  In this paper, a new method is proposed to overcome these obstacles and enhance the learning process.  The proposed approach leverages a two-agent setup, allowing both agents to contribute equally to each other's learning through an alternating policy optimization technique, resulting in improved performance and robustness even when one agent has a performance advantage.  Experimental validations confirm the efficacy of the new method in a variety of interactive tasks conducted within both simulated and real-world environments.

Plackett-Luce models are widely used to analyze and compare rankings. Recent research has introduced PAC distributions as a statistical model for these rankings. Building on this development, we examined the characteristics of PAC distributions, derived estimation techniques, and statistical tests for comparing PAC models based on ranking data. Notably, the non-metric nature of ranking data presents significant challenges for estimation, which we addressed by constructing a new metric and developing an efficient maximum likelihood estimation algorithm. Through simulations and real-world data analysis, the proposed PAC models demonstrated promising comparative results.

A new approach to simultaneous hand tracking and object reconstruction using point cloud data is presented. By using an end-to-end trainable deep model, tracked key palm points serve as input to an implicit model for following objects within a hand's grasp. The model's success in a challenging dataset combining successful and failed grasps highlights its utility in designing improved multi-sensor hand tracking systems.

This study employs the modular reduction technique to a Coxeter group of rank 4 featuring a star diagram with 5, 3, and k= 3, 4, 5, or 6 labels, using the odd primes from the ring Z[tau], where tau represents the golden ratio. It categorizes each reduced group as a reflection group over a finite field and demonstrates that the reduced group retains its properties regardless of the used prime in the reduction process.

A novel, markerless extrinsic calibration and pose estimation system has been developed using a depth-sensing End-Effector with a built-in camera. Our innovative approach leverages a neural network-based depth extrinsic calibration and end-effector pose estimation, eliminating the need for physical cameras on robots. Our system relies on a training dataset of end-effector poses and uses a loss function to optimize the parameters of a point cloud transformation. These parameters enable the accurate transformation of end-effector pose data into a unified coordinate system, resulting in high extrinsic calibration and end-effector pose estimation accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed system, with an average extrinsic calibration error of 0.9 cm and an average end-effector pose error of 0.07 for rotation and 0.03 for translation. Additionally, our system has been validated using real-world data and has shown robustness against varying distances and lighting conditions.

A new approach is presented for identifying and analyzing treatment interference in research. Interference occurs when one treatment recipient affects multiple other individuals. Traditional research methods are insufficient for this situation as they are designed for isolated treatments. The proposed framework involves two key components: a model describing treatment interactions and a hypothesis to check for specific patterns of interference. The initial component assumes that each unit interacts with its closest neighbors up to a certain threshold (K) to determine treatment effects. The second aspect seeks to confirm or reject this threshold (K) based on data. The primary research question is whether the observed data supports units interacting only with its closest neighbors up to a certain threshold (K) over others. The proposed solution utilizes the Mann-Whitney approach to estimate the interference distance metric and establish confidence intervals. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations as well as real-world experiments involving magnetite dosage in East Germany schools.

Calculating neutrino emissions from self-annihilating Dark Matter within a star is complex, mainly due to an unknown location of the process within the star. This position influences both the efficiency of the particles converting into neutrinos and where the neutrinos are emitted, which in turn affects their ability to escape the star. This study focuses on new interactions between the Dark Matter and electrons, specifically through a theoretical model called the derivative interaction, which is consistent with an alternative theoretical framework known as the Standard Model Extension. This interaction has its own characteristics, allowing for an improved understanding of the emission process. A calculation of neutrino emissions from Dark Matter annihilation in a star, which takes into account the new physics and stellar structure, reveals that these emissions can be significantly amplified compared to previous predictions. This increased sensitivity to the new physics may be within the reach of a neutrino telescope like Hyper-Kamiokande.

The ongoing UNIONS/CFIS project utilizes the VLT/MUSE instrument to conduct a comprehensive weak gravitational lensing survey targeting Unclustered Galaxies at redshifts between 0.6 and 1.0. A new pipeline, referred to as ShapePipe, has been developed to perform precise shape measurements for galaxies in the UNIONS dataset. By applying ShapePipe's lensing flags to filter out inaccurate shape measurements, the shear bias in the final dataset is significantly reduced to less than 0.003. A preliminary mass calibration using ShapePipe-reconstructed images reveals a residual mass calibration offset of approximately 0.5 percent. Although ShapePipe demonstrates the potential for conducting cosmological measurements, its current performance primarily makes it suitable for accurate mass calibration in current and future large-scale cosmographic simulations. Additionally, ShapePipe's capabilities enable the study of the evolution of galaxy structure over time.

A notable finding from the 1940s by Weyl and Kronecker demonstrated that certain nonlinear functions, such as square roots, are more effective than linear functions in determining which rational approximations best describe irrational numbers. Our research introduces additional equidistribution findings based on wronskians and higher-order derivative functions derived from irrational numbers or transcendental numbers. Using these discoveries from differential theory, we establish alternative, non-differential methods to traditional arithmetic approaches for solving complex diagonal approximation challenges. Furthermore, our findings have significant implications for a critical yet unsolved problem concerning whether rational approximations can be effectively generated through equidistribution.

We prove that for k-rational singularities of local complete intersections, k-Du Bois classification applies. For hypersurfaces, k-rationality can be determined based on the minimal exponent. Moreover, certain local vanishing properties for k-rational and k-Du Bois singularities have been identified. These properties were also discovered separately by [FL2].

Adding a gauge symmetry to the Standard Model can create a potential source of dark matter in the form of an axion. This axisymmetric property is typically assumed to be dark, but adding a gauge symmetry can cause rapid flavor oscillations between electron and quark neutrinos and sterile neutrinos. The presence of these active and sterile neutrinos disrupts the axisymmetric behavior, causing the dark matter field to oscillate rapidly between these neutrino flavors. The solution to maintaining darkness is provided by a two-field dark matter system consisting of an axion and a sterile neutrino that originate from a $Z_2$ gauge symmetry. The axion's coupling to photons allows it to be produced through misalignment, while the sterile neutrino is created via "freeze-in" from the decays of the axion and heavy neutrinos. The axion's coupling to photons is also amplified by loop effects from charged particles, including both active and sterile neutrinos. The effectiveness of this model lies in its ability to produce the observed dark matter solely through the axion and sterile neutrino, without the need for additional assumptions. The model's parameters are determined by two key factors: a decay constant and a mass for the heavy neutrino. The model's features are explored using a combination of effective and exact solutions, as well as an approximate analysis in three regimes. The model's features are compared to those of a related model based on a $Z_2$ symmetry between two sterile neutrinos. The

This study improves knowledge of how much it costs to break down magic states into basic components that allow full classical computation when combined with them. Our research shows that any magic state of the form $|\psi\rangle = \cos\theta |0\rangle + \sin\theta |1\rangle$, where the square of the sine of the angle is greater than the square of the cosine of the angle, can be expressed as a superposition of at most $d$ computational basis states, where $d$ is upper bounded by $\frac{\sqrt{2}\sin\theta + (1+\sqrt{2})\cos\theta}{\cos\theta - \sin\theta \sqrt{1-\theta^2}}$. Our analysis also reveals that this upper limit can be as low as $2^{\log_2\delta/\log_2 n}$, where $\delta$ is the fraction of the magic state that we want to approximate within the infinity norm, and $\delta$ is greater than the magic state's critical point of $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$. This research significantly improves upon the previous upper bound of $\delta^{-2}$, and we also provide a lower limit on the cost of breaking down magic states, showing the cost is at least $\log_2\delta$, where the cost of breaking down magic states is denoted by $r(\delta)$. This research employs the Tsallis holographic dark energy model in two scenarios, 
non-interacting and interacting with a quantum field. 
We commence by examining the non-interacting case, where a complex form of 
holographic dark energy is examined for its evolution in the state equation of 
quintessence. 
Subsequently, a derivative coupling is introduced to explore the interaction 
between the energy density of Tsallis and the scalar field, 
resulting in the derivation of constraints for the state equation parameter and 
the derivative coupling constant. 
By incorporating observational constraints from Planck, 
redshift, and gamma-ray burst data, we obtain numerical values for these 
parameters, 
demonstrating an expanding universe with a decreasing rate. 
Furthermore, analysis of the state equation reveals a universe transitioning 
from acceleration to deceleration. 
We also investigate the energy conditions and find that 
holographic dark energy fails to satisfy the weak energy condition, 
while the strong and null energy conditions are violated. 
A phase diagram is drawn based on holographic dark energy, 
revealing a non-interacting universe transitioning from an accelerating 
decelerated phase. 
However, interaction with the quintessence field alters this phase diagram, 
resulting in a non-interacting quessence.

Between 2018 and 2019, the LAMOST project conducted a large-scale survey on key galactic planes using four $K$2 plates. This data collection, consisting of 1.4 billion frames, yielded 27.7 million unique objects after processing. Out of these objects, 7.7 million unique sources were identified as variable stars across various categories including AGN, M dwarfs, and objects showing multiple states. The researchers discovered notable patterns in variable stars across different galactic planes, characterized by distinct properties such as variability duration, amplitude, and color. The observed features varied significantly among the four plates, suggesting diverse types of variable stars present. The data collection has also revealed several highly variable AGNs with amplitudes exceeding 3 magnitudes. The LAMOST project's first results have provided valuable insights into various astrophysical phenomena across different sky regions, paving the way for significant future contributions.

In recent years, the SRAM-based True Random Number Generator (SRAM TRNG) has gained significant adoption due to the ease of incorporating it into chips for producing random numbers. A key component of SRNG TRNGs is monitoring the supply voltage to confirm if the generated numbers meet quality standards. To improve upon current methods, which are either impractical on-chip or consume excessive area, a new solution called TuRaN is proposed. This solution uses supply voltage underscaling to create an SRAM TRNG with efficient in-chip health checking that only checks the most critical parameters. As a result, supply voltage monitoring circuitry can be miniaturized, leading to better performance with lower area and power consumption. With simulation results demonstrating excellent reliability and passing industry-standard tests, as well as results from multiple process nodes showing strong performance, TuRaN has the potential to be a game-changer in SRAM TRNG design.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules of $NR_1N^+_R_2$ type, where $R_1$ and $R_2$ denote terminating groups. By integrating molecular resistors into a mesoscopic single-electron circuit, we found that molecular devices can effectively serve as single-electron resistors in such circuits. Furthermore, we observed that certain molecular resistors can induce a quantized resistive switching effect within single-electron capacitors. It was also shown that introducing a linear molecular tunnel barrier led to a quantum resistive switch exhibiting nonvolatile behavior, where the resistive state could be retained even in the absence of an external voltage. By adjusting the molecular structure, we were able to tune the voltage thresholds for switching between the resistive and conductive states.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically calculating complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an alternative to traditional methods. By converting loop integrands into a form where only the desired kinematic regions are identified, this method simplifies the integration process. To enhance this approach, we introduce a causal representation for general scalar Feynman graph functions. Utilizing the Heavisman contour and a set of causal conditions, we express these functions in terms of their on-shell graph components. As a result, the causal representation matches loop-amplitude numerics with loop-integral numerics, providing an exact equivalent. We demonstrate the practical application of this representation in obtaining higher-order loop corrections by applying a Laplace transform to the mass-uniqueness theorem. This method yields finite results at any order of expansion in epsilon and enables an efficient numerical evaluation of multi-loop Feynman integrands. We evaluate the performance of this technique by calculating two- and three-loop box functions for various topologies and kinematic settings. We propose a new numerical approach to evaluate general scalar Feynman integrals, termed numerical causal representation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by accurately calculating two- and three-loop functions for various topologies within milliseconds.

A novel approach to one-dimensional quantum walks with two states is presented, utilizing a complex-valued St\"{u}rmer-Liouville theory to derive a comprehensive eigenfunction expansion formula for two-state walks. By redefining a one-component function and associated measure from the given two-state vector, we translate the two-state discrete quantum walk into a one-component expansion problem. This method effectively bypasses the non-self-adjoint nature of the original two-state system, offering an alternative to traditional techniques like transfer matrices or ansatz-based approaches.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles, taking into account the influence of electrons and a third-type neutrino on structural properties. By combining a model with static quarks and another accounting for the pairing effect between quarks, we simulate a phase transition from a pure neutron star to a hybrid star containing a quark matter core. Core mass limits for such stars, particularly those with 1.5 and 2 solar masses, are established. It is observed that hybrid stars can support masses equivalent to 1.5 and 2 solar masses at specific density thresholds, which also indicate the onset of deconfinement within their cores. Notably, we found that the compactness of hybrid stars exhibits a significant decrease as mass increases, in contrast to conventional neutron stars. Additionally, we determined that hybrid stars containing such a core typically have softer equations of state, resulting in smaller radii compared to their non-hybrid counterparts. It is interesting to note that pure neutron stars generally possess larger radii, and thus, we suggest that future gravitational wave observations, specifically from binary neutron star mergers, could be used to distinguish between models predicting their existence.

The paper examines the optical properties of the $q$-deformed optomechanical system under the presence of non-linear interaction. By analyzing the system's density matrix elements, it is found that the photonic population exhibits an oscillating behavior in relation to time. This relationship is also affected by $q$-deformation parameters. Notably, the system demonstrates delayed light emission, which is influenced by mechanical damping. This occurrence is evident when the mechanical damping is high. Additionally, the phasor model is used to explain this phenomenon. By tuning the $q$-deformation parameter, the system delays light emission. This parameter has a direct impact on transparency windows, as increasing its value leads to fewer and narrower transparency windows. This parameter also affects the refractive index, as its increase leads to an increment in the imaginary part of the refractive index. This result holds for both delayed and fast light scenarios.

In a recent theoretical investigation, we have examined the application of the Two-Rotors Model to describe R-parity broken states, particularly those involving scalar and magnetic components. The model's successful implementation has been confirmed through confrontation with experimental data from several isotopes, including $^{192}$Os and $^{194}$Os. The research also investigated R-parity broken states in Rigid Rotor models and found that certain features, such negative scissors modes, cannot be accounted for within this framework.

In ultrathin films made of transition-metal oxones bonded to a single atom, extraordinary magnetic properties can arise due to extreme dimensional reduction, which significantly impacts local magnetism and the unusual behavior of carriers within these materials. To understand the extraordinary magnetic states at these interfaces, our theoretical investigations into spin and orbital fluctuations have been carried out using a generalized Hubbard model that accounts for local correlations of spins and orbital order. By examining the effects of energy level shifts and crystal-field splittings within our model, we identified a diverse range of magnetic states and their connections to carrier activity. To further refine our theoretical framework, we applied quantum dynamical-mean-field theory, which enabled us to develop a quantitative connection between macroscopic magnetic states and underlying microscopic parameters. The resulting classification of possible magnetic states provides a valuable tool for interpreting experimental data, which we then used to analyze the magnetism in ultrathin oxide films experimentally.

In the last few years, the distribution patterns of laser-cooled atoms within and between dissipated optical lattices have been extensively studied. We present a new distribution pattern of cold atoms in a dissipated lattice setup, demonstrating how a zero-temperature system in the absence of cooling and optical pumping results in a unique distribution pattern, exemplified by the inverse Gaussian distribution. We are also able to experimentally verify the occurrence of a negative binomial distribution, as well as accurately quantify the degree of correlation between atoms, by collecting and sorting single-shot distribution data.

A cryptocurrency trading network was analyzed using an information propagation model based on data from 10 major exchanges. The study revealed a significant increase in the network size over the observation period and observed the formation of prominent communities within it. All major communities were found to be interconnected through high-order connections. An overall correlation network based on cryptocurrency prices was also studied and found to exhibit characteristics of a complex network. Specifically, the network exhibited positive correlations dominating over long durations and a power-law distribution of node degrees. The communities identified in this network exhibited a HUB node in each, with one notable community characterized by a super-HUB node. However, it was discovered that this HUB node relied on a single exchange, leading to its removal causing the community to collapse.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial process that significantly influences the formation of cloud condensation nuclei, a crucial component in predicting climate change. Understanding how particles form and develop requires an accurate representation of the behavior of its component molecules, especially their inherent motion even at absolute zero temperature. This study examines the impact of zero-point motion on the behavior of molecular clusters consisting of sulphuric acid and water molecules using high-precision simulations. The simulations reveal that considering zero-point motion increases the effective binding energy of these clusters and shifts their temperature-dependent stability thresholds to lower temperatures. These findings suggest that accounting for intrinsic motion is crucial for modeling the initial stages of particle formation.

We establish the definitions for a compact perception pair (X,Q) and space (G,X,Q), utilizing these to show the existence of compact subsets within the spaces of non-expansive group equivariant operators (from Q to Q along with an action on Q) and non-expansive compact operators, respectively. The solution involves constructing upper semicontinuous multivalued maps between compact sets, which are then used to define the spaces in question, ultimately allowing for the demonstration of their compactness. The solution also applies to lower semicontinuous maps, which are used to describe the spaces of non-expansive operators that preserve lower hereditary properties, compactly acting on Q. The solution also provides the descriptions of locally compact and countably compact perception pairs and spaces, which are shown to be equivalent under certain conditions.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by drawing a parallel with gravity's effect on crystal lattices. This analogy suggests that when gravity acts on the lattice, it displaces it, generating a flow. However, our research finds that horizontal differences in temperature have no direct correlation with the internal movement within the crystal structure. Instead, we discovered that a combination of temperature and gravity is required to induce movement. This finding has far-reaching implications for the theory of energy transport under the influence of gravity.

In various machine learning tasks, simplicity of learned models is crucial. A key strategy to promote model simplicity is incorporating a regularizer, like the well-known Tikhonov or Tikhonov-Gabors method. This work delves into the complexity of geometric features in neural networks and how their simplicity can be measured, ultimately showing that certain neural network properties can be influenced by regularizers in a specific way.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is introduced and applied to $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within the context of an effective Hamiltonian. This method offers distinct advantages over traditional fit-based methods, utilizing data from multiple experiments to determine the Wilson coefficients in question, specifically $C_7$, $C_{9s}$, and $C_{s'}$. By focusing on specific muon momentum ranges that exclude new physics, a fit based on only three Wilson coefficients is performed, revealing experimental evidence against new physics and indicating a $2.4\sigma$ disagreement between the Belle and LHCb experiments.

Non-native speakers of English often struggle with limited writing samples.
To enhance their language skills, it's essential to expose them to a broader range of text.
Exposing learners to varied data can also improve automated essay grading using machine learning, which historically has been effective with older NLP techniques but less so with more recent transformer models.
This study explores the impact of two forms of data augmentation on the data augmentation for transformer-based automated essay scoring, specifically looking at how it affects the scoring of essays by trained models.
Two forms of data augmentation were examined: word replacement using a thesaurus and word shifting, a technique that reorders words in sentences to maintain meaning.
When paired with the pre-trained BERT model, both types of augmented training data resulted in improved scores compared to the paired data alone, with word shifting showing the most significant improvement and no decline in performance.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals associated with these marginal independence models based on a given design matrix. Specifically, we focus on a particular class of models - marginal trees - and demonstrate a method to determine a fixed point in the interior of the corresponding cone. As an application, we show that any DAG-encoded Markov network has a unique configuration where its specified marginal distribution maximizes entropy subject to those marginals being fixed.

A higher education model is proposed, where students are assigned to colleges based on their families' socioeconomic status and their own abilities. Colleges have different mobility rates, which determine how much a student's socioeconomic status changes when they attend. A key parameter, mobility, ranges from 0 to 1 and has a direct relationship with intergenerational socioeconomic status correlation. The model considers how socioeconomic status changes over generations, where each generation is a fraction of the total population, with families of different sizes making up the whole.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, by addressing a key limitation - the inability to verify whether a sender has obtained permission from sender public keys.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made a significant breakthrough by detecting the simultaneous creation of three massive gauge bosons in high-energy proton-proton collisions at a record-breaking 13 TeV. This groundbreaking discovery was based on data collected by the CMS detector at the CERN's LHC over the course of 2016, 2017, and 2018. After carefully analyzing the results, this study presents the first observation of the simultaneous presence of three massive gauge bosons, which significantly surpasses the predicted standards set by the Standard Model. This discovery involves four distinct processes: simultaneous presence of W bosons (WWWW), one W boson along with two Z bosons (WWZZ), two W bosons along with one Z boson (WWWZ), and a process involving two W bosons along with two Z bosons (WWZZ). These processes were detected across multiple final states characterized by numerous jets and lepton signals. This study demonstrates an impressive 7-sigma significance for the process involving three W bosons, whereas the other process involving two W bosons and one Z boson shows a 6-sigma significance. These discoveries were discovered with a record-breaking 59 inverse femtobarns of data, significantly surpassing previous expectations set by the Standard Model. This discovery also includes the most precise measurement to date of the cross-section values for these rare processes, which were found to significantly differ from previous standards set by theoretical models.

Previous iterations of the widely-used Universal Dependencies paradigm for unsupervised morphosyntactic parsing have been tested on older versions of the Hebrew language. A more recent, manually-created corpus of modern Hebrew has now been developed for the same purpose, providing an alternative to previously-established resources. This new corpus has been analyzed to explore how it compares to the existing manual annotations of other resources and to explore the effectiveness of different methods for automatically parsing morphosyntactic relationships. Results indicate that a specific type of neural network is outperforms other methods in the corpus. Further findings also reveal that the current manual annotations overestimate the capabilities of some parts of speech in Hebrew.

We have two new concepts, the ε-Frechet dimension of a set and the ε-isometric dimension, for a set within a specific range of values. For sets that have incompressible subsets in the set S_{p}, where 1 < p < 2 and the compression exponent is less than one, it is demonstrated that the ε-isometric dimension of such a subset is equal to the real number 1/p divided by the compression exponent. In addition, it is proved that any subset of S_{p} that is incompressible has infinite Fredrich dimension when p < 2 and the compression exponent is strictly less than one half.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial intelligence have led to the rapid growth of data-driven modeling techniques in theoretical physics. However, these models are typically developed through two-step processes: a network is trained on raw data, and its hyperparameters are optimized to achieve the best results. As a consequence, each model is created in isolation, with no collaborative element. Our research aims to address these limitations by introducing a novel approach to data-driven modeling. We propose a framework where multiple AI networks are generated and refined in a cooperative environment. Through our work, we demonstrate the feasibility of this idea by applying it to the estimation of a fundamental constant in the theory of quantum chromodynamics. Our findings are based on training the networks with parameters obtained from our internal optimization process, and we compare the method to traditional, standalone modeling approaches.

Current research on degree-degree correlated LDPC codes has primarily focused on finite block length scenarios, often assuming specific finite distributions for degree degrees, which limits the applicability and efficiency of such codes. In contrast, our work investigates the effects of degree-degree correlation on LDPC performance at infinite block length with arbitrary distributions for degree degrees, allowing for the possibility of correlation. We develop a novel ensemble of degree-degree correlated LDPC ensembles and create a density evolution algorithm to analyze their behavior. Our findings indicate that increasing variance in degree distributions enhances the LDPC performance, while degree-degree correlation can actually decrease performance under certain conditions. Based on our research, we propose an LDPC ensemble that optimizes performance by eliminating degree-degree correlation, verify our findings with simulated results, and suggest practical applications of such codes.

An advanced modular system, which is known as a safety filter, has been designed to adjust a robot's movements and keep it safe from obstacles without changing its original motion plan. Traditional safety filters use local information about a robot's surroundings, but a new predictive safety filter was created that can assess a robot's overall safety and find the most effective way to change its movements. This novel predictive safety filter uses an advanced optimization technique called System Level Synthesis to create and test many safety options for a robot's movements in advance, which allows it to run faster and be more efficient. The performance of this new filter was tested on a self-driving car and a real-world drone, and it outperformed other safety filters in most cases.

A new class of attacks has been developed that targets the security of quantum key distribution systems based on the decoy state method. A recent study demonstrated an attack involving the partial phase randomization of signal states that increased key generation rates above acceptable thresholds. Building upon this discovery, a more potent attack has been devised by optimizing various attack parameters and devising strategies to bypass the monitoring device's error rate constraints. The success of this attack has been verified through simulations using a real-world QKD system and it has been shown to achieve near-perfect error-free counts while outperforming earlier attacks in terms of key generation rate. The attack can also be adapted to decoy state QKD systems employing Gaussian modulation. The findings highlight the vulnerability of real-world QKD systems to entangle-and-reattack strategies combining efficient pair generation with partial phase randomization.

Recent studies have demonstrated the capability of large language models to learn and apply various tasks without explicit training. The underlying mechanism driving this 'in-context' learning in transformers remains unclear, particularly the influence of their pretraining on the model's ability to learn tasks during inference. This research aims to address the following inquiries: Firstly, does a language model's pretraining affect its 'in-context' learning performance? Secondly, can tasks be mastered through 'in-context' learning even if they were not included in the model's pretraining? The study provides experimental evidence to answer these questions and offers the following key findings: Firstly, tasks can be mastered through 'in-context' learning, even if they were not part of the model's pretraining. However, this capability is contingent upon the model's pretraining, with significant variations observed across different pretraining types. The study's results can be attributed to two potential factors: language similarity and representation similarity. The study's pretraining corpus has a significant impact on both of these mechanisms. Galaxy cluster observations reveal that the central areas of these galaxy clusters are home to an equal number of clouds as the rest of the galaxy cluster itself, the presence of which remains unexplained. To investigate the origins of these clouds, we conducted numerical simulations incorporating various physical processes including field strengths of 0.1-10 Gauss, conduction effects, and a detailed analysis of cloud dynamics over periods of 100 million years. When undamaged by radiation, undelivered clouds collapse and break up, the best scenario for survival involves weakened fields of 0.1 Gauss and compensated losses between radiation and heat loss, the presence of which is required for undelivered clouds to survive over long periods of time. However, undelivered clouds still break up and disappear, the best scenario for survival involves weakened fields of 0.1 Gauss and absent turbulence, the presence of which is required for survival of undelivered clouds. To understand the dynamics of undelivered clouds in galaxy cluster environments, we developed a simplified model to predict cloud survival and identified conditions under which undelivered clouds can survive and grow, the presence of which is required for survival of undelivered clouds. Our results show that undelivered clouds can survive and possibly form the observed structures in galaxy cluster observations when weakened fields of 0.1 Gauss and absent turbulence, the presence of which is required for survival of undelivered clouds.

The study of the weak interaction's CP violation in beauty and charm will be
discussed, focusing on experimental outcomes obtained from B-factories, B-factory collaborations, and Tevatron in their respective $\overline{B}$d $e^- \nu_e$ and $D^0$ particle decays. The relevant theoretical underpinnings and the Standard Model's predictions for these interactions are also examined. The presentation begins with an overview of flavor physics fundamentals, the CKM matrix, and flavor observables. It then delves into beauty particle observations, including particle production rates and leptonic, semileptonic, and hadronic decays. A comprehensive examination of charm particle production rates and subsequent decays is also provided. The discussion culminates in an exploration of direct and indirect CP violation in beauty and charm particles.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes have unique properties, such as a specific relationship between n-point amplitudes and their lower-dimensional counterparts. Their mathematical expressions reveal an underlying pattern, suggesting a broader theory at play. This discovery validates and expands previous theories about fermionic interactions, while also revealing new relationships between bosonic and fermionic scattering amplitudes. These results have far-reaching implications for understanding the fundamental nature of open superstring theory.

To effectively manage the growing number of 5G devices, a Core Network (CN) solution is required to streamline operations and minimize manual intervention. The CN plays a crucial role in optimizing resource allocation and ensuring cost efficiency by enabling automated management procedures. By incorporating intelligent cost management strategies, the CN can facilitate dynamic resource allocation based on real-time needs and Market Domain requirements. As a key component of Self-Organizing Networks (SON), the CN helps maintain 5G network stability by facilitating resource reallocation and real-time cost effectiveness.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a speech synthesis technique that operates without any speech samples.  The underlying concept of unit selection synthesis was initially applied to music synthesis in zero-shot conditions.  The technique is then transferred to non-musical conditions. A zero-speech synthesis approach is developed by transforming transcripts of an open-access music dataset into acoustic units based on a model trained on speech data.  The acoustic units are used to train a text-to-speech model that selects the most suitable sequence to reproduce a target sound, based on a dataset consisting of music and voice samples.  The effectiveness of this technique is evaluated using the Mozilla Tims speech evaluation task using a dataset of speech and music samples.  The evaluation results show that the speech produced through unit selection using acoustic units based on speech music appears to be more natural than the speech generated using a text-based model fine-tuned on the same speech sample.

Optimizing motion planning in multiple dimensions often involves non-convex problems, which are challenging to solve due to their computational complexity. To address this issue, a novel multi-stage optimization framework coupled with an data-driven McCormick envelope technique has been introduced. Multiple nonlinear optimization problems are interconnected by shared variables, with each stage utilizing learned relaxation techniques to balance computational efficiency and planning performance. Through simulations on diverse environments, this method outperforms traditional approaches in multiple dimensions.

We have developed a comprehensive set of rules that define the probability of one quantum state being transformed into another through a specific type of quantum operation. This rule set includes conditions that are both necessary and, in isolation, met by certain classes of quantum states. However, for all quantum states, it is not isolating. By removing a specific constraint related to distinguishability, a relevant subset of these rules is obtained, which is not isolating but was previously determined to be sufficiently accurate to fully characterize a specific type of quantum operation. This leads to the discovery of two distinct categories of quantum states for which the removed constraint is the key determinant in whether one state can be transformed into another with the same probability.

We investigated the dynamic behavior of a cup of coffee being carried while in motion, by applying a lumped model that combines the effects of the liquid and the cup. This allows us to see the liquid's motion, which has been broken down into two distinct parts - a high-frequency vibration and a slower-moving component, whose amplitude can be controlled by the rate of oscillation. It has been observed that the peak amplitude of this slower-moving part can be significantly higher than the peak amplitude of the faster-moving part, which can be explained by treating the liquid like a pendulum in a state of resonance. This phenomenon was also linked to historical examples of similar behavior in other systems.

In our research, we address the problem of a regularized distributionally robust learning task in a graph setting, where multiple interconnected agents collaborate to find a robust solution without sharing sensitive data. To tackle non-convex and smooth loss functions under robust optimization constraints, we develop a new decentralized learning algorithm based on the augmented Lagrangian method and proximal operator. Under specific conditions, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithm converges to a solution within a small epsilon of the optimal value. Through theoretical and experimental results, we show that our method outperforms existing distributed approaches in various graph-based machine learning problems.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy states and the number of produced particles in high-energy collisions. By combining this with an in-depth analysis of how energy is distributed and transferred, we obtain a universal equation describing the dependence of the number of produced particles, the entropy generated, and the volume of the system on the time elapsed and the time it takes for the system to thermalize. As a result, our findings demonstrate that the yield of particles produced in these collisions is universally proportional to the initial energy stored in the system raised to the power of one divided by four.

Using data from the ALMA telescope, we studied the gas dynamics surrounding the forming protostar IRAS 00466-3532. This research revealed that the area around the protostar is shaped like an 'hourglass' due to the combined effects of the protostar's wind and two opposing jets, labeled Jet A and Jet B. Jet A has a distance of 148 astronomical units and a speed of 10 kilometers per second, whereas Jet B is 75 astronomical units away and moves at only 3 kilometers per second. Simulation results indicate that the protostar's wind has a significant impact on the area around 50 astronomical units, causing the speed of Jet A to drop to 3 kilometers per second, while the protostar's wind has little impact on Jet B even at 148 astronomical units. This suggests that the high speed of Jet A is likely not the primary cause of the low velocity of the other jet.

This study focuses on enhancing the robustness of nonlinear systems with constraints, 
specifically robust constraint management. The proposed approach utilizes an outer-inner loop architecture, 
where the outer loop regulates the system's aggressiveness and the inner loop ensures its stability. 
A nonlinear model predictive controller is employed for the outer loop, employing an inverse dynamics technique 
to generate a reference trajectory, and an integrator is incorporated in the inner loop to handle model discrepancies. 
The suggested strategy is demonstrated through two robust constrained nonlinear examples.

This research project focuses on offering precise analytical approximations for various analytical solutions for several key orbital elements connected to the Fatio-Wollaston lines and also provides a crucial argument supporting the necessity of implementing second-order J2 analytical solutions for long-term orbit predictions for large solar-powered satellites. The study also examines how these effects cause secular resonances in the sky for specific elements.

We suggest a method based on first-principles theory to develop the spin orbit coupling Hamiltonian within a tight binding framework. Our approach is non-local and maintains gauge invariance. The methodology is demonstrated using gauge invariant numerical examples. Furthermore, the method is applied to simulate a tight binding model for a non-centrosymmetric material. This simulation allows us to calculate the spin polarization properties relevant to the spin Hall effect. This technique can be generally applied to tight binding models derived from more comprehensive ab initio methods to incorporate various parts of the kinetic energy operator.

In a world full of diverse objects, understanding an object's appearance can be both challenging and complicated. This is particularly true in scenarios where an object is seen from multiple angles or in different states. This paper focuses on an advanced form of object perception, where an algorithm is required to identify and locate a specific object in an image or point cloud without prior knowledge of which object it is. This is achieved by leveraging large datasets of objects and focusing on their essential features, known as semantic keypoints. Once an object is found, the next step is to determine its position and form, even if some parts are hidden or damaged. This is especially important in scenarios where an object is seen from an angle that hides some of its features. This paper presents two methods for solving these problems, with the first being an optimized approach that uses a database of objects and their likely positions and shapes. The second being a method for shaping 3D objects from a limited set of viewpoints, even in scenarios with occlusions or damage. Both methods have been tested and shown to be effective in a variety of applications, with the first being used for locating objects in 2D images and the second for shaping objects from 2D images or three-dimensional cloud data.

We develop a profile likelihood for estimating a probability distribution, focusing on the Cauchy distribution, and derive a profile likelihood estimator using a distribution-based approach. This method yields a profile likelihood estimate that solves a specific equation, for which we prove the existence and uniqueness. The estimate's properties in a local area are examined through an asymptotic analysis, which shows the profile likelihood estimator converges in distribution to a specified function of a Chi-squared distribution, and this convergence also occurs uniformly.
