The profile likelihood estimator's properties in a profile neighborhood are also examined. The profile likelihood estimator's performance is compared with other maximum likelihood estimators, including a median-based estimator, and we present "confidence discs" and "squares" for various types of estimators.

A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups under one protocol. This approach uses a Bayesian framework to determine an appropriate sample size by considering the likelihood of showing positive treatment results for the subgroups. The success of adjacent patient subgroups is believed to provide valuable information about their clinical trials. Two methods are created to calculate the required effective sample size (ESS) by first examining the likelihood of significant results in bivariate trials and then generalizing this knowledge to large sequences of clinical trials. The first design focuses on equally sized patient subsets while subsequent designs accommodate varying patient subset sizes. By incorporating uncertainty about clinical trial outcomes and potential differences between historical and current trials. This new approach demonstrates its utility through simulation, analyzing real-world oncology trials and a clinical trial recruitment study.

To improve the robustness and convergence speed of visual servo control under varying environmental conditions, an adaptive gain feedback controller is needed.  Proportional-derivative controllers have limited environmental adaptation capabilities.  The performance of a typical cascade controller for 2D/3D visual servoing can be enhanced by employing a Linear Parameter Varying (LPV) controller that uses interpolation between a set of nominal gain matrices based on a measured adaptation signal. In this paper, we develop a sequential loop-closing strategy for 2D/3D visual servoing that incorporates an LPV controller in the image space. By incorporating LPV control into the command generator and observer, we are able to improve response times and robustness. Image coordinates that are reference-dependent images signals serve as LPV scheduling variables for nominal gain matrix interpolation. The development of a theoretical framework for continuous and differentiable LPV sequential loop-closing motion control is guided by a high-performance, high-robustness requirement. A real-world experimentation on a high-precision research platform validates the proposed strategy's effectiveness.

We introduce a general registration method called Partial Recalling Network (PRNet), specifically designed for aligning partial point cloud representations with varying coverage rates. Unlike existing methods that require a complete scene or extensive memory, PRNet can handle complex scenes and extensive point clouds by replacing traditional global encoding with adaptive sampling techniques. The proposed method reconstructs a complete representation from available partial views, eliminating the need for a complete model or pre-trained knowledge. Experimental results show PRNet's superiority in handling varying coverage rates compared to other cutting-edge methods.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. In such cases, we determine the $R_\infty$-nilpotency degree of G when it comes from a generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar group, which corresponds to the smallest positive integer n such that its nth lower central series quotient is $\varphi$-$R_\infty$. Our analysis reveals that for the BS-m groups, we have the inequality $n \leq m$ and in several instances $n$ equals m. Additionally, we prove that if G is a nilpotent group with a specific series of subgroups, we have the inequality $n \leq n_2$ and the condition for $n$ to be the smallest possible value in this scenario.

Beyond the Standard Model physics in the heavy landscape could be crucial for solving its fundamental instabilities. Heavy landscape parameters might be out of reach for future colliders like the 33 TeLCLIc or 100 TeV projections. A proposed solution to this issue is to utilize precise Higgs measurements at the "Higgs factory" to determine the landscape's instability. However, this approach has its limitations, as heavy parameters affecting the Higgs are subject to large theoretical uncertainties. To overcome this issue, a heavy parameter's identification through rare collider processes could serve as an effective filter. Specifically, the rare decay $B \to X_s\gamma$ is highly sensitive to top quark parameters. The measurement of this decay at a B-factory or a B-factory upgrade can effectively distinguish between a 1-TeV and a 10-TeV cutoff, making 33 TeLCLIc or a B-factory upgrade the optimal options for this scenario.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results demonstrate that solutions obtained from experiment and advanced computer simulations can be validated by matching the electron density profile obtained from the optimization with diffraction patterns. This enables the identification of molecular structures that may be obscured by noise or limited resolution. The technique also provides a reliable way to extend findings beyond the experimental resolution. These discoveries illustrate the potential of a new optimization method to make full use of the information contained in time-sensitive data from experiments.

Lattice QCD calculations from the Fermilab/MILC collaboration are used to derive the distribution amplitudes of a specific type in an entirely data-driven manner. This type of distribution describes the internal structure of a particle known as a meson. Two types of lattice data are employed: static quark correlation functions combined with the mass of a meson and the distribution amplitudes of light-valence quark mesons. A theoretical framework called the twisted mass fermion formulation is employed to calculate these distributions at their fully non-singular values. Although these values cannot directly match certain experimental quantities due to mass differences, their shapes can be compared by removing mass dependencies. This comparison shows good agreement with results from other theoretical approaches and demonstrates the reliability of these calculations for further analysis. Additionally, these lattice data are used to calculate the distribution amplitudes of a specific meson and compare its first moment with theoretical predictions.

We establish key fairplay conditions for Schwartz classes with the property that its subspace consisting of functions with exponential decay in specific parts of the time domain, when convolved with a particular function, results in entire functions with localized growth in specific parts of the time domain. The growth of these functions is also limited to specific parts of the frequency domain beyond a certain threshold. Our non-triviality results for these spaces rely heavily on the application of an inequality by Beckovicibekov and the use of iterative arguments, which are also applied to the study of Toeplitz operators.

Segmenting diverse modalities in medical images is a challenging task.
While some datasets are available for training, their scarcity often poses a
problem when attempting to segment other image types for which corresponding
annotations are unavailable. To overcome this difficulty, we propose a cyclic
segmentation approach that leverages generative adversarial networks to train a
cycle-consistent image-to-image translator for cross-modal image segmentation.
The proposed method allows us to train on existing modalities and apply it to
other types of images, producing consistent results despite the lack of direct
supervision. It performs comparably to state-of-the-art methods on standard
datasets and delivers satisfactory outcomes on new image modalities.

For a robot to execute tasks efficiently, it must forecast users' intentions based on partially observed body movements.  Features extracted from video footage are often high-dimensional, hindering learning.  Using an RNN with a novel memory unit and a radial basis function kernel for non-linearly mapping features, our method allows the model to adapt its long-term dependencies and achieve optimal prediction results without the need for extensive training.  When tested on a dataset featuring human arm gestures, the proposed method outperformed other RNN methods and performed on par with a method that uses linear mapping for the features.

Recent observations of white dwarf flare stars reveal significant astrophysical insights.  Specifically, studying their energetic flares is crucial.  A comprehensive study of the ultraviolet continuum modeling of the AD Leo's Great Flare on April 12, 1985, was conducted.  Observations from the UV1 and UV2 filters of the International Ultraviolet Explorer Satellite were analyzed.  Deconvolution of blackbody spectra from 1300 Angstroms to 4000 Angstroms was achieved.  The analysis revealed an increase in temperature from 28,000 Kelvin to 80,000 Kelvin during the flare, accompanied by a decrease in flux.  Furthermore, the temporal evolution of temperature and flare energy release rate showed distinct peaks at 11:53:00 UTC.  The findings suggest that the flare originates from the accretion of matter from the secondary star onto the primary white dwarf star.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantans on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one correspondence exists that relates the space of infinitesimal G2-instanton deformations to the fourth de Rham cohomology space with self-duality, modified by the Lie algebra of G2.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is termed $C$-normal if the commutator $TC - CT$ is a compact operator. Under this definition, we examine the $C$-normality of weighted composition operators on the Hardy space $H^2$, where the domain consists of analytic functions on the open unit disc of the complex plane.

This paper addresses a query initiated by Dixit and initially by Hammen regarding core partitions. We demonstrate the hamming distance between any two p-core p'-partitions is at least 2. Using this finding, we establish the large p-core p'-partitions correspond to shortest paths on the additive residue graph, providing a generalization of Hammen's 2-core 5-partition results. These results enable counting high-p-core high-p'-partitions as a walk-based issue on the additive residue graph, extending Dixit's previous work.

Three-dimensional object recognition can be effectively achieved using point cloud representations, which can be directly applied to both single and three-dimensional video scenes. Nevertheless, point cloud videos suffer from significant instability, primarily caused by variations in point cloud transformations, such as shifts, rotations, and irregular surface fluctuations. These smoothening issues can be effectively addressed by a proposed approach called Transformation-Specific Smoothing (TPC), which generates a coherent three-dimensional scene by eliminating inconsistencies across video frames. Unlike other methods that produce generic output, TPC takes three-dimensional time-series input and generates input-specific geometric representations, thereby enhancing video-based three-dimensional scene understanding. Thorough testing on various datasets, including LASER-3D, MHEVAL, OCHIB3D, and real-world data, such as KITTI and KITE, has demonstrated the effectiveness of TPC in producing stabilized point cloud videos.

We examine media access methods in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks, acknowledging the necessity to prevent interference between radar transmissions and analyzing the impact of network size and frequency sweep settings on performance. To address this problem, we compare two AALOHA-based and two CSMA-based protocols, assessing their suitability and efficiency within AALOHA and CSMA framework. Our research focuses on two existing AALOHA protocols and introduces a novel method to optimize FMCW radar transmission parameters to minimize packet loss and reduce time waste. Additionally, we present an enhanced CSMA protocol that incorporates a novel mechanism to eliminate range resolution ambiguity using negative sweep time, a concept not previously applied in FMCW networks. To evaluate these protocols, we developed a simulation tool based on an extended version of the ns3 network simulator, specifically tailored for simulating FMCW networks.

Recent experiments employing a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometer have enabled the investigation of the entangled two-photon absorption process, with results published in Nature Communications in 2016. A non-linear interaction was facilitated in a silicon waveguide by coupling a pump beam with a spectral separation of 750 nm from the interference source. The findings indicated that absorptance outcomes are sensitive to temporal coherence. However, we argue that spatial considerations cannot be disregarded when analyzing these results, especially given their diverse scales. The experiment involved lengths of 500 micrometers for the silicon waveguide and 3 millimeters for the temporal coherence. The effective interaction is influenced by the interplay between diffractive and refractive effects, with the former governing coherence in free space and the latter, by the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, dictating energy scale coherence. The spectral window for observing HET A should be on the order of gigahertz, corresponding to a nanometer time scale, consistent with prior experimental findings.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre99, and shown to be constructible in Gr10, rationally equals the construction presented in BB18. This equivalence allows us to leverage the techniques developed in BB18 for the computation.

Temporal knowledge graphs (TKGs) document relationships between entities, attributes, and events occurring at specific times. Although multiple approaches have been proposed to address TKG temporal reasoning, their performance can be hampered by two main issues: the complexity of their representation models and computational demands of their prediction methods. To overcome these limitations, we suggest a two-component solution. Firstly, we introduce a compact representation model for time that preserves essential information through a neural network with a low-rank structure, thereby minimizing overfitting in small TKGs and reducing computational costs in large TKGs. Secondly, we develop a prediction model called neural relational evolution (NRE) that generates event representations and predicts future relationships based on past temporal patterns. Notably, our proposed model is model-agnostic, enabling it to be applied across various existing prediction methods without incorporating relation representations. Through comprehensive evaluations, we verify the effectiveness of our proposed model and demonstrate the benefits of our low-rank time encoding in both predicting future events and conducting triplets link prediction.

In the physics of binary collisions, the impact sound produced by two objects can reveal subtle information about their movement and interactions.  By theoretical analysis and computer simulations, the sound generated by the collision of two spheres is found to be dependent on several factors, such as the sounds emitted by each individual sphere.  The pressure amplitude of the pressure wave from the impact is found to be proportional to the square root of the involved velocities and inversely proportional to additional parameters.  An important discovery is that the impact sound can be significantly amplified when a specific frequency related to the geometry of the spheres is satisfied.  The theory also explains how acoustic properties and energy dissipation influence the pressure wave, and similar patterns are observed in the radiated intensity and the long-range part of the elastic wave.

A groundbreaking concept known as Bell nonlocality without inequalities has been demonstrated through the means of the correlation matrix factorization check. Building on this method, we found that it can verify nonlocality in cases where correlations are imperfect, and we specifically realized a seven-outcome scenario where four parties' correlations deviate from the local model entirely, confirming novel nonlocality that was previously unverified. In addition to showing its applicability in the seven-outcome case, we found that our correlation matrix factorization method can also verify nonlocality in situations involving multiple subsets of parties, each with different outcomes. As a result, we developed a Bell nonlocality without inequalities protocol that can be applied to the multi-subset scenario and successfully verified nonlocality in the seven-outcome case even when parties' measurements are noisy.

In flat band systems, constrained environments cause the loss of magnetic translation symmetry, which our study shows leads to the breakdown of this symmetry and the emergence of local moments with a finite Chern number, resembling the characteristics of Chern insulators. These features can be observed through experimental measurements, such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy. Furthermore, our analysis within the Hubbard model, considering Hubbard and kinetic broadening, demonstrates that localizations give rise to distinct spectral functions for each site, which collectively form the flat band's shape in the Hubbard model. This discovery enables a more precise understanding of spectral functions in numerical calculations and material-specific systems, such as the kagome lattice, moire systems, and the triangular lattice with a flux pattern, which mimics the structure of the moire pattern in twisted bilayer graphene, and may explain its observed local density of states.

A recent experimental study found that superconductivity in hydrogen boride exhibits critical transition temperatures around 30K. A theoretical investigation utilizing advanced computational methods has revealed that the B2H3 monoclinc structure demonstrates mild mild superconducting traits, characterized by an energy gap of 100meV. Nevertheless, self-consistent calculations revealed that within the superconducting range, the electronic state at the Fermi level primarily originates from the sp2 hybridized electrons of boron, accounting for approximately 70%. Conversely, the contribution from s and p orbitals of boron and sp2 hybridized electrons of hydrogen collectively accounts for 70% of the total superconducting response. Despite this, the low state density at the Fermi level is the primary cause for the low critical transition temperatures of hydrogen boride's superconducting range.

The count of ways to write a number as a sum of other numbers, where the count of numbers is fixed, is referred to as a "run distribution" in the context of the distribution of parts within a partition. The goal is to demonstrate the multiplicative relationship between the generating functions for the run distribution on flattened partitions in the following area: A = (a_1, a_2, ..., a_k), which can be represented as sums of parts [a_1, a_1, ..., a_k, a_k], given that the elements within the partition are in non-increasing order. The demonstration is achieved by first defining a new type of algebra based on the area A, using a foundation that consists of the direct sum of symmetric function algebras S((a_1), x S((a_2), ..., x S((a_k). The element x within this algebra corresponds to the conjugate of a partition, allowing the multiplication to be defined in the following manner: (a_1, ..., a_k) x ((b_1), ..., b_m) = (a_1, ..., a_k, b_1, ..., b_m). The generating functions for the run distribution on the areas within the given area can then be expressed in terms of these flattened partitions.

We categorize as robust certain irreducible arithmetic subgroups within the special linear group of matrices with a rational identity eigenspace, and demonstrate that a discrete subgroup is virtually free-abelian if it keeps the boundary at infinity, and has a weakly finite-amplitude action on a metric space, and a metric group is considered virtually discrete if it has a uniform bound on the diameter of its metric space, and has a bounded action on a metric space.

Highly automated driving systems are designed to maintain functionality even in the event of primary system failure by incorporating a fail-safe backup system. In this scenario, the primary system shuts down and the fail-safe takes over, making critical safety decisions and either transferring control back to the primary system or bringing the vehicle to a controlled stop. A modeling approach using UML state machine diagrams is proposed to model and analyze these systems. The approach was applied to an existing automotive driving system model developed in MATLAB/Simulink, with subsequent formal verification using the UPPAAL Synchronization and Communication tool confirming the validity of the assumptions made about the system's behavior.

Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, and brain science is a pressing need. Recent advancements in machine learning have made possible the detection of clusters in systems that operate independently. Our contribution lies in extending this capability to systems which are interconnected and can affect one another, using real-world examples like power generators, brain signals, and stock prices. We present a novel approach to partition such systems into separate, autonomous parts, relying on data alone, and present multiple verification methods to validate the accuracy of our results.

In recent years, there has been a resurgence of interest in Leibnizian infinitesimal calculus. The key procedures of this calculus can be viewed as solutions to specific mathematical problems, which in turn rely on three fundamental concepts: the transition from non-differential to differential expressions, the movement from non-integrable to integrable expressions, and the conversion from non-differential to differential expressions that are already integrated. Leibniz characterized these concepts using four distinct metaphysical frameworks: physical, mechanical, geometric, and mathematical. This account aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of his characterization by representing each of his models within the contexts of continuous function theory, non-standard analysis, and coinductive reasoning.

We generate forecasts for HI intensity mapping experiments by applying large-scale structure theory and then use them to evaluate the impacts of removing the dominant foreground noise. The outcomes depend on whether the data is analyzed using the full theoretical framework or whether some higher-order infrared cross-spectra are neglected. In the case of the latter scenario, the theoretical assumption leads to an underestimation of the signal strength by approximately 10% when considering the HI signal beyond the k-max limit. However, using more accurate theoretical representations of the foreground noise can significantly improve our understanding of the HI signal. Specifically, in scenarios where the data is collected with long baselines, this neglected contribution could account for as much as half of the total theoretical forecast uncertainty.

Stated simply, a dimensionality concept for a Banach space is considered "white" if it aligns with the standard Euclidean dimension in n+ dimensions, implying all "white" concepts should meet this criterion. We have discovered that the "independence" criterion in a certain theorem does not meet this requirement by presenting two instances - operators on c0 and a specific space constructed from operators on c0 - which have different dimensions according to both theories yet share identical white dimensions with all (n +) dimensional Euclidean spaces. Consequently, this indicates that any "white" dimensionality concept for Banach spaces must attribute the same dimension as the Euclidean (n +) dimension.

One major hurdle in recommender systems is the inherent limitation of only suggesting a minority of available items, thereby missing items that could also be highly recommended. In the realm of online document retrieval, this problem is particularly pressing as it hampers user satisfaction. A potential solution to this issue is incorporating context-aware document clustering into recommender systems. A series of studies have shown that OviReco, by integrating cluster information, outperforms traditional methods in terms of recall and relatedness. Building on this insight, this study proposes a two-phase hybrid approach that first leverages content-based clustering to group similar documents, and then applies collaborative filtering to identify relevant clusters for each user, before recommending all user-related documents. Our experimentally-validated results demonstrate the efficacy of this new method in enhancing the recall of recommender systems.

Using finite-perturbed matrices to model a type B framework, we demonstrate how to represent both freeness under conditional independence and freeness itself through large random matrix products. This approach enables us to derive the required large matrix implications from essential assumptions via the semi-circle law and trace-based calculations on unitary U(n) matrices, ultimately simplifying proof of these implications into assertions of stated assumptions alone. Leveraging this semi-perturbed framework on large matrices to simulate type B free variables, we successfully prove a de Finetti-type implication in step prior to establishing a small perturbation version of a key result from Nica and Speicher's work on moment/cumulant formulas for type B free probability. This pivotal finding is then utilized to decompspose the aforementioned large matrix prior into determining the appropriate large random matrix outcome.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties expressed in two powerful temporal logic frameworks: Metric Interval Temporal Logic and Temporal Safety LTL. We propose a novel monitoring algorithm that generates increasingly precise system behavior assessments, starting from limited data. In addition, we develop a translator to automatically create monitors from general LTL safety formulas, ensuring optimal error indices through applications of safety margin-based reasoning and interval tightening techniques.

The decay process $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi\pi^0\eta$ is studied in detail. A key aspect that significantly impacts this reaction is rescattering between $K^+K^-$ and $\pi^-\pi^+$ in the energy range of 0.8 to 1.4 GeV. Utilizing an effective Lagrangian approach, calculations are performed to estimate the branching ratio and angular distribution properties. A notable observation is made that $a_0(980)$ and $f_0(980)$ produce distinct signatures in both the $\pi^0\eta$ angle integral and the $J/\psi\pi^0\eta$ Dalitz plot. A suggested methodology is presented for identifying a potential signal in experiments searching for the $a_0(980)$ through the $\pi^0\eta$ channel in $\bar B_s^0$ meson decays. Furthermore, a suggested methodology is presented for identifying the $f_0(1500)$ and $f_0(1710)$ through their contributions in angular analysis and Dalitz plot investigations.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical configurations to track multiple points in space with high precision across various wavelengths in the near-infrared spectrum. A notable achievement of this camera is its capacity to track extremely faint objects as dim as K=16.5. A comprehensive characterization of the camera's performance has been carried out, revealing a root mean square error of 60 microarcseconds for objects brighter than K=12 and 80 microarcseconds for objects dimmer than K=15. These figures are consistent with the design specifications under ideal conditions, although real-world operations may result in a 2 to 3 times decrease in precision. The inherent stability of the system allows for the reuse of calibration parameters, facilitating the production of in-situ calibrations within a period of 30 minutes.

We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs with complex structures, specifically focusing on the impact of doubling dimension and pathwidth on this problem's solvability. For general doubling dimensions, our work presents an algorithm adapting to input size for both metric spaces and graphs, achieving a related running time of $k^O(\text{doubling dimension})$. This improvement upon previous solutions with exponential growth related to the doubling dimension is notable, especially considering the minimal increase with small values of $k$ in certain instances. Furthermore, we demonstrate that using a data structure known as relative $(z,\tau)$-map allows for efficient approximation when certain conditions are met, regardless of the doubling dimension. Conversely, our findings also reveal that when certain pathwidth-related parameters are present, finding even a rough approximation of the problem is an intractable task under a widely accepted hypothesis.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_2\Delta_{\eta}^{l}f=0$ is unique, given the conditions that the equation has finite order and satisfies $0\leq k<k+1$, with constants $Q_1$ and $C_2$. Additionally, the equation of the form $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-\Delta_{\eta}^{l}f=0$ is shown to have only the trivial solution for the same set of conditions.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation method. The study aims to derive tighter bounds on the system's size for specific error limits. A novel early termination technique is also introduced to skip unnecessary evaluation steps. The theory is supported by examples that demonstrate early termination and yield a revised bound on the system's size. Additionally, an extended model is considered that takes into account a fixed error limit.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we've discovered a new type of coherent photon paritiesymmetric bundle emission originating from a single quantum dot. The generated photons exhibit an even value for even-quality interference and a zero amplitude for odd-quality interference. The even and zero amplitudes are protected by the parity symmetry of the system. The research focuses on a setup where a quantum dot is positioned in a one-dimensional photonic crystal with a strong cavity. The quantum dot has two possible states based on the spin orientation of the excited electron. The system has an ultrastrong coupling when the ratio of the quantum dot emission rate to the cavity frequency exceeds 0.1. The system has a ultrastrong coupling when the ratio of the quantum dot emission rate to the cavity frequency exceeds 0.1. The degeneracy of the two quantum dot states is preserved in the ultrastrong coupling regime. The two states are connected by the spin flip operation which acts as a parity symmetry. The parity is a good quantum number in the ultrastrong coupling regime. The quantum dot emits photons in the parity eigenstates. The parity eigenstates have even and odd values. The even and odd values are protected by the parity symmetry. The even-valued amplitude is protected by the parity symmetry. The odd-valued amplitude vanishes due to the parity symmetry. The research provides a new approach to study paritiesymmetric emission in the ultrastrong coupling regime. The new approach can be used to develop new quantum

A unified model is developed to assess the thermodynamic properties of equimolar group-IA plasma across all temperature and density conditions. This analytical model, applicable within a limited set of constraints, accounts for ionization and pairing effects and exhibits smooth behavior under extreme conditions. However, it displays discontinuous changes when applied outside its limited set of conditions, rendering it unsuitable for widespread use. To overcome this limitation, we propose a new approach that extends the model's applicability to encompass all conditions, while preserving its simplicity and accuracy within the limited set of conditions. This model approximates the ionization energy and pair fraction analytically, thereby enabling efficient computation of thermodynamic properties without resorting to computationally intensive methods.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are examined. This consideration arises from the chiral current's non-zero expectation value within such mediums as a result of the chiral anomaly. As a consequence, masses for the vector mesons $V$ change, splitting into components with both parallel and antiparallel momenta in relation to the chiral imbalance's direction. This phenomenon indicates that vector mesons can decay into a pair of photons with an energy difference spanning a few hundred MeV.

We examine small-network estimation in a setting where a network of $n$ nodes, each interacting over asynchronous random time intervals, is modeled after an asynchronous graph with unreliable message delivery, some of which may be compromised by up to $f$ Byzantine nodes. The network in question is assumed to be composed of two interconnected parts: one consisting of $n_1$ nodes forming a fully interconnected subgraph with message-delivery time $t_1$, and another consisting of $f$ edges linking nodes from the first subgraph to $n_2$ nodes, each taking an average time $t_2$ to interact with messages from these links. Our focus lies on estimating the size of nodes within the second subgraph when estimates for nodes within the first subgraph are already established. To achieve this, we introduce two estimation algorithms - one producing estimates over multiple rounds and delivering a probabilistic guarantee, and another producing estimates in a single round but requiring specific conditions to be met for an accurate estimate.

In simulations of numerical relativity with multiple objects, the Hamiltonian constraint can lead to significant numerical instabilities, particularly when data is nonlinear. The method of constraint projection has been widely used to ensure a satisfied Hamiltonian constraint by modifying the constraint equations before data selection. The method of Constraint Projection with the Conformal Transformed Kounter (CTPK) previously demonstrated good results for certain scenarios. The method of Constraint Projection with Kounter (CPK), a revised approach that eliminates the conformal transformation step and restores the original Hamiltonian constraint format, showed improved performance. The new method, CPK2, further optimizes the modification term in the Hamiltonian constraint by incorporating an extra conformal transformation, resulting in a more conformal and stable conformal metric for the initial data. This optimization also leads to a simpler and more straightforward momentum constraint, making it more efficient to solve. Numerical tests on various scenarios, including black hole collisions and rotating black holes, have demonstrated that CPK2 provides better momentum and Hamiltonian constraint resolutions than both CPTK and CPK.

The large neutrino experiment JUNO will utilize over 20,000 nitrogen-on-junction neon 081441 night large-voltage units, each measuring 0.29 cubic meters, to detect low-energy neutrinos from the Sun and the Earth. To ensure optimal performance and minimize potential biases in data collection, all JUNO PMTs underwent a thorough quality testing process at the experimental site, involving the analysis of 44 distinct parameters. This involved using high-pressure lamps and both radioactive and laser sources, resulting in the evaluation of the PMTs' optical and electronic components. As a result, the PMTs were categorized into various levels of quality, and approximately 97% met the required standards for installation in the detector. This paper outlines the techniques used for testing the PMTs and presents the outcomes of the quality assessment.

For precise long-term weather forecasting, accurate prediction of air temperature trends over extended periods is essential. Although conventional methods like linear regression and neural networks have shown limited success in predicting long-term temperatures, recent advancements in machine learning, including the development of Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) and attention-based models, have opened new possibilities. By representing time-series data in a specific format and applying graph-based operations, these methods can effectively capture temporal patterns. However, defining the structure of the GCN and its transformation for conventional time-series prediction remains unresolved. In this study, we introduce an innovative framework for GCN-based time-series prediction that automatically defines the network structure through recursive recursion. By defining a new node and edge meaning in the framework, we can define the GCN's operation for traditional time-series prediction. Theory and experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms other methods, such as conventional neural networks and specific GCN-based models.

A comprehensive study has been established to model the atmosphere's dispersion across the 0.35-2.55 $\mu$m wavelength range by analyzing over 1500 measurements from the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope. By incorporating various factors such as atmospheric depth, observatory altitude, air mass, temperature, relative humidity, and atmospheric pressure, the study successfully expressed the dispersion spectrum in terms of these parameters. By comparing different measurement sets, the study found distinct atmospheric characteristics at the VLT's two sites, Paranal and La Silla, and determined the optimal atmospheric conditions for obtaining accurate on-sky data. Furthermore, the study presented new formulas for calculating the dispersion components and demonstrated their applicability to astronomical observations, highlighting the importance of accurate atmospheric dispersion correction for obtaining high-quality spectra.

In recent years, knowledge distillation has emerged as a popular technique for achieving remarkable results in a wide range of tasks. Utilizing the guidance from pre-trained large-scale models, this approach can yield high accuracy even with relatively small datasets. Nevertheless, employing multiple teachers in distillation can be computationally expensive, especially in resource-constrained settings. Therefore, developing an efficient method for multi-teacher distillation remains an important area of research. We introduce Pairwise Iterative Logits Ensemble (PILE), a novel approach for aggregating logits from multiple teacher models in a computationally efficient manner. By designing a scalable method for combining the outputs of teacher models, our proposed technique outperforms current state-of-the-art methods, while also offering improved generalization capabilities. Furthermore, we demonstrate that PILE achieves a notable speedup of up to 2.4x in inference time, making it a practical and efficient solution for multi-teacher distillation.

Bosonic dark matter, when it forms a wave-like state, creates an oscillating pattern, resulting in correspondingly fluctuating SM particle interaction rates with it. The changes in interaction rates are linked to the mass of the dark matter. Since dark matter with masses less than the inverse of the Planck mass exhibits interaction variations matching local amplitude differences, they are influenced by the environment's geometry and composition. The variations in interaction rates can be amplified using a detector array, taking advantage of the coherent response of multiple components. The environment's geometry can also be probed by observing the fluctuating interaction between quantum systems and bosonic dark matter, potentially within their quantum states.

The basis pursuit problem is a non-convex optimization issue that arises when seeking the sparsest solution for a set of linear equations. This issue has various applications in areas such as network analysis, where the goal is often to identify the underlying connections. We have proven a crucial theorem showing that the degree of sparsity in a given network determines whether a unique sparse solution exists. The proof involves analyzing the geometric properties of the equations using concepts such as Grassmannian matrices. Based on this finding, we have also developed an algorithm to calculate the minimum sparsity required for obtaining a unique solution. This theory allows us to categorize the networks into three types: those with a unique sparse solution, those that cannot support a sparse solution, and those on the boundary. In addition, we have applied our result to find the closest network structure that has a unique sparse solution for an input with a known non-zero pattern. This helps in distinguishing between networks with a sparse connection and those that are fully connected.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring hardware network elements, with various P4 compilers supporting different P4 versions and target architectures. The CompCert compiler for validating the P4 Java frontend in P414 has now been extended to work with the P416 language, and an open-source compiler backend for reconfigurable switch hardware based on the Broadcom SDN architecture has been developed. This compiler allows for reliable and efficient compilation of P416 programs to programmable switch hardware, and research into the compiler's correctness has already been conducted.

In numerical simulations using the finite element method, Raviart-Thomas elements are commonly employed to approximate vector fields. Transport equations are crucial across various scientific and engineering disciplines, necessitating an accurate implementation of transport-shift operators aligned with these elements' geometry for preservation of key physical properties. Although existing methods for quadrilateral meshes exist, they often sacrifice accuracy or simplicity. This research presents a new, geometrically-based transport-shift operator tailored to the elements and mesh structure, ensuring accuracy and property preservation.

The remarkable effectiveness of deep learning has sparked numerous efforts to enhance its efficiency and longevity.  Federated learning, for instance, can improve efficiency by allowing multiple devices to contribute data, while federated averaging and differential privacy work to safeguard user information.  However, research into how federated learning can ensure equitable outcomes remains relatively underdeveloped.  This review examines the latest advancements in federated learning, with an emphasis on addressing challenges related to fairness and privacy.  It also explores the potential impact of incorporating novel methods to overcome "gradients leakage" and "client data homogeneity" issues, which could hinder fair and secure federated learning outcomes.

Scientists analyzed collision data from the LHCb experiment to identify excited states of a particular subatomic particle, known as the B-c plus. They found two peaks in the data, each corresponding to a possible state. One state has a mass of around 6841.2 MeV and fits expectations for a particular predicted state. A second state has a mass of around 6872.1 MeV and may be consistent with a different predicted state.

In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems.

This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel method that utilizes specialized networks to accelerate optimization. By segmenting the main network into separate layers and assigning each model a corresponding critic, computational efficiency can be increased by factor of M (the number of model nodes). We observe that this technique not only reduces training time but also maintains comparable final accuracy when compared to a model-single-node setup. To further optimize performance, we implement an original algorithm for exchanging and integrating information between model nodes. Experimental results confirm the potential of this approach to achieve an $O(M)$ speedup.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering exhibits a basins boundary fractal structure that forms only when there are multiple unstable periodic orbits, resulting in a Wada property for all basins. Our research finds additional instances of Wada boundaries in three dimensions that were not seen in two-dimensional cases. Focusing on the 3D Spherical Top, a system with multiple unstable periodic orbits, we discovered that all basins share the same fractal boundary with different orders. Through numerical simulations and visualizations, we represent the boundary using a level-set function that effectively distinguishes between the different basins. Moreover, we discovered a key finding: basins with higher stability experience the most significant effect from dissipation, which not only influences them the most but also enhances this phenomenon.

A theoretical model involving an expanded U(1) B-L (baryon minus lepton) symmetry has been explored where a related gauge boson, denoted as $Z'$, interacts with particles like electrons and heavy right-handed neutrinos. These interactions, triggered by the mixing of heavy right-handed neutrinos with light neutrinos, are proportional to the latter's mass differences. When combined with small coupling constants, this results in a long-lived $Z'$ particle. We have examined various scenarios and used tools like effective field theories and Boltzmann equations to understand how a $Z'$ with flavors can act as a dark matter candidate and influence the universe's evolution. Additionally, we have analyzed how this scenario is constrained by experiments such as LHC and precision collider studies. Our findings show that under certain conditions, the $Z'$ can be stable and constitute a significant portion of the universe's dark matter, with its properties able to match observations from particle colliders and astrophysical data.

Human action recognition in complex videos has far-reaching implications, 
but the large amount of unstructured data poses significant challenges. 
To address this, we present the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN), which is 
designed to tackle these challenges. HAN is an action recognition model that works 
directly with raw video frames in a temporal context. It operates under a setting 
where the network must learn to focus on crucial spatial and temporal segments 
in the absence of clear structure. Evaluations on three benchmark datasets show 
that HAN outperforms state-of-the-art action recognition models and achieves 
notable results, particularly on the JHMDB dataset where it surpassed a 
10% top-1 accuracy rate. Furthermore, diverse ablation studies provide insights 
into the effectiveness of various network components and the significance of 
enforced attention mechanisms.

Investigating a Reissner-Nordstr$\ddot{o}$mn anti-de Sitter black hole in the presence of a non-standard scalar field with a potential, a test scalar field with a specific potential is introduced near the horizon to perturb the system and calculate the first law of thermodynamics using a generalized Smarr formula. The theorem of weak cosmic censorship is then evaluated under various conditions. Our investigation demonstrates that when the specific heat is negative, disturbances by matter fall into the black hole, confirming the validity of the weak cosmic censorship conjecture. Furthermore, we found that if certain inequalities are met, the charge can increase while mass decreases, confirming the conjecture. However, in the absence of these conditions, the singularity may become naked if the mass reduction exceeds the initial mass.

This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progress over the past two decades, as well as current advancements, will be discussed. Using star formation efficiency and its relationship with dust emission as examples, the advancement in understanding star formation through observational studies, as well as its progress over the past two decades, will be highlighted. Ultimately, the challenges and future prospects in understanding star formation through observational studies, as well as its progress over the past two decades, will be discussed.

This paper proposes a new computational method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, for complex probability distributions that can't be directly calculated. By leveraging Nested Sampling, this approach enables evaluation of such quantities even when only sampling data is available. Three case studies are provided to illustrate its effectiveness: one with a straightforward Gaussian distribution; another with a real-world experiment involving observation scheduling for signal period estimation; and a scenario with predicting future outcomes from past data under heavy-tailed conditions.

We introduce an extended framework for interpreting and analyzing weak measure-valued solutions of a nonlinear equation, reducing to Lebesgue-based solutions in one dimension when they are regular. This framework integrates hyperbolic conservation laws with oscillatory behaviors not captured by traditional models. Specifically, we establish a weak formulation for the problem:

$$
\partial_t \mathbf{m} + \partial_x \mathbf{q} = 0,
$$

where the product $\mathbf{m}\mathbf{q}$ adheres to a specific interpretation. Our model incorporates time-dependent initial conditions, oscillating measurements, and handles situations where $\mathbf{m}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are out of sync. Additionally, we examine the convergence of oscillatory solutions as they approach regular Lebesgue-based solutions under regular initial conditions, and the associated energy calculations in such scenarios.

The surge in IoT devices is accompanied by a corresponding rise in the threat of network attacks, which can compromise device integrity and disrupt services. The challenge lies in the fact that existing intrusion detection systems are either unable to identify novel attacks or are too resource-intensive to efficiently classify incoming network traffic. This paper introduces a code-based machine learning approach that leverages the strengths of both encoder and naive bayes models to detect and classify network attacks, thereby addressing the limitations of traditional supervised learning methods. By using binary codes to represent input data, the proposed method enables the use of unsupervised learning for feature extraction, thereby facilitating the detection of both known and unknown attacks. The codeboarding algorithm combines the advantages of encoder and naive bayes in a two-stage process, which includes using a self organizing map to generate unique codes for SCPIoT attack labels, followed by a naive bayes classifier to classify traffic. The study demonstrates that NBcoded achieves a high accuracy of 99.82% in identifying network attacks, outperforming existing intrusion detection systems.

For finitely generated groups G, the focus of this article is the geometric property of growth in graphs representing faithful G-actions. We investigate group actions by solvable groups of both finite and infinite rank, as well as by affine groups over finitely generated extended valuations fields. Our findings reveal that, for amenable groups G, the asymptotic growth rates of non-amitable actions can vary widely. We establish a mapping from non-amitable G-actions to homomorphisms G->R, which we use to compare G-actions with each other. We establish a connection by showing that, for G-elements g, the growth in spheres under the action of g is directly related to its image in R. We make further contributions by presenting a lower bound for non-amitable G-actions and by demonstrating both upper and lower bounds for general G-actions. We achieve this by introducing a group function that, for all G-elements g, accurately measures the leading exponent in the growth of g-actions on balls.

Animals have evolved various movement strategies to navigate their environments efficiently. By analyzing video footage of insects in motion, researchers can gather essential information about an insect's type and behavior. This knowledge has significant applications in multiple fields, including insect control methods. However, the complexity of motion detection algorithms is a major challenge due to biological movement's unique characteristics. In this research, an approach is proposed to identify and track moving insects in real-time using learning-based motion detection. By creating a dataset of real insect videos, the method is demonstrated to outperform existing techniques. By integrating motion analysis with biological features, the framework also achieves more accurate tracking and classification, resulting in a notable enhancement of tracking stability.

Maximizing efficient electricity usage across transmission power networks requires optimized surplus management to minimize costs.
In our study, we demonstrated the effectiveness of using quantum annealing for optimizing power networks by defining the QUBO problem and implementing solutions on both purely quantum and hybrid architectures.
The hybrid approach combines quantum annealing with traditional methods like gradient descent, and we compared it to using quantum annealing alone.
We experimented with these methods on real-world networks supplied by a German utility company and assessed their effectiveness through our results.

Recent breakthroughs in machine learning have made significant advancements in using observed behavior to identify governing physical principles. Despite numerous achievements, key inquiries remain unresolved. For example, how can machine learning account for situations where observed phenomena deviate from established theoretical models? Can the robust generalizations provided by traditional physics still be realized, accounting for the numerous exceptions evident in real-world data? To address these questions, we developed a unified framework that simultaneously extracts both consistent and changing patterns from observed data. This framework represents continuous curves as a combination of a finite set of basic building blocks, representing universal laws, along with the residual errors, which indicate discrepancies between theoretical models and actual observations. We successfully applied this framework to a synthetic data set, mimicking the complex nature of human vision, and to actual physics experiments, yielding promising results.

A search for massive, enduring, positively charged particles occurs using data from the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider. This study utilized $pp$ collisions that took place at a 13 TeV energy level with a collected dataset totaling 137 fb$^{-1}$, amounting to 70% of the ATLAS-R2-13 TeV dataset. Unique features of this search include enhanced sensitivity due to employing missing transverse momentum $\not\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\!\

We have developed a numerical approach to enhance coupling efficiency of a specific type of optical source, consisting of a quantum dot at the end of a waveguide made of a different material. The interaction between this optical source and a different material leads to strong coupling, resulting in a unique phenomenon where energy is periodically transferred between the two. By periodically constricting the waveguide, we observed an even greater transfer of energy, which allowed for a very high efficiency of coupling of the optical signal out of the source and into a specific material. The average efficiency of this optical signal was found to be very close to unity for certain conditions, which were found to be very common. The design also allows for a very short distance of coupling, making it very practical for real-world applications.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a key tool for studying the boson peak, enabling a detailed analysis of its nature. The technique allows for the direct observation and characterization of low-frequency vibrations at the atomic level. The variation of the boson peak with temperature, temperature, sample history and isotope composition has been used to gain insights into the phenomenon's origin. The ability to study the glass-forming liquid above the glass transition using the same method has further contributed to the debate on the nature of the boson peak. The discussion presented highlights the accomplishments of recent research, as well as the remaining challenges.

Particle physics predictions rely heavily on theoretical calculations, with
precise physics demands two-loop, multi-scale framework corrections to
accurate order accuracy. This lecture series introduces key concepts and
tools for complex multi-loop calculations, with an emphasis on general
techniques and precision applications. Highlighted ideas include differential
equation solving, polylogarithmic function usage, annihilation methods,
harmonic polylogarithm extension, differential equation solving within
$\overline{\rm{MS}}$, hypergeometric differential equation solving, iterated
integral solving, and non-multiple zeta value basis searching. Each topic
includes an introduced problem, with relevant mathematical and physical
context.

In random systems, the scattering matrix correlates input and output channels, with a disproportionate number of inputs required to maximize output power in some cases. This is particularly evident in the context of ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays, where the most intense low-lying eigenvalues of the scattering matrix dictate the minimum number of inputs needed to detect rare events like very high energy gamma-rays. This work demonstrates that the scattering matrix develops a distinct set of eigenchannels, with associated sum rules governing their behavior, and that these eigenchannels remain stable under minor perturbations to the system. Furthermore, we show that very high-energy cosmic ray antiprotons exhibit similar properties, and that the eigenchannels in the gamma-ray case are predominantly real and non-negative, and can be determined through the analysis of forward solutions, which simplify the eigenvalue problem by incorporating available energy directly into the system's core.

Researchers have discovered a new spiral structure in the inner regions of the Milky Way, located approximately 3-4 kpc from the center, based on gas and dust observations. This finding aligns with a previously identified feature found in stellar data. Analysis suggests this spiral has physical characteristics similar to other inner spirals, including a large mass and a specific inclination. Furthermore, this spiral structure is likely a result of the same star formation process that creates other nearby spiral arms, and it may be linked to an elongated bar-shaped area in the galaxy. These results support the hypothesis that multiple spiral patterns exist within the galaxy and that a central bar-shaped area plays a significant role in its formation.

To assess the variety of outcomes produced by multi-agent collaborative learning in optimization, our research focuses on the underlying factors contributing to outcome diversity. By comparing the traits of these results, we uncover a strong correlation between their quality and the characteristics of these outcomes, revealing that higher-quality solutions tend to exhibit less diversity. Additionally, the concept of phenotypic diversity is found to effectively predict the number of additional solutions that can be generated without significantly altering the network's architecture, while also being shown to be influenced and, in turn, influencing, the collaborative learning process.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing individuals into couples, avoiding
stable but incompatible relationships. A more complex variant of this problem
involves triads instead of pairs, and we adapt this to scenarios where relationships
are not just incompatible, but form a continuum, and preferences are expressed
as separate value assessments for each triad. Our goal is to prevent both
incompatibility and one-sided deviation from relationships, and in scenarios where
individuals' likes and dislikes are measured additively and are balanced by their
respective values, we find a solution to this modified problem. Furthermore,
assuming bi-additive preferences, we show that such a solution exists when the number
of individuals is limited to 5 or fewer. However, when the number of individuals
is 7 or more, we know that additively invariant problems without a solution are
inevitable; we demonstrate the existence of such problems under a specific condition
of one-sided consistency. By exploring the relationship between the concepts of
stable roommates and triads, we establish a connection and explain its significance.

Our study delves into how different electron-phonon interactions influence valley behavior in two-dimensional materials, and uncovers their varying degrees of impact. In contrast to long-range Coulomb interactions, which are the primary focus in existing theories of valley physics, our investigation reveals that short-range interactions significantly contribute to valley drift, while intermediate electron-phonon couplings significantly affect valley behavior. Based on these findings, we propose a revised valley drift theory that incorporates these mechanisms. This updated theory specifically considers two important interactions: the interaction between electrons and atoms as they shift from equilibrium positions, and the interaction between electrons and atoms during their acceleration. Our research demonstrates that these positions-based interactions significantly contribute to valley behavior in two-dimensional graphene and black phosphorus, with their effects varying significantly compared to long-range Coulomb interactions. Additionally, we find that taking these positions-based interactions into account substantially improves agreement between theoretical and experimental measurements of valley drift in these two materials. Our updated theory also provides accurate predictions for valley drift in additional materials, including phosphorene, antimony black phosphorene, and certain other two-dimensional materials with strong spin-orbit coupling. Our expanded understanding has significant implications for valley electronics technology, as it enables the engineering of materials with customized valley drift characteristics.

We investigate a specific collection of Gromov-Hausdorff classes containing metric spaces with measured distances. This class is characterized by spaces where the-diameter "clouds" of $\epsilon$ is less than or equal to a certain threshold. Clouds here refer to subsets of a metric space with a diameter no larger than $\epsilon$. The upper bounds provided by this structure theorem determine that for any infinite space, its representation within this class accurately captures its fundamental metric properties. This confirmation was challenged by previous research, and our analysis resolves the issue by demonstrating that a particular subclass of our structure, comprising uniformly bounded, non-compact metric spaces, holds true. This subset includes spaces where the existence of a maximal compact subspace within a given class can be shown to exist uniquely.

A microstrip antenna designed to operate at millimeter wavelengths incorporates a unique microstrip feed with significant resistance to fabrication errors in phase center height. The proposed widepatch antenna operates within the 26.1 to 31.6 GHz frequency range with approximately 17 GHz bandwidth and covers more than 150 degrees in the in-plane direction. The design features a simple rectangular shape that can be easily and cost-effectively manufactured using standard techniques. As a result, this simple design is highly suitable for integration into applications requiring large aperture arrays. The angular range of the radiation pattern remains consistent across the frequency band, exhibiting minimal variation of less than 1 dB in gain and less than 2 degrees in phase. The proposed patch antenna exhibits strong potential for use in millimeter wave applications due to its high gain and wide angular range.

Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models, providing a potential alternative to traditional decoding techniques.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. The ability to efficiently monitor the behavior of individual atoms over extended periods is crucial for its implementation. This is currently achievable for small groups of atoms but remains an outstanding challenge for larger atomic ensembles. This study presents a novel approach to quantum precision measurement based on a complex network of two interconnected cavities, each containing atoms, where non-Markovian effects can be utilized to efficiently monitor single atoms for longer periods, as evidenced by the formation of a Heisenberg-scale first-order coherence peak. The research further demonstrates how this advantage can be maintained over extended monitoring times and what non-Markovian characteristics are required to ensure efficient measurement.

The PHENIX Collaboration has studied direct photon-hadron correlations in Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions at a velocity of $v_{\text{lab}}$ of 200 GeV per nucleon pair. Compared to simulations of free parton fragmentation, data from $d$$+$Au collisions show suppression of hadrons in specific momentum-velocity ranges, while a combination of direct photons and hadrons reveals suppression in Au$+$Au collisions, with more significant effects at higher momentum fractions. Above a photon transverse momentum of 5 GeV per mole, the ratio of Au$+$Au to $d$$+$Au collisions exceeds expected values by 10 to 20 percent, indicating enhanced particle interactions in the nucleus.

In this hybrid digital-analog approach to quantum computing, any quantum algorithm can be implemented without needing a universal quantum computer by combining two techniques. One technique involves using a technique that is insensitive to errors, known as the Pauli trap, which is insensitive to the specific nature of the problem being solved. By combining this with a digital method of breaking down the problem into smaller steps, our framework achieves minimal overhead, making it very efficient. We demonstrate this approach for solving complex fermionic systems, such as the non-staggered and staggered versions of the Hubbard model, and find that the digital method accounts for less than 10% of the operations, while an alternative approach using a technique based on the Cayley form of the problem leads to significant increases in the number of operations. We apply our approach to specific fermionic systems, using the electronic properties of the material NiO as an example, and find that our approach is very promising for quantum computers that are likely to be built in the near future.

One main challenge in optimizing a variational objective lies in the intricate balance between its two key components: the precise definition of probabilistic forecasts and the rich feature set required to generate accurate predictions.  To tackle this issue, we've developed a multi-stage approach that begins with a basic, efficient network for out-of-sample optimization, followed by a second and third network for retraining, aimed at producing richer output variables.  This solution yields a significant improvement in the accuracy of our probabilistic weather prediction models, with the first and second optimization stages resulting in AAR scores of 0.1135 and 0.1105, compared to the initial AAR of 0.1135.

Achieving a desired light field or multiple patterns within a medium is often called optical shaping, and it's widely used in various applications such as controlling self-assembling particles, performing photothermal therapy, and inducing 3D neuronal connections. Most experiments are conducted in a transparent environment, and shaping light within a medium with a scattering agent, such as tissue, is more difficult and typically results in deformed or indistinct patterns. Achieving multiple complex structures within a 3D volume of tissue simultaneously is particularly challenging. An advanced iterative algorithm is introduced here for designing a complex feedback loop to produce multiple target patterns within the tissue. This novel algorithm uses tissue as part of the feedback loop and incorporates feedback from both the real and imaginary components of light field polarization to optimize the phase mask of a device called an axial-symmetric Fourier lens-based continuous-phase axial-symmetric spiral phase modulator. A computational experiment demonstrates the effectiveness of this system in generating six different patterns within the tissue simultaneously, and confirms that a high degree of correlation between the original and measured structure is achieved with an average of 0.95. This method offers an efficient approach for optical shaping in complex media and has the potential to significantly advance applications involving scattering materials.

We appreciate the discussion opportunities provided by several insightful comments and discussions which helped to clarify key points and open up exciting areas for future research. Our initial work aimed to demonstrate that certain distributionally robust methods can effectively achieve personalized treatment goals. The robustness of these methods can be justified by the concept of transportability, which we believe offers a solid foundation for their application beyond the targeted population. Following this, the discussion centered on whether specific assumptions underlying these methods are practical in real-world scenarios. The robustness of these methods relies on specific assumptions about how the target population and support approximations are derived from related populations. The degree of "closeness" between these populations is quantified using a transportation cost, which we define as a measure of divergence between probability distributions. We employ this measure to derive bounds on the gap between the optimal treatment rules from related and target populations, which can be estimated from observational or interventional data. This general approach enables the effective transfer of treatment rules across diverse populations, such as medical settings. The robustness of these methods also has implications for applications outside of medical settings, such as cross-geographic analyses. The robustness of these methods relies on specific assumptions, which could be addressed by leveraging transferable features or by collecting additional data through targeted studies. The discussion also raised important questions about the identification of optimal treatment rules when support approximations are used, for which we provide a positive answer.
