The LHC can initiate ultra-peripheral collisions (UPC) in Pb-Pb encounters at high energies, producing lepton pairs or heavy vector mesons through its massive, charged nuclei' virtual photons. In a recent study, UPC data from forward J/psi production was collected and analyzed by ALICE at 5.02 TeV, yielding 28,364 signal events after background subtraction from 2018 data. Cross-sections were determined to be $514 \pm 13$ (stat.) $ \pm $ $23$ (syst.) $\mu$b/GeV for p_T < 1 GeV/c and $10.9 \pm $ $1.4$ (stat.) $\pm$ $1.3$ (syst) $\mu$b/GeV$ p_T^2$ for $p_T > 1$ GeV/c. Cross-sections were found for various p_T intervals and rapidities. For the latter, UPCs were found to comprise a substantial portion of UPC production in Pb-Pb collisions.

Recent advancements in AI technology have enabled the development of visually-guided sound generation models that can create contextually-appropriate sounds based on objects or scenes. This is particularly valuable in areas like virtual audio for augmented reality and audio synthesis for visually-driven non-photorealistic sound design. This study presents an improved method for visually-guided sound generation, moving away from traditional text-based sound descriptions to a more direct and efficient synthesis approach. This new method leverages latent vector space, enabling the generation of coherent sounds that are aligned with a reference image, scene, or object, while maintaining control over the generated sound's temporal characteristics. This innovation is demonstrated to outperform previous methods on various audio synthesis tasks, including vehicle sounds, animal noises, and sound design.

Recent advancements in machine learning have made significant progress in detecting abnormalities in continuous time series data using Hidden Markov Models. This is particularly evident in healthcare, where it's applied to tasks like epilepsy detection and heart rhythm analysis. Although recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have shown great potential in handling time series data, its application to continuous monitoring remains limited. To bridge this gap, we have developed a novel B-LSTM model, an improved version of LSTM that can provide real-time data in a streamlined manner. By pre-processing streaming data into short, overlapping segments, our model can perform efficient anomaly detection without compromising its performance. When compared to the standard LSTM, our B-LSTM model has demonstrated superior results, particularly in evaluating epileptic seizure prediction.

Achieving a balance between pandemic control and economic considerations is a complex task, as it is highly sensitive to the adoption of measures and initial infection rates. A fundamental principle suggests that early implementation of effective measures can mitigate economic losses, although this outcome may not be possible in the long run. A key factor influencing this outcome is the variety of measures employed. When a wide range of measures is tested, a time-sensitive relationship between infection levels, economic activity, and the effectiveness of measures emerges. Specifically, a rapid sequence of events where early implementation of effective measures can lead to lower economic losses. When a single measure is tested, this time-sensitive relationship may not be possible, requiring instead a later point of inflection for measures to be optimal. Employing multiple measures, on the other hand, enables for lower economic losses at all stages, suggesting that a diverse range of measures can be both economically and epidemiologically advantageous.

The objective of data debugging is to pinpoint inaccuracies or biases in training data that are likely to impair machine learning models. Our method involves applying the Shapley value concept to a two-stage data enhancement process: first, we frame data corrections as a combinatorial optimization problem and utilize the GRPO algorithm to generate an updated dataset, then we integrate this modified dataset into machine learning models and leverage the Shapley explanation tool to assess its influence on model outcomes. Our Shapley-based approach enables the model to highlight data samples that are crucial for maintaining high model performance and should therefore not be compromised. The developed tool is applied to a natural language processing task, where we examine the impact of shrinking or removing irrelevant text from machine learning training datasets on the model's performance.

This work reveals underlying relationships between various, seemingly unrelated branches of mathematics: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. We emphasize discrete invariants, which have strong ties to the concept of Lorentzian polynomials. A common thread among these fields lies in a linear space of matrices.

This study provides an in-depth examination of how pressure affects the anomalous Hall effect in Mn$_3$Sn, an antiferromagnetic metal with a triangular structure. Experiments revealed that low pressure can switch the anomalous Hall effect, and this behavior can be attributed to the lattice's structural distortion. Structural examinations indicate that Mn$_3$Sn's triangular arrangement transforms into a pyramidal shape under pressure, and this structural alteration can switch the anomalous Hall effect. Furthermore, this research demonstrates that Mn$_3$Sn's triangular structure can be manipulated through chemical means, and this structural adjustment can be used to switch the anomalous Hall effect, which may provide new insights into similar materials like Mn$_3$Ge, and potentially influence the development of antiferromagnetic data storage technology.

Formal knowledge acquisition is essential for developing intelligent systems capable of high-level reasoning. A crucial initial step in this process involves identifying relationships within a given knowledge base. A significant portion of research in the field of NLP has centered around relation extraction (RE), which encompasses several key tasks essential for informed decision-making in clinical settings, including semantic role labeling, text classification, and link extraction. This paper will provide an in-depth analysis of recent advancements in role labeling and link extraction, emphasizing the advantages of deep neural networks, including their structural, training, and aggregation strategies. A comprehensive evaluation will be conducted using publicly available datasets, emphasizing the significance of this work in enabling efficient knowledge extraction and enhanced clinical decision-making through optimized RE methods.

This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we consider a problem involving a domain $\Omega$ situated between two concentric balls with radii $r$ and $R$. The corresponding eigenvalue problem combines Steklov boundary conditions on the inner ball and Robin boundary conditions on the outer ball. By leveraging the variational characterization of the lowest Steklov eigenvalue, we identify a critical combination of the Robin parameter and the inner ball's radius at which the lowest eigenvalue transitions from positive to negative. Furthermore, within a particular parameter space, we show the existence of at least one negative eigenfunction.

We've developed an innovative approach to reconstructing hypergraphs using supervised learning. Traditional graph reconstruction methods often produce inaccurate or incomplete hypergraphs due to the use of graph-based approaches. By leveraging the unique features of data points, our novel deep neural network can directly identify two essential hypergraph components - the adjacency matrix and the Laplacian - which in turn enable the efficient reconstruction of the original hypergraph. The proposed approach has demonstrated superior performance in various tasks including hypergraph generation, image reconstruction, and a range of tasks like classification, clustering, and registration when applied to synthetic and real-world datasets.

In medical radiology reports, doctors document their visual analysis of imaging techniques like CT, MRI, and X-rays. These documents, written by doctors, serve multiple purposes including tracking a patient's medical history and aiding future physicians in diagnosing through past reference. The information contained within these reports is invaluable for non-radiologist doctors to comprehend a patient's medical condition. Unfortunately, the data in radiology reports remains unstructured, making it difficult for AI models to learn from it. Our proposed solution involves a novel report annotation technique that uses computer-generated synthetic X-rays based on 3D CT scans to mark regions visually identified in the actual X-rays. We've also developed an approach to train an image classifier that can utilize these X-rays to pinpoint disease locations. Through testing on 1,000 lung cancer cases, our model demonstrated an 80% accuracy in identifying and correctly locating tumors.

Bill Thurston initially found a connection between Euler classes and sutured geodesics on surfaces, which was later re-examined using different methods to establish a similar relationship. A similar relationship exists for contact structures as well, which can be expressed in terms of sutured tight geodesics. The concept of a tight geodesic is a discrete version of an embedded Lagrangian straight line in a symplectic space, which has been defined independently of previous concepts of a tight contact structure. Using this new definition, we are able to prove a converse statement to the initial relationship and establish that every surface carrying a sutured geodesic also carries a tight contact structure.

We propose an advanced concept for measuring directional emission in microcavity lasers, relying on entropy to quantify and compare the distribution of emitted photons across all directions at each time step. This innovative approach offers a clear, energy-normalized metric that can gauge the degree of order or coherence in the emitted light. Furthermore, our method can effectively distinguish between directional and nondirectional emission patterns, showcasing its practical applicability through simulations of a 2D distributed feedback photonics integrated cavity laser.

Our findings indicate that cryptocurrencies fulfill two key conditions - they are in demand and their prices are relatively stable - suggesting that they can serve as a medium of trade. Specifically, we have found that individuals are actively purchasing cryptocurrencies, and when these currencies are first introduced, their prices remain stable with only minor fluctuations, similar to a random walk pattern. However, as time passes, the volatility of their prices begins to increase, ultimately exceeding that of emerging stock markets, particularly for certain cryptocurrencies like Dash, Dogecoin, Monero, Nexo, and Stellar after a period of about one year.

The exact solution method using the inverse scattering technique is demonstrated for a specific type of trigonometric seed-based solitonary-traveling wave framework in the presence of random noise. This framework corresponds to the large-scale height variations in the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang equation under its large-scale height variation scale, particularly for the case of a single soliton height variation. The large-scale height variation scale, including soliton height variations, can be characterized by a particular parameter. This parameter is derived from the reflection coefficient of a noise-free soliton solution and a particular mathematical constant. The height variation of the noisy soliton solution can be expressed in terms of this parameter and additional random phases, which are independently and identically distributed random variables with a uniform distribution over a certain interval. An analogous result is proven for the case of a double soliton solution, leading to the derivation of the height structure function with a cubic dependence on a particular scale, which is in agreement with the known theory of weakly nonlinear systems.

The solar wind's compressive turbulence at sub-ion scales is analyzed using magnetic and electric field data from the MMS spacecraft.
Two spacecraft separation distances are considered: 110 and 41.2 km.
The larger separation shows clear signs of coherent structures,
while the smaller separation reveals more fine-grained, less coherent electric and magnetic fields.
Analyzing the data using the minimum variance technique,
we find that the 110 km separation shows a magnetic field spectral slope of -2.2,
and the 41.2 km separation shows a magnetic field spectral slope of -1.9.
Both 3D magnetic and electric field spectra show similar slopes for both separations.
However, the 41.2 km separation shows a larger anisotropy in wave number,
and the 110 km separation shows a smaller anisotropy in wave number,
which is consistent with theoretical predictions.
Additionally, both 110 km and 41.2 km plasma measurements are found to be collisionless,
and both magnetic and electric field contributions to the Poynting theorem are found,
which supports various theories of plasma turbulence closure at sub-ion scales.

In SASE FEL schemes, short pulse durations are achieved through the propagation of a short electron bunch, typically resulting in pulse lengths of a micrometer or more, corresponding to several optical cycles. To generate attosecond pulses, a modified technique involves applying a chirp to the electron bunch, which causes the self-amplified spontaneous emission to build up more gradually and create shorter pulses. By implementing this approach, we can generate extreme ultraviolet and soft X-ray attosecond pulses, which will be applicable to various facilities such as LCLS, FXELSC, PETRA III, and SACLA.

A mathematical model examining the impact of turbulence on a stratified flow is investigated. By combining three key factors - vertical velocity shear, horizontal temperature gradient, and the Earth's rotation rate - a specific non-homogeneous equation arises, which describes half-space half-wave propagation. This scenario generates two distinct eigenfrequencies associated with the Earth's inertia waves, influenced by both turbulence and the Coriolis effect. Analyzing these frequency behaviors through various limits reveals new relationships between Ito and Havrda-Charvat approximations, providing insights into turbulence's effect on turbulence models.

Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy.  Several metrics have been developed to assess the extent of distortion caused by manipulated district boundaries, yet there exists no universally accepted standard for measuring it.  This study presents a real-world experiment employing a district-redrawing procedure based on dynamic systems, which we call annealing, mirroring a well-known statistical digitization technique.  By analyzing multiple simulations of this process, implementing various levels of randomness, we can establish reliable confidence intervals for standard grievance metrics applicable to the final generated maps.  The method proves effective in identifying unfairly biased electoral manipulation and has already been applied to a newly created state map for Oregon, USA.

A novel defect detection approach is introduced that utilizes a direction-sensitive Gabor Hough transform and matrix decomposition techniques. Firstly, a directional gradient map is created from the input image, followed by a direction-sensitive Gabor filter bank. The transformed image, derived from analyzing the map's structure, is then subject to a matrix decomposition that separates the background and defect components, resulting in a reliable defect detection result. Experimental results, particularly for patterned fabric images, demonstrate the method's high detection accuracy and a rate of true positives near 99%.

To enhance the robustness of learning methods in control problems, we introduce a new Gaussian distribution relaxation that incorporates an I-KL penalty for better performance in uncertain environments. Building on this framework, we develop a novel regularization technique for deep navigation problems in uncertain real-world settings. By incorporating our relaxation and resulting gauge function into offline reinforcement learning, we achieve improved robustness. In contrast to traditional offline reinforcement learning, which relies on fixed experience, our method introduces an information-theoretic regularizer based on the maximum mutual dependence between states, actions, and navigation policies. Experimental evaluations in a simulated uncertain environment demonstrate the efficacy of our techniques in both standalone and combined applications, showing that they combine with standard offline reinforcement learning to navigate a 3D real-world scenario with greater resilience.

For asymptotically flat spacetimes that adhere to the Einstein field equations, a specific condition can be established, indicating how quickly mass can be lost according to the Bondi mass, a measure of mass at infinity in general relativity. By applying a previously created framework for time-dependent spatially homogeneous spaces, we can determine the minimum rate of mass loss under certain energy and dominance conditions, which hold under both classical and quantum theories of relativistic mass, including菲利普 mass. This enables us to set upper limits on how long mass can be stable, a crucial factor in mass stability. This has significant implications for the formation of black holes and neutron stars from large mass disturbances, including mass disturbances that span the entire sky. Furthermore, we find that mass loss may cease before the Bondi mass changes by an extremely small percentage, less than $10^{-11}$, even for mass disturbances that span the entire sky. This means that mass loss may effectively end while the Bondi mass remains nearly constant, less than $10^{-11}$ change, even for mass disturbances that span the entire sky.

We've created a star cluster simulation to study the fate of Population III binary black holes after they form through direct collapse in massive, metal-free clusters. We focused on populations of these black holes predicted to remain in clusters that formed the first Population III stars in 10-20 million year old regions with high densities of star formation, located far from galaxies with high rates of star formation. Our results indicate that these Population III binary black holes have high probabilities of surviving and remaining in such environments, where they would interact dynamically with other stars to eventually merge and produce detectable gravitational waves. Based on our findings, we estimate a minimum of one binary black hole merger per year in these regions, with the most massive mergers having the highest detection rates by observatories like LISA. Our results suggest the most likely outcomes of Population III binary black hole interactions are either escaping the cluster or becoming the central black hole binary, with the latter scenario having a high potential for contributing to the observed supermassive black holes in early galaxies.

In modern power distribution networks equipped with energy storage systems (ESS) and advanced control systems, the standard monitoring methods need to be reevaluated since they often rely on predefined rules that might not be sufficient to cover all scenarios. Incident-aware data mining techniques can enhance monitoring by allowing the system to learn and adapt through real-time data analysis. This study develops a data-driven approach to identify and distinguish different types of events in low-voltage power distribution networks, including over/undervoltage, over/under frequency occurrences, and power flow reversals. By utilizing historical SCADA data, a two-stage method combining binary classification and feature importance analysis is implemented to ensure accurate detection and feature relevance. The proposed algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through its ability to achieve a high F1-score of 0.99 in event detection, while also identifying the most impactful features for each category.

Our study focuses on how the $\rho$ and $\omega$ mesons contribute to the radiative decays $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi \gamma$ and $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$. The first process is predominantly influenced by the $\rho$ meson, consistent with $X(3872)$ having a higher population of $c\bar{c}$ over $\sigma \pi$ or $\rho \pi$. The $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$ decay can arise from either the $\rho$ (or $\omega$) in the $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi$ decay decaying itself, or as a direct two-body decay of $X(3872)$ into a $\rho$ (or $\omega$) and a $\pi$ (or $\omega$) component. The latter scenario is the most plausible, with the $\omega$ contributing significantly. The $X(3872)\rightarrow J/\psi \pi\pi\gamma$ decay via the $\rho$ (or $\omega$) direct path is 10 (100) times stronger than the three-body decay process involving the $\rho$ ($\omega$).

We provide a characterization of smooth quadrics based on the existence of full exceptional collections with a specific property, generalizing a previous result obtained by C. Vial for projective spaces.

A recent breakthrough at one million steps per second enables researchers to efficiently evaluate and compare AI models by rapidly testing AI capabilities, such as learning abilities, across various scenarios. The faster simulation timeframe also provides valuable insights into the effects of AI limitations, like restricted computational power, on real-world applications.

Using an analog of Cartan's elemental method for spaces with irregularities, we create a generalized model for a 2D topological insulator with various imperfections, similar to a material with varied properties. Building upon this foundation, we extend our method to include analogs for the Berry phase and curvature, which allow us to calculate the conductance in systems with irregularities by applying modern theories of topological insulators. The resulting formulas have been analogously applied to specific cases, such as a 45-degree rotated lattice and a lattice unevenly stretched along one axis, and the outcomes are matched with expected material conductance values.

Consider a sector in the plane with a finite angle, denoted by $\Omega_\eta$, bounded by $p$-lines meeting at the origin. For a $C^1$ function $u$ that satisfies the condition of $p$-harmonicity in a region within $\Omega_\eta$ but does not include the origin, we establish an estimate for the oscillation of $u$ in smaller disks centered at any point within the region. This estimation is expressed in terms of the oscillation within a larger, specified disk and its distance from that point. Notably, we achieve this result without assuming the function $u$ is bounded in that larger disk. For the specific case where $1 < p \le 2$, we derive specific constants for this oscillation estimate in terms of the sector angle $\eta$. However, when $p > 2$, we find that this constant depends on an additional parameter $R > r$, which represents a larger disk, implying that without boundedness assumptions, no universal constant can be determined.

Using a joint multivariate spatial model based on the work of Heffernan and Tawn, the relationship between satellite wind speed data, wind direction data, and data on significant wave height, all located in the North Sea, is examined in a study. This model is applied in a bivariate and trivariate context for various sites. Multiple parameters are estimated using the Markov chain Monte Carlo method by combining direct extreme value parameter estimates and the approach by Patefield and Rothenberg. The results show that severe conditions exist across the North Sea, particularly around Germany, Denmark, and Holland.

Inspired by intermediate Lang conjectures concerning hyperbolicity and rational points, we establish new theorems on the finiteness of non-constant morphism sets from a specific fixed variety to another, also defined over a specific number field, by adapting Faltings's work on the finiteness of maps in moduli spaces.

A key concept in robotic manipulation, the manipulability domain, helps robots plan and execute movements. Although many human studies have shown the value of using the manipulability domain to improve hand-over-hand transfer of manipulation skills between humans and robots, there are still significant challenges in making this a reality. A major obstacle is adapting the manipulability domain from one robot to another due to differences in their structures. A recent study proposed a method to transfer 6DoF pose estimation tasks by mapping the manipulability domain between two robots. However, this approach has so far been limited to simple tasks. To overcome this, we develop a new technique for transferring the manipulability domain between any two 6DoF manipulators, which we implement in a hand-over-hand human-robot manipulation task. Our approach involves using an iterative closest point algorithm to match manipulability boundaries and incorporating a novel metric that considers the geometric properties of the manipulability ellipsoid. This enables us to successfully transfer a wide range of manipulability domains and accurately transfer a variety of manipulation tasks.

To study non-resonant Higgs boson pair production in the $\textrm{HH} \to 
\textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ channel at the LHC, the matrix element method has been applied. The approach used accounts for final state particle fragmentation and the underlying parton distribution functions in the proton, allowing for a precise comparison between simulated and actual data. The results demonstrate the feasibility of employing the matrix element method for studying Higgs boson pair interactions.

A novel method is introduced for automatically creating accurate 3D shape models of everyday objects using only images of the objects from a rotating surface. By the nature of their creation, these objects provide unique features for 3D pose estimation, eliminating the need for artificial features. Our research focuses on developing a system that can learn 3D pose from these objects without relying on specific features. This is achieved by creating a network that can be retrained with different datasets, allowing it to generalize to various objects. Our approach is evaluated on multiple datasets, producing results comparable to state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, we create a large dataset with accurate 3D pose information, allowing us to test the effectiveness of our approach. Our objects, along with their specific features, can be publicly accessed at a provided link.

A rapidly growing number of individuals are falling prey to vaccine misinformation on social media, which is attributed to a combination of factors including inaccurate information and emotionally charged messages. Despite this, research on how to effectively counter such misinformation has received relatively little attention. This study seeks to address this gap by developing a computational framework for categorizing social media discussions about COVID-19 vaccines as supportive, opposing, or unrelated. By leveraging a diverse dataset of Twitter posts, the proposed framework combines multiple NLP techniques and LLMs to analyze the posts and identify supportive messages as well as those conveying misinformation. Experimental results show that the proposed framework outperforms existing benchmark models, showcasing its potential in real-world applications where it can be utilized to identify and counter misinformation on social media platforms.

A key challenge in attosecond science lies in achieving precise control over the production of these electron waves from a target and their direction. A novel technique has been developed to exactly control isolated attosecond pulse generation by altering the characteristics of the driving laser. Utilizing a highly-optimized laser field, researchers can target electrons with greater precision, resulting in improved efficiency and output energy. A highly-efficient, isolated attosecond pulse source has been demonstrated using a target in a 3D-optimized laser field, yielding an enhancement of over 100 times compared to conventional techniques.

Recent observations from TESS and Gaia have prompted a re-examination of the binary star system Algol. By analyzing the light curve and astrometric data, researchers discovered a broad, periodic dip in brightness with a 69.3-day period, indicating the presence of a new object. Although the amplitude of this dip, around 2%, is relatively low, the light curve exhibits multiple peaks and an irregular pattern, making it unsuitable for exoplanet classification. Assuming the object is an eccentric edge-on binary system, the semi-major axes of the three components in the Algol system have been calculated. Furthermore, the magnitude of the new object, M_2, was found to be 7.73. By combining TESS and Gaia data, the mass and orbit of a binary system within the M_2 system were discovered. This system, M_2a and M_2b, has a 77.5-day period and lies 166.4 AU away from x Algol. It was found that M_2a has a mass of 2.5 M_sun and M_2b a mass of 1.0 M_sun.

This paper investigates a half-space Schrödinger equation outside a convex obstacle with a subcritical nonlinear term. Near the point of the obstacle with the smallest radius of curvature, the problem can be approximated by a half-space equation with a Laplacian operator in two dimensions. We demonstrate that the data of initial energy and mass uniquely determines the blow-up time, which is then used to derive optimal constants for the given nonlinear Schrödinger equation.

In recent years, Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have gained attention for fusing the benefits of data-driven and physics-based modeling approaches.
To enhance PINN training efficiency, we propose an innovative Residual-based Adaptive Node Generation Method (RANG).
By dynamically creating new data points where the network's prediction is farthest from the residual mean in each dimension,
the method optimizes training resource allocation.
Additionally, a residual-based weight is applied to adjust the influence of existing data points based on their distance from the residual mean.
Experimental results confirm that RANG accelerates the PINN training process,
yielding more accurate solutions with minimal training time compared to a standard VarINNN method.

This research focuses on developing a compact model for multi-domain ferroelectric FETs (FEFETs), incorporating a drift-diffusion numerical simulator to investigate domain walls in multi-domain FeFETs and examining their impact on channel capacitance. The simulator is comprised of two parts: one accounting for the self-consistent Poisson and current continuity equations, and the other incorporating additional equations for domain evolution based on the time rate of change of domain area fraction. The model's results demonstrate the presence of negative capacitance behavior in multi-domain FeFETs, influenced by domain walls, and its dependence on ferroelectric layer thickness. The underlying physics is also examined through energy analysis. To fast-track simulations, we develop a set of closed-form equations, namely the analytical compact model. By integrating various effects, such as sub-threshold swing enhancement, variability, and short-channel ones, the proposed model successfully replicates complex multi-domain FeFET transfer characteristics.

A study of computer security has shown that most analysis focuses on how a single vulnerability spreads across operating systems and web applications, but the cargo ecosystem, a vast collection of software libraries, has seen very little research into vulnerability propagation. A new construction approach for a cargo ecosystem dependency-vulnerability knowledge graph enables the examination of how vulnerabilities spread within the cargo ecosystem, based on a comprehensive dataset of 242,492 cargo packages. By analyzing real-world vulnerability data, it was found that the cargo ecosystem vulnerability propagation rate is significantly higher at 22.5%, compared to other ecosystems like Python's PyPI at 0.6%. An analysis of vulnerability types revealed that 40.4% of the cargo ecosystem's vulnerabilities propagate, and 60.4% of these can be transmitted due to incomplete version control of software libraries.

For analyzing long-term behaviors of stochastic complex Ginzburg-Landau equations受到纯跳跃扰动影响, we establish a sufficient condition related to their irreducibility and invariant measures. The established condition relies on a S. Verducci-type theorem regarding Dirichlet distributions. The approach involves expressing the small noise in the form of a random complex exponential linked to a positive-definite matrix, which in turn yields a condition ensuring irreducibility and invariant measures through the existence of a solution to a linear system.

For a finite noncyclic nilpotent group G, we're analyzing the minimal vertex degree in its power graph. This power graph connects vertices based on one being a positive power of the other. By examining the group's prime divisors and Sylow subgroups, we've pinpointed vertices related to its cyclic subgroups. This allows us to establish a connection between the group's properties and its minimal vertex degree in the power graph. This study provides degree calculations for specific types of noncyclic abelian groups.

Hadron-hadron collisions in the intermediate Feynman-x region (between 0.1 and 0.9) have not been thoroughly investigated at high-energy ranges above sqrt(s) = 63 GeV using the CERN Intersecting Storage Rings. I have developed a prototype fast trigger for the Large Hadron Collider that can identify this area in real-time by detecting fragments from collisions between 13 and 14 TeV. These fragments are measured over a large angular range (from 3 to 50 degrees) and across various energy thresholds (from 2 to 50 GeV). By analyzing these measurements, we can derive crucial information about the behavior of these particles, including their cross-sectional behavior, the distribution of energy, and the movement of charge in these collisions. This data will enable us to make direct comparisons between observed results and theoretical predictions, such as the color interaction model by Lund. By analyzing these measurements, we can also determine the properties of an unknown particle called a "soft pomeron," including how its shape changes with energy, its coefficient of exchange, and how it influences our understanding of the behavior of particles, ultimately connecting this knowledge to the behavior of particles from cosmic rays.

Deep learning models, specifically deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs), have become the gold standard for task-dependent image analysis, but they often require images to be in a fixed orientation. Developing an orientation-invariant CNN would enable handling of 2D images without needing image alignment, a challenging task in itself. Our work presents an orientation-invariant convolutional neural network (OICNN) capable of automatically determining and rotating images to a consistent orientation before processing, thus making the orientation estimation process robust and precise. The OICNN's novel design, with its special filter bank structure, allows it to accurately predict image orientation, and our experiments demonstrate its superior performance compared to other methods. The OICNN's novel architecture also offers potential applications beyond orientation estimation, including automatic image preprocessing by aligning images based on their estimated orientation.

Recent advancements in learning from 3D data have been driven by the success of
deep learning, with graph convolutional networks (GCNs) emerging as a prominent approach for processing graph-structured data. Notably, GCNs have found applications in 3D shape analysis by employing point clouds as input. However, using GCNs for point cloud learning presents challenges, including increased computational complexity due to graph connections and difficulties in leveraging local and global features from unstructured point clouds. To address these issues, we introduce Geometric GCN (G-GCN), which optimizes computational efficiency by directly using Euclidean distances for calculating convolutions, thus eliminating the need for graph-related operations. Moreover, we propose a novel attention-based pooling method to effectively aggregate features from local neighborhoods and global contexts. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets for 3D shape analysis reveal that G-GCN outperforms existing state-of-the-art models, demonstrating its superior performance.

We introduce a groundbreaking type of Trojan attack, which uses fixed images in
the out-of-distribution dataset as a semantic marker for backdoor triggers,
unlike existing research that relies on adversarial examples to identify
activation patterns. Our testing reveals that this novel approach has a high
success rate in both clean and poisoned images, exceeding that of existing
techniques by a significant margin (27.7% higher in the semantic-preserving
attack and 37.7% higher in the semantic-altering attack). Additionally, our
research shows that this type of Trojan attack can be implemented without
access to the target model, making it possible to inject the attack at a minimal
computational cost. Our tests demonstrate that this approach can successfully
trigger the attack in 91.9% of the images at a loss of only 0.0126 for the
semantic-preserving attack and 0.0201 for the semantic-altering attack,
compared to 0.0691 for the FNDT approach.

We are developing an image slicer for an integral field unit, ROSIE IFU, to integrate with the IMACS spectrograph on the Magellan Baade Telescope. The designed ROSIE IFU will split a 2 degree field of view into different segments and capture their spectra across the 0.5-1.0 micrometer wavelength range with high spatial and wavelength resolution. The project involves an upgrade in technology with higher sensitivity and efficiency detectors, thus allowing for more detailed observations. In addition to this, we have created an advanced software for processing data and tracking moving objects in real-time to enhance observational capabilities.

In this paper, the carbon-carbon fusion research is revisited in light of recent findings.
Experimental evidence indicates an oscillating pattern of the fusion cross-section near the barrier,
which is more pronounced for equal-mass nuclei.
A key theory, the diabaticity model, suggests that the fusion process loses coherence when the reaction time exceeds the unitary time.
Interestingly, a predicted fusion minimum at a certain energy is in line with the diabaticity model.
Furthermore, an attempt is made to apply the diabaticity model to proton capture reactions, specifically in the case of 12C + p.
We also discuss a novel approach of the inverse Trojan horse method to measure these elusive fusion and capture data.

A crucial initial step in understanding terrestrial exoplanets is obtaining their precise mass and size to calculate their density, which in turn provides valuable insights into their composition. Recent studies have revealed a correlation between stellar metallicity and exoplanet mass, suggesting a compositional link between stars and their respective exoplanets. This paper expands on previous research by incorporating more accurate mass values and incorporating oxygen content into the element correlation models. By applying these updated stellar compositions to existing planet radii and assuming formation within a specific star-planet element relationship, this study explores the compositional makeup of hypothetical terrestrial exoplanets using advanced numerical simulations. Two distinct scenarios are considered based on different star-planet composition dependencies. Depending on these assumptions, such exoplanets could have mineral compositions ranging from 10-40% metallic core by mass. Additionally, this research indicates a significant increase in their metallic core mass fraction, with values as high as 40-60%. These findings can be further applied to planetary bodies within our own solar system, such as Earth, Mercury, and Mars.

Deep neural networks have become popular in recent studies for predicting Channel State Information (CSI) features and using them for location estimation. However, accurately extracting CSI features remains a major challenge due to the adverse effects of noise and multipath interference. To overcome this limitation, our proposed method focuses on utilizing attention mechanisms to identify and emphasize the most relevant CSI features that contribute to accurate localization. After removing unnecessary features, our approach achieves better performance and lower computation costs. When tested in a real-world environment, the proposed model demonstrated higher and more consistent localization accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This paper presents a comprehensive framework for modal logic semantics by linking different types of logical meaning in the literature to the topological categories theory. Building on similar methods in categorical logic, we will thoroughly examine the relationship between the structure of the categories and the principles of the logic, thereby enabling the comprehensive expression of the principles within the categories framework. As a result, it becomes possible to achieve a unified approach to the semantics of the different types of modal logic.

A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance criterion, effectively mirroring the requirements of color indexing in a squared graph. Researchers previously made the claim that bipartite cubic graphs could be colored using a maximum of 17 different colors; however, it was later discovered that a specific case did not hold, leading to the revision of the bound. Although the new upper limit for coloring these graphs was set at 21, it was later found that the original conjecture did not hold for one graph, but it does remain valid in other cases, such as 3-connected graphs, where the bound is still 17. Furthermore, an algorithm exists to determine the exact number of colors needed to properly color any 3-connected bipartite cubic graph.

This research examines functions defined on the vertices of a $d$-dimensional Hamming graph, which adhere to constraints imposed by the eigenvalues between $-d$ and $-d+2$. We demonstrate that the functions have supports of a minimum size with a cardinality not exceeding the product of dimensions $d$ plus one. In addition, the research identifies the conditions under which the size of the support equals $d+1$, especially considering functions supported on specific elements within the Hamming graph's vertex set, which include points with supports limited to specific levels within the graph. Furthermore, the research explores cases where functions within the Hamming graph's support size have specific properties and lists small support sizes for these cases. Lastly, the research connects the properties of functions within the Hamming graph to those on hypercubes and provides their respective support sizes.

COPASI is a widely-used simulation and analysis tool for biochemical networks.
After in-depth analysis in MATLAB using copasi2matlab, users can now view
results through a web interface with the ShinyCOPASI application. This allows
for visual inspection of model and analysis results, as well as providing an
in-depth analysis within MATLAB, before finally sharing the results via a web
interface on R.

A burgeoning trend in science and engineering is to employ data-driven methods in conjunction with traditional numerical techniques to resolve intricate problems. These methods, referred to as Scientific Machine Learning (ScML), are particularly effective in handling high-fidelity datasets and are applied to various domains such as partial differential equations and image-based reconstruction. Despite the significant improvements in accuracy that ScML methods can offer, there is a lack of understanding regarding their reliability and limitations, which is a crucial aspect to consider in science and engineering applications. The need for accuracy uncertainty quantification in SchML is even more pressing due to the high cost of errors in these fields. The purpose of this work is to provide an in-depth examination of uncertainty estimation techniques within SchML methods, including Bayesian Neural Networks, Deep Kernel Networks, Multilayer Perceptrons, and Dempster-Shafer Theory, and to highlight the importance of using proper confidence metrics. The study also includes a direct comparison of these methods, highlighting their ability to accurately quantify uncertainty in a regression problem, and discusses the implications of this research for future SchML applications.

We are investigating quantum group analogues of the free group factors' radial subalgebras. These have been studied extensively within the context of the free group von Neumann algebras by specific researchers, who have demonstrated key properties such as being maximal abelian and having a specific relative property S. We aim to verify the latter, and also hope to verify the former, for the full quantum group subalgebras, in class function spaces, particularly for quantum permutations. We have found that the full subalgebra is maximal abelian in quantum permutations, and have made initial progress in proving it is property S, before needing to consider a more in-depth study for a complete demonstration.

Policy iteration comes with computational drawbacks in large-scale Markov decision processes due to its requirement for an exact solution of a linear system and the convergence to zero of the residual for both Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel iterative methods. In contrast, inexact policy iteration still guarantees the movement between value iterates in distinct polyhedra as the residual approaches zero. Informed by this observation, a new class of iterates has been developed using a combination of inexact solutions and specific directions, with the resulting policy iteration algorithm demonstrating convergence to an $\varepsilon$-optimal solution in a finite number of steps when inexact solutions with an $\varepsilon$ that decreases over time are used. In addition, by applying this framework to a time-varying LSTD algorithm, a finite policy iteration algorithm has been applied to large-scale continuous MDPs, with the resulting method showing improved efficiency and optimality.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. In comparison to the general oriented case studied by Schwartau and Tuncalan, the current research focuses specifically on weighted directed graphs. The study establishes a criteria to determine when the $s$-th symbolic power of $I(\mathcal{D})$ contains the $s$-th ordinary power, where $s$ is a positive integer, based on the concept of $s$-path cover in $\mathcal{D}$. A specific condition for binary oriented graphs is identified under which the $s$-th symbolic power of $I(\mathcal{D})$ is equal to the $s$-th ordinary power. Additionally, the study proves that for the class of oriented cycles, the $s$-th symbolic power of $I(\mathcal{C})$ contains the $s$-th ordinary power for all positive integers $s$.

This paper examines the solution to a inverse problem through a computer simulator that generates complex data over extended periods. To address limitations of current methods, which often require multiple evaluations of an expensive function, we utilize the output values of our simulated data to our advantage. By applying the mean squared error to determine the optimal combination of these values, we develop a class of estimators for an unknown parameter across various points on a predetermined boundary. By leveraging the inherent correlations within the simulated data, our method allows for multiple parameter estimates with enhanced precision compared to traditional methods, requiring only a few additional simulations for verification purposes.

Research has shown that certain distributional assumptions are required for algorithms to learn under adversarial conditions, even simple concepts like parity require up to $O(n)$ assumptions when queries are unrestricted. However, the situation changes when queries can be made locally, defined as having limited Hamming weight. We investigate the robust learning capabilities of local queries, finding an efficient learning algorithm for parity with Hamming ball depth $d=\Omega(\sqrt{np \log(1/\delta))}$. This is comparable to the query complexity of exact learning ($d = O(\sqrt{np \log(1/\delta))}$ Hsu et al., 2022) and shows a robust learning gap of at most factor two. Moreover, we show a at most factor five difference in the required query complexity for a black-box approach. While our research highlights the robust learning potential of local queries, we also raise an open question regarding query depths up to $d=\Omega(\sqrt{np \log(1/\delta))}$.

For the first time, fragmentation functions for jets associated with a solitary isolated photon have been measured in collisions involving protons and a lead–lead nucleus. This analysis employed data from the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider, specifically, a total of 29.3 inverse nanobarns of collision centrality between 0 and 20\% was captured at $\sqrt{s_\mathrm{NN}} =$ 5.02 TeV. Comparing these results to predictions for proton-proton collisions, a significant decrease was observed in the energy of the heavier nucleus, starting approximately five baryon number units away from the jet axis, within the region of less than 400 MeV. This discrepancy is consistent with theoretical expectations regarding energy loss collisions involving a heavy nucleus, specifically a large decrease in fragmentation function and an altered energy profile, also known as the "jet shape," when comparing proton-proton and lead-lead proton collisions.

Recent research involving Feynman integrals has highlighted the significance of Apéry-type inverse binomial series. Building upon previous findings by the third and second authors in collaboration with Borwein, new nontrivial series identities will be proven through a different approach. The new proof relies on demonstrating functional equations for certain hypergeometric functions as well as establishing an underlying motivic differential system. This leads to an underlying motivic differential system. This leads to representation of the values of the Apéry-type series as well as weighted sums of multiple zeta values and polylogarithms evaluated at $-1$ via integration. A novel connection to the underlying motivic differential system has a novel connection to colored multiple zeta values will be established. A novel connection to colored multiple zeta values will be established. This research provides a novel relationship between the values of the Apéry-type series and colored multiple zeta values.

The initial production yield measurements of various particles are presented for the most central Xe-Xe collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.44$ TeV reported by the CMS Collaboration at the LHC. Key characteristics of these yield measurements are the rapid increase in the photon photon to hard parton conversion probability with increasing rapidity, and a substantial enhancement in the yield of certain particles compared to those of others as a function of transverse momentum. Notably, this enhancement is more pronounced in the yields of certain particles than others at high rapidity and transverse momentum. Furthermore, this enhancement exhibits dependence on the charge and mass of the particles involved. When compared to theoretical models, these measurements imply an enhanced probability of certain particles being produced in the collisions relative to those of other particles at the given energy.

We introduce a novel, numerically efficient approach to solving DGLAP equations for single and double parton distribution functions by leveraging Chebyshev interpolation techniques. This method enhances numerical precision with a reduced number of grid points for PDF evolution, achieving improved efficiency. The developed algorithm is now incorporated into the DGLAP API for LPFMS-based PDF evolution.

For missions to Mars and the Moon, in-depth geological and astronomical studies are being conducted by analyzing regolith samples provided by both planetary rovers and orbiters. These samples can be utilized to create in-situ building materials through a process called 3D printing with binder technology. To create the printed material, the raw material must first be processed into a fine grain size of less than 150 micrometers. To achieve this, the material is milled and then sintered to remove volatile compounds and make it suitable for use in constructing habitats or other constructions on another planet or celestial body. This research focuses on the Sintering process for the material, specifically the Sintering temperature, and its effect on the material's microstructure and mechanical properties. To better understand the material, the Sintering process is monitored using the in-situ monitoring, and the mechanical and microstructure of the material is analyzed. The Sintering temperature is optimized for the material, and the effect of Sintering temperature on the material's mechanical properties is studied. The material's microstructure is analyzed using the electron microscopy, and the material's mechanical properties are evaluated using the universal testing machine. The results of the in-situ monitoring, mechanical testing, and microstructure analysis are used to optimize the Sintering process for the material, and the effect of Sintering temperature on the material's mechanical properties is studied. The material's mechanical properties are improved by the Sintering process

A research study has used linear stability analysis to examine the effect of slip boundary conditions on a film of liquid flowing down a curved cylinder with a specific curvature. The study found that at higher slip values, the film becomes thinner and more prone to break up into droplets. A proposed slip-enhanced Rayleigh-Plateau instability mechanism suggests that in films with very low viscosity and moderate to high slip values, break-up into droplets can occur more quickly than previously reported. The study has also validated theoretical findings with three-dimensional numerical simulations and is relevant to understanding and controlling droplet formation in systems that experience slip boundary conditions, such as those with liquid overhangs.

By combining observations from the VLT/VISIR and James Webb Space Telescope, we've obtained precise spectral data for a large group of distant galaxies, providing a crucial benchmark for accurately determining the dust temperatures and forming masses. These results are essential for correctly calculating the star formation rates and luminosity temperatures of galaxies at various wavelengths, from 3 to 28 micrometers, by fitting their spectral energy distributions. The VLT/VISIR data revealed a notable trend of increasing far-UV brightness with greater far-IR wavelengths, while the addition of the JWST data further highlighted a significant far-UV component, consistent with a two-temperature blackbody model. This discovery led to a significant overestimation of far-IR brightness when using a single blackbody model to fit the data. Notably, incorporating far-UV observations from the Hubble Space Telescope into our analysis further amplified this effect. These results underscore the critical need to account for a potential far-UV component when estimating far-IR dust temperatures and, by extension, galaxy forming masses. This is particularly crucial for accurate interpretation of far-IR photometric data, such as that provided by the Hubble Space Telescope, in conjunction with near-IR and mid-IR observations. The inclusion of a far-UV component in our analysis significantly impacted the estimation of star formation rates, resulting in a significant overestimation when using a far-UV-free model, such as the common far-infrared fitting method. This is the initial paper in a two-part series aimed at categorizing a substantial number of the type II quantum subgroups within the $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1})$ quantum group. We employ a method that leverages the categorified local action of the quantum group on highest weight $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_{r+1})$-modules. By defining the action on tensor products of these modules, we identify the smallest quantum subgroup capable of acting categorically on the infinite direct sum. It is crucial to note our approach is distinct from traditional methods, which rely on a similar concept but act on the modules themselves, and often require the modules to be simple.

The fundamental equation describing non-stationary diffusion in a bounded area with varying internal and boundary conditions lacks a general analytical solution, which precludes using classic methods to determine it in the presence of significant nonlinear terms or fractional orders in the time derivative of the diffusion equation. A novel approach based on representing the solution as an infinite series of Heavistheta functions allows to formulate both homogeneous and non-homogeneous solutions for such equations. These solutions can be applied to solve a wide range of physical problems involving integer and non-integer order diffusion equations with various boundary conditions.

This work presents an approach to identifying written mathematical expressions on a sheet of paper using inductive reasoning. By employing a simple sensor, we can capture the movements of a person writing math equations by measuring the angles between two lines. These angles serve as input for a series of classifiers trained with basic signal processing techniques. The writing movements are first preprocessed to extract key information, which is then used to create a set of features to be fed into the classifiers. The experiment involves writing mathematical equations on a sheet of paper and collecting the corresponding sensor data, which is then processed and used to train the classifiers. The average accuracy of the final model is around 80%.

This paper introduces an innovative method for duration modelling in statistical parametric speech synthesis by training a recurrent model to predict median durations of target words. Unlike existing approaches that rely on complex duration models, this simplified system uses only median durations as input. A crucial aspect of this approach is that it avoids the traditional "hidden & mean" duration framework, instead utilizing a distinct set of networks to predict median durations. Extensive experiments were conducted on the Libritox-2b corpus using three target lexicons with varying sizes, showcasing the effectiveness of this new approach.

Species distribution modeling has grown rapidly in recent years, driven by advances in computing power and the widespread availability of large-scale data. A key limitation often encountered when analyzing such data is computational complexity. To overcome this issue, spatial occupancy models have incorporated unobserved states. However, even these improvements can result in persistent computational challenges. To address this issue, a novel R package called spOccupancy has been developed to enhance the efficiency of single-species, multi-specpecies, and integrated spatial occupancy models. Through the utilization of integrated nested Laplace approximation and Bayesian hierarchical modeling, spOccupancy successfully mitigates computational difficulties while maintaining accuracy. This package can analyze various data formats, including repeated surveys from various sources such as camera traps, acoustic monitoring, or visual observations. To validate its efficacy, a simulation study was conducted comparing the performance of the new package to existing alternatives. Additionally, real-world data applications were examined, including an analysis of acoustic monitoring of bird distributions in a European forest and an examination of species distributions from multiple taxa in recent camera trap records.

The Skincare project aims to create an innovative, interactive deep learning system for assisting dermatologists in identifying skin lesions and providing a comprehensive diagnosis, encompassing accurate descriptions of lesions' characteristics. This cutting-edge system leverages a newly developed deep learning technique to analyze high-resolution images of lesions, enabling rapid diagnosis. In the domain of computer vision, this cooperative approach represents a groundbreaking innovation in diagnostic tools. The Skincare project's design prioritizes an intuitive, non-invasive diagnosis process, beginning with a thorough visual examination that complements traditional methods, such as clinical interviews. The project employs cutting-edge technologies, including a high-precision camera and cutting-edge software, to enhance diagnostic accuracy. The Sklearning framework is used to develop and train a deep learning model on a vast dataset of skin lesions, enabling an efficient and accurate diagnosis. The model's core functionality revolves around analyzing high-resolution images of lesions, which are captured using cutting-edge technology, including a high-precision camera. The Skincare project's design philosophy revolves around an intuitive, interactive diagnosis process, which begins with a thorough visual examination of the lesion and complements traditional methods, such as clinical interviews. The Skincare project's development has been guided by a number of cutting-edge technologies, including a newly developed software framework for interactive diagnosis and state-of-the-art hardware for rapid lesion analysis. The Skincare project's design has been informed by the principles of cooperative diagnosis, which emphasizes the importance of a thorough visual examination of the lesion and accurate clinical interviews

To obtain the most accurate cosmological results, it's essential to derive reliable estimates of key parameters from various surveys of Type Ia supernovae. By utilizing a probabilistic autoencoder, researchers can effectively capture the correlations inherent in the sequential data provided by individual supernovae. This encoder enables the calculation of the total likelihood of the sample by condensing high-dimensional spectral information into a compact latent representation. As a result, more precise estimates of the underlying acceleration of the universe can be achieved, taking full advantage of the data's complex characteristics.

A massive neutral gas outflow has been observed in a heavily magnified star-forming galaxy, which is significantly affected by dust interference. Using a custom code to analyze gas emission, we found that the outflow moves at around 800 km/s and covers around 40% of the visible part of the galaxy. Despite high dust levels in the galaxy, we were able to detect the outflow by combining measurements of different ion states. The outflow's gas mass loss rate is estimated around 1000 solar masses per year, which could be the source of the galaxy's hot gas supply. This hot gas could eventually form the galaxy's observed intragroup medium after it merges with another galaxy. The discovery of the outflow in this magnified galaxy provides valuable information about gas dynamics in early galaxy formation.

To study the movement of fluid into a swirling plume filled with turbulent currents, we performed high-speed experiments using a setup that simulates natural phenomena through controlled releases of fluid. The experiments involved plumes that transport fluid in both upward and downward directions, formed by a fluid source with adjustable control parameters. High-speed cameras captured fluid movement within a transparent plume medium, allowing us to analyze fluid intake patterns in a plume environment. Our observations revealed that fluid movement dynamics are influenced by fluid viscosity and fluid density variations, but novel effects emerge when the fluid contains suspended particles. These unique effects cause fluid movement behavior to deviate from standard prediction models, particularly when particles settle into fluid currents due to differences in fluid and particle density. Fluid intake patterns in plumes with particles are significantly affected when fluid movement shifts from a rapid, fluid-like motion to a more gradual, particle-driven motion, leading to significant discrepancies between observed and predicted results, especially in plumes with unstable fluid stability.

Over the past decade, the interplay between epidemic dynamics and complex network interactions has become a focal point in the study of the former.  However, traditional networks, represented as collections of pairwise connections, may not adequately capture the unique features of intricate systems.  Hyperedges, capable of interpreting multi-way interactions, serve as a more comprehensive tool for interpreting their underlying structure.  In this research, we advance the understanding of epidemic dynamics on systems that interact through multiple ways by integrating the concept of stochastic processes and spectrally characterized data.  The generalization of matrix theories that underpin network analysis to hypergraphs leads to the development of a new analytical framework that outlines the conditions under which an epidemic will be contained, thereby providing valuable insights for controlling disease outbreaks in complex systems.

Recent breakthroughs in understanding 2D magnetic materials have led to the identification of a unique spin system, the 2D ferromagnet CrI$_3$. This unique system combines ferromagnetism with anti-symmetric exchange interactions called Rashba-like Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (RDMI). As a result, the ground state of CrI$_3$ exhibits a non-zero chirality, which can be observed through the alignment of spins within the material. Using advanced computational methods, we've calculated the spin structure factor to identify this alignment and determined that it can be controlled by applying an external magnetic field or creating moiré patterns through the integration with a hBN substrate. These findings provide a framework for exploring the unique properties of 2D magnetic materials and 2D/2D interfaces, which could lead to the development of advanced spintronics devices.

By incorporating rotation effects into mean-field solar-type dynamo models,
we're able to demonstrate the significant influence of rotation on dynamo
cycles. In particular, our results show that the rate of differential rotation
is the primary determinant of these dynamics. In stars with slow rotation,
it's possible for magnetic cycles to emerge only when the rotation gradient
points in the opposite direction to what would be expected from pure Coriolis
forces. This characteristic is also observed in the rotation patterns of the
Sun. Consequently, modeling the rotation dynamics in solar-like stars is
crucial for accurately simulating their magnetic cycles.

Deep models like the K-fan network are highly effective for processing complex data but struggle with information loss during feature extraction process. Our novel Generalized k-fan (GK-FAN) multimodal deep model addresses this limitation by efficiently capturing and fusing features from multiple information sources. The model's structure allows it to learn from diverse inputs simultaneously, while its progressive representation sharing mechanism retains critical information throughout analysis. The integration of a shared representation layer in GK-FAN significantly boosts its performance in tasks such as classification, error prediction, and dimensionality reduction when dealing with multidimensional data. Experimental results confirm GK-FAN outperforms the K-fan model for processing complex information, particularly in scenarios involving information compression.

The use of model checking has become a crucial tool in verifying the correctness of single-threaded applications, yet single-threaded programs often lack the precision required for accurate runtime simulations, especially when compared to multi-threaded programs that can be easily compiled and executed using modern compilers. In contrast, using a model checker for single-threaded programs can provide a crucial step towards ensuring the correctness of multi-threaded programs, as it can help catch errors that a traditional single-threaded runtime would miss. However, developing a model checker for single-threaded programs poses significant challenges, primarily due to the need for precise modeling and efficient deadlock detection. In this paper, we introduce McMini, a novel model checker for single-threaded programs that overcomes these obstacles by utilizing an innovative approach based on dynamic partial order refinement to efficiently handle large programs and automatically detect deadlocks. Our evaluation demonstrates that McMini can verify a wide range of programs, including those used in real-world applications, and identifies errors that are both reproducible and valid.

The global prevalence of WhatsApp has made it a primary source of information for billions of people, yet its role in spreading misinformation poses a significant concern. Although structure-driven, the propagation of messages on WhatsApp is often influenced by human cognitive biases. In an effort to mitigate the spread of misinformation, researchers have devised an anomaly detection system that identifies suspicious patterns of forward messages in real-time. To curb the spread of verified false information, we propose a pinning mechanism where authorities can restrict the forwarding of both new and existing posts. By simulating the diffusion of messages on WhatsApp, we evaluated the impact of different strategies, focusing on how personalized recommendations and pinning mechanisms can encourage accurate information sharing and reduce the spread of misinformation.

We introduce a broad class of population models based on branching processes and derive frequencies of unique alleles in both discrete-time and continuous-time scenarios. In discrete-time settings, our findings generalize previous results by Galambos and Newman as well as Loreto, in the context of a specific population type. In continuous-time models, we extend work by Galambos and Newman to a wider range of population types. Our work demonstrates a common approach applicable to an extensive range of population types, encompassing a hierarchical range of distribution types commonly used to model unique allele frequencies in humans and other species.

The primary goal of our spoofing countermeasure system is to identify artificial effects in voice samples that signify spoofing. To achieve this, we incorporate an novel activation function called the attentive ReLU, designed to highlight key time-frequency regions in input samples. By giving a K-fold weight distribution, samples within these regions can enhance the detection of artificial artifacts. Our system's effectiveness is demonstrated through a state-of-the-art EER of 08% on the Voxforge AM-SPEEC spoofing corpus and 10% on the NIST 2020 spoofing corpus. Additionally, the incremental ability of our activation function is showcased by comparing it to standard activation functions like the hyperbolic tangent and the rectified linear unit.

Supergravity, an extension of the Standard Model that encompasses supersymmetry and general relativity, offers a promising framework for formulating the fundamental principles of nature, potentially reducing it to a supergravity theory at low energies. Although supergravity presents challenges in achieving slow-roll inflation, recent developments have made significant progress in slow-roll de Sitter vacua and supersymmetry breaking mechanisms. This review outlines the constraints imposed by supergravity on cosmological models and examines the most supergravity-compatible inflationary scenarios based on their resilience under higher-order corrections.

Nonreciprocal optical systems have diverse applications that manipulate the transmission of light based on its propagation direction. This study examines a distinct class of nonreciprocity related to the correlation of photon pairs rather than the transmission of light. An experiment was conducted and supported by theoretical findings, showing this nonreciprocity through second-order coherence functions of photon pairs created by spontaneous four-wave mixing in a silicon microdisk. Changing the direction of the pump's propagation leads to significant diminishment in coherence functions while maintaining the transmission.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as the leading platform for quantum computing, with superconducting phase qubits being a prominent example. However, detecting single photons in the gigahertz to gigahertz range poses a significant challenge. This research presents an innovative approach, combining terahertz time-domain spectroscopy and near-field scanning optical microscopy to overcome this challenge. The method involves using a terahertz pulse to both excite and detect a superconducting phase qubit, with the qubit acting as a superconducting single-photon detector. The finding that qubit-based sensors can be effectively operated at microwave frequencies suggests new possibilities for superconducting quantum technology.

We argue in favor of Borel determinacy, by demonstrating how the real line can be divided into Borel sets, with each set containing either winning positions for Player I or Player II in a specific game involving real numbers.

In the past few years, numerous hedge funds have entered the cryptocurrency market due to its immense growth and untapped potential. However, this surge in activity has also led to considerable controversy and criticism within the community. To better understand the underlying dynamics, we employed agent-based models to examine the cryptocurrency market, comparing our analysis to a traditional benchmark. The CEO of BitMEX, the world's largest derivatives exchange, previously stated in a blog post that the market was experiencing an excessive influx of funds, saturating available investment opportunities. Our model effectively replicates the sentiments expressed by BitMEX's leadership, underscoring the disproportionate impact that new investments from multiple institutions have on existing players, ultimately leaving little to no opportunity for price appreciation in the cryptocurrency market.

Identifying the application protocol is crucial for network security monitoring and threat analysis. The dynamic protocol detection method uses existing features to determine the application protocol without pre-defined rules. A significant limitation is the existence of dynamic identification methods that can mislead network security monitoring tools. This research focuses on exposing this vulnerability by developing a deceptive technique to mislead dynamic protocol detection algorithms in network security monitoring tools. The experiment targets and successfully manipulates Grumpypcap and Zeek's dynamic protocol detection algorithms.

Electrostatic gating has limitations in controlling magnons due to their short exchange interaction range. A potential solution lies in using superconducting proximity effect, which has an longer range, but the practical implementation is challenging due to the short superconducting energy gap, making magnon-based circuits difficult to operate. Our study demonstrates the efficient control of magnons via 2D proton doped graphene in a Josephson junction array, where magnons are gated by domains with distinct magnetic orientations, facilitated by 2D proton doped graphene. The superconducting current generates a range extended Zeeman field, enabling gate voltage controlled magnetic order and precise magnon gating. This novel approach offers a viable pathway for superconducting quantum circuits based on magnons.

A prominent challenge in federated learning is adapting to emerging classes at various participating devices. This study introduces a novel approach for addressing this challenge in audio classification through federated learning. First, a pre-trained audio model is utilized as a reference guide for unknown classes. Next, the knowledge from participating devices is seamlessly integrated with the reference guide, forming a complete knowledge base that encompasses both local and overarching knowledge. Experimental outcomes in audio classification reveal that the proposed method yields comparable results to a centralized training paradigm with existing classes and exceeds performance in unknown classes by approximately 10%.

A comprehensive theoretical model is offered in this paper for analyzing any complete set of greenberger-horne-zeilinger states in any number of dimensions using a method of post-selection combined with measurements of complementary bases. We confirm through experiment that any assembly of complementary bases can be analyzed by applying a specific set of unitary transformations and subsequent checks for post-selection compatibility. A similar model is also provided for measuring any set of generalized Bell states in any configuration of sources, any complexity of multi-source states, any arrangement of complementary bases, any high-dimensional Greenberger-horne-zeilinger state, and any combination of these elements.

A recent innovation in wireless communications is the use of intelligent reflecting surfaces (IRS) to enhance signal quality and overall system performance. In a setup with multiple users, base station, and passive reflector, this paper focuses on an uplink system where direct and reflected links coexist. Due to the complex interaction between these links, estimating all individual channels is an intricate task. To address this complexity, a new approach is proposed where direct channels are estimated first, followed by indirect channels. By doing so, this paper significantly reduces the number of pilot symbols required and greatly improves estimation accuracy compared to existing methods. The performance benefits of this innovative ULS-CE algorithm are demonstrated through comprehensive numerical results.

This study provides a comprehensive analysis of U.S. local news consumption during the COVID-19 pandemic by examining data from 2019-2020. The research focuses on relationships between market characteristics, audience sizes, disease severity, and news consumption patterns. The data reveals that larger markets with higher case and death rates tend to have more news coverage, while smaller markets are relatively more dedicated to reporting COVID-19 in proportion to their overall news.
